text:
9:46 EDT - Why ask others to do what you can do yourself? Colombia's government, after begging to no avail for the central bank to increase its dollar purchases to weaken the local currency, started buying greenbacks on its own this week, at least $300M worth, and said to expect more of the same in the following weeks. This is $60M a day, far more than the $20M daily by the central bank, and it's worked well so far: COP is at 2-month high of 1,823 for a dollar, up 1.8% from its close at end of last week. (dan.molinski@dowjones.com)

9:35 EDT - With the 10-year yield, at 1.82%, back just below the start-of-year's 1.86%, "yields have normalized somewhat from emergency levels," says Dan Dektar at Smith Breeden. Just three weeks ago, it hit an all-time low of 1.38%. Still, Dektar calls current levels more of a safe-haven play than an investment proposition. His firm remains light on Treasurys; it's more willing to take on credit risk for better yield with high-grade corporates. (cynthia.lin@dowjones.com)

9:33 EDT - Whether it's uncertainty about Europe, fears about another Knight Capital Group-like (KCG) trading glitch or vacations to the beach, the summer doldrums are in full effect. On average, 4.35B shares have traded daily this week. Another session at those levels would put this week's total volume at the lowest so far this year, excluding weeks shortened by holidays. (matthew.jarzemsky@dowjones.com)

9:32 EDT - An encouraging sign for the sliding Treasury bond market -- foreign central banks have been buyers for the past two weeks, even as many other investors cashed out. The Fed's custody holdings data late yesterday show foreign central banks' Treasury bond holdings increased $8.4B in the latest week, following $9.5B addition in the previous week. "We continue to...see the [Treasury] market as a buy," says David Ader, head of US government-bond strategy at CRT. "We await our opportunity and proof, via the price action, that the call is a correct one." If the 10-year yield closes below 1.77%, Ader says it'll be a convincing signal to get into the market. The 10-year note recently 5/32 higher to yield 1.819%. (min.zeng@dowjones.com)

9:31 EDT - Brean Murray is no bull on Idenix's (IDIX) hepatitis C treatment, calling it "incapable of being the cornerstone of a competitive all-oral regimen" for the drug maker. But IDIX has another virus-treating drug in the pipeline that the investment bank considers more promising. So after Thursday's 29% stock slump after the FDA put a partial hold on clinical trials for the hep C drug, Brean Murray upgrades IDIX to hold while pulling its $6 price target. It's up 4.3% in early trading at $6.09 but has fallen 24% this week. (andrew.fitzgerald@dowjones.com; @drewfitzgerald)

9:28 EDT - Prepare to sift through some fancy branding campaigns along with deluge of information when hedge funds are allowed more leeway to advertise. PR firm Walek & Associates says many funds are quietly preparing to make more information publicly available on their web site and build a media profile. Firm says branding matters because investors also look at "visibility differentiation and credibility" on top of performance. Adds branding doesn't necessarily mean performance: None of the billion dollar money raisers last year were found to be on the year's top performer lists. The SEC will meet on Aug 22 on the matter. (amy.or@dowjones.com)

9:17 EDT - The Chilean peso trades nearly unchanged against the dollar after the central bank held the interest rate at 5% for the seventh consecutive month, as expected. Some market participants expected the bank would raise the curtain for a possible intervention, but it only said "the peso has appreciated." Peso recently trading at CLP483.00 versus Thursday's close of CLP482.80, according to Valor Futuro newswire. (graciela.ibanez@dowjones.com)

9:13 EDT - Increases of the number of US Krispy Kreme (KKD) stores, including the first for company-owned ones in 7 years, and "already industry-leading international growth could result in sustained high-teens to low-20% EPS growth and an expanded valuation," says Wedbush as it starts coverage of the restaurant chain at outperform and sets a $9 price target. The investment bank sees international earnings more than doubling within 5 years. That as July's efforts around KKD's 75th anniversary "could have resulted in 'best month in years', as some stores put it." Shares are up 2% premarket at $6.68. (kevin.kingsbury@dowjones.com)

9:03 EDT - "The Bank of Canada's tightening bias is increasingly looking untenable," National Bank's Krishen Rangasamy says after July's softer inflation report. Total inflation rate is now tracking 1.00% in Q3, Rangasamy says, short of the Bank of Canada's estimated for 1.2% for the quarter. The core rate, meanwhile, is tracking 1.2%, significantly lower than BOC's 1.9% estimate. The Canadian dollar is shrugging off the report, even trimming some losses in the wake of it, with the US dollar now at C$0.9883, from C$0.9866 late Thursday. (karen.johnson@dowjones.com)

9:01 EDT - A Peruvian delegation has arrived in Venezuela, and the countries are expected to finalize a new accord replacing trade pacts that lapsed when Venezuela withdrew from the regional customs union of the Andean Community of Nations in April 2011. Venezuela completed its long-pending exit with only temporary accords in place with Colombia and Peru. Current CAN members also include Bolivia and Ecuador. (ezequiel.minaya@dowjones.com)

8:58 EDT - Morgan Stanley says WellPoint (WLP) could face more pressure from an unfavorable mix of commercial health-insurance prices and medical costs as it downgrades WLP to equal-weight and says the company's "risk-reward looks less compelling" than peers. WLP cut its 2012 guidance during last month, mainly citing faster-than-expected erosion in its membership ranks, and shares have fallen 5.8% since. But Morgan Stanley sees more problems afoot than membership levels and cites "concern that poor cost-trend visibility has led to a mispricing of the commercial book." WLP, inactive premarket, has rebounded 8.6% this month. (jon.kamp@dowjones.com)

8:57 EDT - As emerging market currencies lose ground to the dollar, Morgan Stanley recommends that investors buy some of the currencies at these cheaper rates. "We continue to believe we are in a risk-positive environment," the analysts said. They recommend going long the Russian ruble on the expectation that Russia will hike rates, giving investors a chance to get higher carry. Long the Mexican peso vs the yen, on the stronger growth prospects of the Latin American country. USD/MXN is up today at 13.2113 as is the USD/RUB at 31.926, according to CQG data. title: Colombian Coffee Growers Demand Stronger  Forex Intervention
text:
MANIZALES, Colombia--Colombia's coffee sector Tuesday joined a chorus of critics of the country's central bank who feel the institution isn't doing enough to prevent excessive strength in the peso.

Mario Gomez, a longtime board member of the National Federation of Coffee Growers, said the bank should "at least double" its daily dollar purchases aimed at offsetting gains in the peso against the U.S. currency.

The central bank currently buys a minimum of $20 million a day in the spot market.

The Colombian government and some bank board members, including Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry, have been urging for months for the bank to buy more dollars.

But so far the majority of the seven-member board resisted such a move, arguing it is important to keep a hands-off approach to forex markets as much as possible to avoid inflationary pressures and other economic imbalances.

"The bank should be buying more dollars," Mr. Gomez said on the sidelines of a tourism-promotion event in the central, coffee-farming region city of Manizales.

He noted a recent drop in coffee production in Colombia, along with lower global prices for coffee beans, have put the iconic Colombian coffee farmer in dire straits.

"We know the problem--production is low and export prices aren't sufficient," Gomez said, adding a weaker peso would help in this regard. "So let's buy more dollars and see what happens."

Mr. Gomez pulled no punches in his criticism of the bank's board, which is led by bank Chairman Jose Dario Uribe.

"This is what happens when you have people leading powerful institutions who haven't done real business work in the real world," he said, saying he wasn't referring to the chairman specifically but rather the board in general.

Mr. Gomez said he personally believes the peso needs to weaken to COP2,000 a dollar. The peso closed Tuesday at COP1,803.05 to the dollar. It is 8% stronger this year, but little changed versus 12 months ago.

Mr. Gomez said he expects coffee production of around eight million 60-kilogram bags this year. That is well below the 11 million bags Colombia produces in a good year.

President Juan Manuel Santos, meanwhile, said he "believes there is space for the central bank to buy more dollars" to weaken the peso, which he said would help coffee farmers.

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso up on rising inflation, Brazil real gains
text:
* Brazilian real seen testing 2-per-dollar level

* Colombia finmin "prays" for stronger intervention

* Brazil real gains 0.28 pct, Mexico peso up 0.53 pct

(Repeats to additional subscribers; Recasts, adds comments)

By Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso gained on T hursday as high inflation boded steady interest rates ahead while Brazil's real got a lift after weak factory data in China backed hopes of more stimulus in Brazil's top trading partner.

Mexico's annual inflation accelerated to its highest rate in more than two years in July on a surge in egg and fresh produce prices, reinforcing bets that policymakers will hold interest rates steady at 4.50 percent in the coming months.

Mexico has held interest rates steady this year even as Brazil slashed borrowing costs to support growth. Rock-bottom interest rates in the United States and Europe have boosted the appeal of higher-yielding Latin American currencies.

Mexican annual inflation rose to 4.42 percent last month, above the central bank's 4 percent comfort zone. Even though there are signs Mexican growth may be slowing, high inflation should keep policymakers from cutting interest rates.

Lower benchmark rates would curb the gains investors can make from borrowing in dollars or euros to invest in Mexican fixed-income assets.

"With expectations that inflation could stay above 4 percent in the coming months, we think that the central bank of Mexico cannot cut interest rates," said Rafael Camarena, an economist at Santander in Mexico City. "In the short term, this helps the peso."

The Mexican peso strengthened 0.53 percent to 13.0860 per dollar, also boosted by data showing claims for unemployment benefits unexpectedly fell in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

Meanwhile, expectations for additional Chinese stimulus rose after data showed growth in the country's factory output slowed to the weakest pace in three years.

China is the largest consumer of Latin American commodities, and prices of raw materials have great sway over currencies in the region.

The Brazilian real gained 0.28 percent to 2.0160 per dollar, leading some analysts to forecast the market could soon test the central bank's willingness to defend the level of 2 reais per dollar, considered by investors an informal floor for the currency.

"The real is nearing the level of 2 per dollar and, with a possible decline in risk aversion, markets may test this level today," said Andre Perfeito, chief economist at Gradual Investimentos in Sao Paulo.

Government officials have repeatedly said that a real stronger than 2 per dollar could hurt Brazilian exporters, leading investors to believe the central bank would step into the market to defend that level.

The tide of yield-hungry global investors has been strengthening currencies around Latin America and pressuring exporters.

Colombian Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry called on industrialists to "pray" that the central bank boosts dollar purchases to ease gains in the currency after noting foreign direct investment in Colombia could reach $17 billion this year and boost the peso.

Echeverry said the monetary authority, which is independent from the government, should step up dollar purchases to $40 million a day to strengthen its arsenal to fight the gaining peso. The bank currently buys at least $20 million a day on the spot market.

title: Colombia Central Bank  July  Forex Intervention  Was $400 Million
text:
BOGOTA--The Colombian central bank said Monday it had purchased $400 million in the spot market in July under its policy of buying at least $20 million a day to drain U.S. currency from the foreign-exchange market and build up international reserves.

The central bank's dollar purchases in the spot market are aimed at preventing excessive strength in the peso. The bank has bought $2.36 billion this year and has pledged to continue the daily purchases through at least Nov. 4.

The central bank used a similar strategy in 2011, when it purchased $3.72 billion until October, then ended its policy of daily purchases as fears over the European debt crisis caused the peso to weaken on its own, rendering such intervention unnecessary.

The Colombian peso weakened slightly agains the dollar Monday to close at COP1,788.50 to the dollar, from COP1,786.00 a day earlier.

title: DJ Foreign Investment Into Colombia Surges in First Half of Year
text:
BOGOTA--Foreign direct investment into Colombia surged in the first half of this year, the latest indication that the peso's strength against the dollar is being driven by flows of the U.S. currency into this Andean nation.

Preliminary data released Monday by the central bank shows that foreign direct investment into Colombia jumped to US$9.38 billion in the first six months of 2012, up 26% from the year-earlier period.

The surge in foreign direct investment, which is largely geared at Colombia's oil and mining industries, is commonly cited by analysts as one of the key factors behind the peso's strength against the dollar. The peso has appreciated more than 7% so far this year and ranks as one of the world's best-performing currencies.

On Monday, the peso traded at COP1,777.2 after closing at COP1,776.60 on Friday.

Despite recurrent calls from exporters for the government to curb the peso's strength, Colombia's intervention in the foreign-exchange market consists of having the central bank buy at least $20 million daily in the spot market, a move designed to mop up excess dollar liquidity.

Over the course of this year, the bank has bought $1.96 billion, and it has vowed to continue the daily purchases through at least Nov. 4.

The government has called for a more aggressive foreign-exchange intervention by the central bank while also steering away from implementing capital controls, which limit foreign investment.

The trading volumes in the spot market can easily reach about $1 billion daily, leading many analysts to project that even if the bank steps up its dollar purchases, it will not be able to reverse the peso's appreciation.

title: POLL-Colombia cenbank seen holding rates steady on Fri
text:
* Policymakers to decide interest rate on Friday

* Most analysts see rate at 5.25 pct through 2012

By Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, June 25 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank is seen keeping its benchmark interest rate unchanged at its policy meeting on Friday as inflation expectations remain contained and worries over the European economic crisis ease, according to the unanimous view of 30 analysts polled by Reuters.

The monetary authority has held the rate steady since March at 5.25 percent to provide economic stimulus amid concerns that weakness in the global economy could spill into Colombia.

The bank has raised borrowing costs 225 basis points since early last year to prevent Latin America's No. 4 economy from overheating and ease bank lending over fears that households are becoming too indebted.

The majority of the 30 analysts, based in Colombia and on Wall Street, c onsulted by Reuters thought the bank would keep the rate unchanged for the rest of 2012.

The number of analysts who expected the bank to raise rates again this year to cool the pace of consumer lending have gone down while more now believed that a rate cut could be on the table in the coming months.

Economic figures in the first quarter and in April come in stark contrast to 2011 when Colombia's full-year gross domestic product grew at its highest level in four years.

In the first quarter of 2012, the economy grew at its slowest rate in more than a year as last year's rate hikes took effect and the mining sector was weakened by lower commodities prices and renewed attacks by rebel groups.

The economy grew 0.3 percent in the first quarter versus 1.2 percent in the previous three months - the slowest quarterly growth rate since the third quarter of 2010.

Since Colombia's last policy meeting at the end of May, worries that Greece might leave the eurozone have subsided after elections that brought a conservative-led government to power.

"April activity numbers were negative, but we think still not bad enough so as to sway the majority of the board, some of whom remain concerned about credit growth, to act by loosening monetary policy," Bank Of America Merrill Lynch said in a note.

"We expect (the central bank) to remain on hold. Although the minutes showed significant concerns about the global economy, concerns about a slowdown have somewhat diminished relative to the moment at which the last meeting was held, given the outcome of the Greek elections."

Colombia's slow economic growth in the first quarter and a fall in industrial production and retail sales in April showed that the economy was nearing its potential, according to one of the central bank's seven board members.

Monetary policy is determined by the seven-member central board, which meets monthly.

Some board members have said that the authority could adopt a countercyclical monetary policy if there were a significant deterioration in Europe.

Colombian policymakers are concerned that continued credit expansion is pressuring consumer prices even though inflation has remained relatively steady in recent months.

Consumer prices rose 3.44 percent during the 12-month period through May, slightly above the 3 percent midpoint of the central bank's 2- to 4-percent annual target range.

The majority of analysts ruled out additional measures to stem the rising peso currency, which is the strongest gainer among the world's 36 most-traded currencies.

Two experts polled by Reuters, however, believed the central bank would increase the amount of dollars it is purchasing at auction from the current $20 million or more daily - the peso has firmed 7.7 percent so far this year.

Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry, a board member, has said he favored more aggressive intervention into the foreign exchange market to stem the peso.

Colombia has become one of the best performing economies in Latin America and attracted a flood of foreign investment, mainly into the oil and mining sectors.

Last year the country was granted an investment grade credit rating from Fitch, Moody's and Standard & Poor's.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies  and Debt Gain Modestly
text:
Emerging market currencies and debt were a tad improved Friday, riding on hopes that central banks would ride to the rescue or Greece's pro-Europe party would take the lead in Sunday's election.

Emerging market currencies are on the cusp of what could be a hefty market rally. The May selloff of these currencies has brought most of them to levels investors find attractive and reasonable.

"A lot of these currencies don't look fundamentally overvalued, as they had, and are becoming a more attractive investment," said Keith Brakebill, a portfolio manager at Russell Investments. While the fund is long on emerging markets, it also has instituted a proxy hedge with a basket of developed-market currencies, such as the Canadian dollar, Australian dollar and the euro against the dollar.

His Russell Global Opportunistic Credit Fund (RGCAX), with $853 million in assets, also began buying U.S. high-yield and high-quality emerging-market dollar and local-currency bonds in May, once it was clear there would be another election in Greece. His reasoning is that if markets recover after the election, these two asset classes would provide high returns. However, if markets sell off, these bonds could be traded to raise liquidity and seek investments in other distressed opportunities.

Like him, many other investors returned to emerging markets in the latest week, according to data from EPFR Global. Net capital flows to emerging-market bond funds totaled $361 million, reversing three weeks of outflows.

But many other investors are on hold, worried that an unfavorable result in Greece could trigger another selloff, and prefer a larger-than-usual dose of cash.

The rally in equities Friday is another instance of investors getting overly optimistic without reason, cautions Jamie Stuttard, portfolio manager of the Fidelity International Bond Fund (FINUX) with $394 million in assets. He says investors expect coordinated central bank action and some more direction from the spate of policy meetings next week.

"It's another cycle of rescue versus reality," he said. The reality is Spanish bond yields are near 7%, and there is another bond auction next week that the beleaguered European sovereign has to clear.

"Portfolios should be pretty liquid in the current environment, and cash is healthy," he said.

In addition, he has been buying up options to hedge out risk of an extreme situation like the euro collapsing on Monday.

Others such as Nomura's trading desk, protectively, have gone long on the dollar, because there is only upside against the Colombia peso. Colombia's aggressive verbal intervention has helped keep the dollar above 1,783 Colombian pesos, giving the currency a break from its continued appreciation versus the dollar. If the weekend brought a positive outcome in Greece, the dollar's weakening beyond COP1,760 would be curbed by Colombia's central bank. If Greece's elections results were unfavorable, the dollar would gain. Currently, the dollar is trading at COP1,784.70, down 0.31% on the day, according to CQG data.

The Brazilian real also is gaining on the dollar. Investors have taken note of the country's indication that it may backtrack on some of its more aggressive moves to depreciate the currency, and see this as an opportune time to buy the real. The dollar, currently, is trading at BRL2.0441, down 0.57% on the day.

Meanwhile, emerging market debt was trading five basis points narrower at 386 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt Rally on Hopes of Coordinated Action
text:
Emerging-market currencies and debt were eerily calm most of Thursday as investors hunkered down ahead of Greece's elections on Sunday.

A late-afternoon report of global coordinated central-bank action helped lead a mild rally in these currencies, though market participants wondered about the endurance of such a move.

For most of the day, though, investors preferred dollars and stayed out of making any major moves. Earlier in the day, Brazil's backtracking on some of its aggressive taxes on foreign loans elicited little reaction from the currency.

One trader called it a case of "too little, too late." However, late in the day, as other higher-yielding assets rallied, the real also found its legs. The dollar was trading at BRL2.0574, down from its earlier high of BRL2.0770, according to CQG data.

Other proxies for emerging-market risk, such as the Mexican peso and the Chilean peso, made a strong late-afternoon recovery, too. The dollar, against the Mexican peso, slipped below MXN14, to trade at MXN13.9050, down nearly 0.9% on the day. Similarly, the dollar was more than 1% weaker against the Chilean peso at CLP498.20, according to CQG data.

The only commonly traded Latin American currency to buck the trend was the Colombia peso on central-bank intervention. On Thursday, Colombia's finance minister renewed calls for "aggressive" intervention to curb the peso's volatility. Such a move may halt the appreciation, but it won't weaken the peso, said David Rees, an emerging-market economist at Capital Economics.

The dollar is down 10% against the peso for the year, making it the best performing emerging-market currency this year. The central bank has been buying dollars daily to weaken the peso. But continued flows of foreign-direct investments into Colombia, its exports to the U.S. and stable commodity prices have made Colombia resilient. CapEcon expects the dollar to stick around the COP1750 range on interventions from its current level of COP1790.20, according to CQG data.

Elsewhere, emerging Europe remained hardy. The Hungarian forint, Czech koruna and Polish zloty were all up against the euro, and showed little signs of stress during the course of trading.

There was no sign of stress in local-debt markets of emerging economies, with foreign holdings of the bonds resilient despite the broader weakness globally, said Benoit Anne, head of emerging-markets strategy at Societe Generale.

Meanwhile, emerging-market debt was stronger by eight basis points on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index-Global, at 386 basis points over comparable Treasury yields. Emerging-market issuers continued to stay out of the market.

title: Colombia  Finance Minister Renews Call for Aggressive Peso  Intervention
text:
BOGOTA--Colombian Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry renewed calls for a more "aggressive" intervention policy by the central bank in the foreign-exchange market, a measure that could help curb sharp volatility in the peso.

Echeverry said Thursday he is advocating a "more aggressive intervention" by the central bank, which has been buying U.S. dollars at a rate of about $20 million daily in the spot market. The finance minister is one of the seven members in the central bank's board of directors.

"I'm seeing jobs at risk" because of the peso's appreciation, Echeverry said Thursday during a presentation. The peso has appreciated sharply against the dollar this year and has suffered bouts of sharp volatility.

On Thursday the peso trades at COP1,788 after closing at COP1,784.90 a day earlier. The central bank's foreign exchange intervention policy consists of buying at least $20 million daily in the spot market, a move designed to mop up excess dollar liquidity.

Over the course of this year, the bank has bought $1.58 billion, and it has vowed to continue the daily purchases through at least Nov. 4.

Echeverry in the past has called for a more aggressive foreign-exchange intervention by the central bank while also steering away from implementing capital controls, which limit foreign investment.

The finance minister said Thursday the central bank could increase its dollar purchases without spawning faster inflation, which the central bank would like to see end the year at around 3%. He added that intensifying the central bank's purchases could help limit some of the volatility in the exchange rate.

The trading volumes in the spot market can easily reach around $1 billion daily, leading many analysts to project that even if the bank steps up its dollar purchases it will not be able to reverse the peso's appreciation.

Capital Economics, a London research firm, said in a report "we doubt that the authorities will succeed in significantly weakening the peso."

Colombia has attracted record foreign investment since beating back leftist rebels over the last decade, which has fueled the economy but also put appreciation pressure on the peso, making exports less competitive.

In a move to counter the strengthening currency, the central bank board of directors, of which Echeverry is member, is buying at least $20 million daily until early November.

"I maintain it's necessary that in the central bank we have a more aggressive intervention with immediate sterilization," Echeverry told lawmakers during a debate on the peso.

"The exchange rate remains a worrying variable. I've asked the central bank board to look at what other similar economies are doing like Peru. We can learn from them if one can have controlled inflation and a more aggressive intervention."

Colombia's peso is one of the world's strongest gaining currencies, firming about 8.5 percent so far this year although in the last month the rising trend has slowed due to worries over the crisis in Europe.

Latin America has absorbed huge amounts of money as investors look for higher yields in what some policymakers have called a global "currency war".

Europe's debt crisis and China's economic slowdown pose new threats to Latin American economies and markets, and as the region begins to cool down, governments are doing what they can to protect themselves from a wave of cheap goods.

While the United States and many European nations struggle to shore up their fiscal accounts, Colombia's financial management, buoyant economy and security advances were rewarded last year with an investment grade from major rating agencies.

title: Colombia's  Central Bank  Expected To Hold Rates As Inflation Slows
text:
--Economists say central bank likely to keep rates at 5.25% at Monday meeting

--Lower inflation data, elevated global risks reduce need for rate hike

--Bank's board may announce more intervention in forex market to stop peso's gains


 
   By Dan Molinski 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's central bank is widely expected to leave interest rates on hold at its meeting Monday as recently lower inflation and somewhat elevated global risks put the bank in a wait-and-see mode.

All seven analysts surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires said they expect the central bank's board will vote to hold its benchmark rate at 5.25% at its monetary policy meeting. The bank also left rates on hold at last month's meeting, following nine rate hikes going back to early 2011.

While economists unanimously agree the bank will leave rates on hold Monday, there's less agreement as to whether the bank may act to try to stem a strengthening peso that's 9% stronger this year and 0.6% stronger over the past week, at COP1,763 for $1.

The bank already intervenes in the forex market, buying $20 million daily to remove excess U.S. currency, and some analysts say the bank may announce Monday it's increasing this amount.

One of the bank's board members, Juan Carlos Echeverry, who also is Colombia's finance minister, has been urging more aggressive intervention in the peso, saying exporters of bananas, flowers and other products cannot be competitive abroad unless the peso weakens to at least COP1,800 for $1.

Colombia's economy has performed well for several years in a row, and is likely to expand more than 5% in 2012, fueled by a record levels of foreign investment into its oil and coal sectors.

Amid the strong growth, the central bank increased interest rates for much of the past year due to concerns that consumer spending was accelerating too quickly, which might cause inflation to spike. But board members have recently indicate they're confident the rate hikes already implemented will be enough for now to rein in spending habits and keep inflation comfortably within the bank's 2% to 4% target range.

Consumer price inflation for the 12 months through last month was 3.4% after March saw a lower-than-expected 0.12% inflation rate as food prices declined.

Economic data out last week came in higher than forecast, with retail sales rising a sharp 9.4% in February, year-on-year, and industrial output climbing 4.5%. But Alejandro Reyes, at Bogota brokerage Ultrabursatiles, says the sharp gains were likely a result of February being a leap year this year, meaning the month had one additional day for shoppers to spend.

Reyes also said he believes the bank's seven-member board will take into account a slight uptick in investors' concerns about the global economy. Countries such as Spain and Italy are battling with debt problems similar to those seen in Greece.

"There's a moderation in optimism," the analyst said. "And so I think the bank will choose the so-called wait-and-see approach."

20 Apr 2012 16:58 EDT DJ  Colombia Central Bank President: Global Economy In Line With Outlook

-- Colombia central bank sees global, domestic outlook playing out as expected

-- Central bank governor sees growth this year at 5%, inflation at 3%

-- Central bank always ready to intervene in forex market when benefits outweigh costs 


 
   By Matthew Cowley 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The global growth outlook remains largely in line with the Colombian central bank's outlook, although oil prices are slightly higher, and domestic growth and inflation are also on course, the president of the central bank, Jose Dario Uribe, said Friday.

"In the global situation, levels of uncertainty are high but lower than they were," Uribe said in an interview on the sidelines of the spring meetings of the International Monetary Fund.

Recent data "goes in the direction of what we had as the basic scenario" from the last quarter of last year, although oil prices are "a little bit higher" than the central bank had expected, Uribe said.

The higher oil prices are driving up Colombia's trade surplus, which may be the highest in many years, he added.

Growth will probably be slightly negative in Europe, with a decline in gross domestic product of around 0.5%, while the U.S. could grow between 1.5% and 2%, he said.

The Colombian economy, meanwhile, is also responding to the series of interest rate hikes made last year and earlier this year.

"All the information we have now suggest that growth will be around 5% and inflation is around 3%, which is exactly where we want to be," Uribe said.

Uribe said that changes in interest rates have an almost immediate and significant impact on the market's inflation expectations, which are currently around 3%, as well as market interest rates. The final impact of interest rates can be a lag of between nine and 18 months, he said.

Colombia's benchmark rate stands at 5.25%.

Meanwhile, Uribe said that the country's free-floating currency remains the best option for Colombia, and helps the country absorb shocks such as the increase in terms of trade.

Yet, he said, "as we've been saying for some time, it would be appropriate for the Colombian economy to have a currency that is less appreciated."

The official said efforts by the government to save some of the revenues from oil exports are crucial in terms of reducing the impact on the currency.

The central bank has continued to build foreign currency reserves, "and at some moments when we've seen that the behavior of the exchange rate appeared to have some speculative aspects, where there's been a misalignment, that has also motivated us on some occasions to intervene."

The central bank is always prepared to act in currency markets when benefits of intervention outweigh the costs, Uribe said. The central bank has in the past required a deposit on foreign borrowing, and that could be used again, he said.

The bank currently buys $20 million daily in the forex market to prevent excessive peso gains, and is committed to continue doing this at least until early August.

title: Bancolombia Head Says Colombia Needs To Live With Strong Peso
text:
--Bancolombia chief Yepes says strong peso is here to stay

--Yepes says he opposes more aggressive forex intervention to stem peso's gains

--Bancolombia chief says bank's loans to grow up to 20% this year


 
  By Darcy Crowe 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

CARTAGENA, Colombia -(Dow Jones)- Carlos Raul Yepes, the head of Colombia's largest lending institution Bancolombia (CIB, BCOLOMBIA.BO), said the country's business community needs to learn to live with a strong peso even as the government considers stronger intervention measures to curb the currency's strength.

Yepes, who heads of one of the largest market makers in the Colombian foreign exchange market, said he doesn't believe "much stronger measures" should be taken to limit the peso's surge.

Colombia's intervention in the foreign-exchange market has been limited to the central bank buying $20 million daily. The government also has decided to put a strict limit on the amount of dollar profits it repatriates from its oil sales abroad, which run in the billions of dollars.

Colombia Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry has signaled that those measures aren't enough, and is urging the central bank's board, on which he sits, to act.

Colombia's peso closed Friday at COP1,776.20 for a dollar, little changed from Thursday but 8% stronger since Jan. 1.

Yepes said the peso's strength is being driven by forces such as a boom in foreign investment and a strong economy. "We need to learn to live with the peso trading at this range," Yepes said in an interview during a business conference at the Summit of the Americas that will includes more than 30 heads of state.

Bancolombia has benefited over the last year from a surge in economic activity in Colombia. The country's gross domestic product expanded 5.9% last year and the government expects that this year it will grow between 5% and 6%.

That growth is being driven by a boom in consumer borrowing, which triggered the central bank's decision to begin increasing interest rates last year. The bank paused at its last monetary policy meeting and the rate now stands at 5.25%.

Yepes said that if inflation remains under control, the central bank was unlikely to hike its key rate beyond 5.75%. Twelve-month inflation through March stands at 3.4% compared with 3.55% in the 12 months through February, and is within the central bank's target range of 2% to 4% for the year.

The central bank's interest-rate hikes, however, have triggered a "moderation" in lending, Yepes said. He added that he expects the banks loan portfolio to expand between 18% and 20% this year.

Yepes said the bank is not planning any new stock or bond sales and that it will finance its operations with its own cash flow. He added that the bank, which has a strong presence in Central America, has been examining potential acquisitions overseas but has not yet found any suitable purchase targets.

"There are not a lot of options out there right now and the ones out there are too expensive," Yepes said.

The bank, however, believes it has plenty of room to grow in Central America and is also looking at Mexico, Peru and Chile as countries to expand its operations.

title: UPDATE 3-Colombia rate hike cycle may not be over - minutes
text:
* Some board members say "adjustments" may be needed

* Continued credit expansion could pressure prices

* Q1 growth seen robust after Q4 slowdown

(Adds analyst quote, details on global situation)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Brian Ellsworth

BOGOTA, April 4 (Reuters) - Colombia's cycle of interest rate hikes may not be over despite a pause in March, after several central bank board members noted that "additional adjustments" to monetary policy may be needed, according to minutes published on Wednesday.

The seven-member board voted unanimously in the March 23 meeting to leave the benchmark lending rate unchanged at 5.25 percent following a year-long, 225-basis-point rise that has helped cool inflation in one of Latin America's fastest-growing economies.

The minutes signaled concern among Colombian policymakers that a continued credit expansion may be pressuring consumer prices even though inflation has decelerated and tighter monetary policy helped slow growth in the fourth quarter.

"Given the data now at hand, and even considering the recent trend in inflation, several board members noted that inflationary pressures continue to weigh on the (balance of risks), which means additional adjustments in monetary policy might be necessary," the minutes read.

Other board members noted that "the neutral range of the bank's intervention rate has been achieved already."

Inflation slowed in February to 0.61 percent from 0.73 percent in January.

Though growth in the fourth quarter was the slowest in a year at 1.3 percent, compared to 5.9 percent for all of 2011, the bank noted that first-quarter expansion appeared robust, providing further justification for central bank hawks.

"With respect to the economic situation in the first quarter of 2012, the figures on hand point to good performance," the minutes said. "Household consumption continues to be favored by consumer confidence, which is relatively high, despite the decline witnessed in February."

The bank also noted there has been no sign that "contagion" from the crisis in Europe and slower world economic growth is affecting Colombia, adding that exports continued to grow firmly while foreign direct investment remains strong.

RESERVE REQUIREMENTS

Changes to monetary policy could include "macro-prudential measures," which are meant to restrict liquidity and combat inflation without raising interest rates.

One central bank member requested the creation of a "reserve requirement for consumer lending."

This would likely require banks to set aside a percentage of all new consumer loans, according to one expert consulted by Reuters, in contrast to broader reserve requirements in which banks must leave a percentage of deposits with the central bank.

Policymakers have raised concerns in recent months about the risks of Colombia's growing middle class taking on too much bank debt to buy new cars, real estate and home appliances.

"The central bank is still somewhat uncomfortable with the overall exuberant pace of demand ... rapid consumer credit growth, and low level of nominal and real rates," Goldman Sachs analyst Alberto Ramos said in a research note.

Higher interest rates make the peso more attractive to investors given near-zero yields in the United States and Europe. It has rallied nearly 9 percent since the start of the year.

Though Colombia has been largely shielded from the global downturn, industry leaders including coffee and banana growers have complained that a stronger currency makes their exports less competitive in global markets.

The minutes made no mention of measures to stem the strengthening currency. Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said in a recent interview with local media that Colombia is considering "aggressive" intervention to prevent the peso from appreciating further.

(Editing by Helen Murphy, Chizu Nomiyama, Gary Crosse and James Dalgleish)

BOGOTA, March 26 (Reuters) - Colombia wants to see more "aggressive" action to help stem gains in the currency and will ask the central bank to consider stepping up dollar purchases, Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said in an interview published on Monday.

Echeverry told central bank board members ahead of a policy meeting last Friday that President Juan Manuel Santos prefers a "model that requires much more intervention in the exchange rate," Colombian daily newspaper El Tiempo reported.

Colombia has seen record foreign investment flows as security improvements lowered the risk of exploring for oil, coal and other natural resources.

The flood of money, coupled with attractive yields compared with near-zero interest rates in developed nations, has bolstered the value of the peso.

"We have been in agreement with the amount of intervention and with the instruments we've used. Now we are inclined toward a more aggressive strategy, more intense, deeper," Echeverry said. "The bank has the muscle."

The bank said it has a dollar purchase program underway of "at least" $20 million a day that runs "at least" through Aug. 4 to help ease the rise of the peso. The currency has strengthened 9.4 percent this year, the most among major Latin American currencies.

The government has also maintained funds from the sale of bonds and dividends from state oil company Ecopetrol overseas to prevent a flood of dollars entering the country.

Echeverry, who represents the government on the central bank's board, joined three other members who have expressed concern about the level of the peso, which on Monday opened at 1,758 per dollar.

The central bank held the benchmark lending rate at 5.25 percent at its policy meeting last week, a move that could help slow pressure on the currency following nine rate hikes of 225 basis points in just over a year.

Santos has faced pressure from exporters to ease currency gains. Banana, coffee and flower growers have complained that high interest rates boost the peso, which dulls their competitive edge for goods sold abroad.

title: Emerging-Market Investors Faced With Fewer 'Carry'  Currencies
text:
--Central bank interventions limit carry-trade options

--Investors continue to seek higher-yielding paper

--Focus turns to Mexican peso and South African rand


 
   By Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Investors remain bullish on emerging-market currencies and now that Greece has concluded its debt restructuring, low volatility in global markets offers an ideal time to initiate trades.

The problem, however, is these investors' options are less plentiful now that central banks in emerging markets have built walls to protect their currencies.

One favorite play, selling the dollar and buying Brazilian real assets, lost its luster recently after a rash of central-bank actions to prevent further appreciation of the Brazilian currency. Central banks in Turkey, Colombia and Peru also have intervened either directly or indirectly to stop their currencies from rising too quickly.

The genesis of this "currency war" is the rapid gains among emerging-market currencies in the first two months of the year. Investors, especially those in developed countries like the U.S. and U.K. with a capacity to borrow cash at ultra-low yields, sought out assets in emerging currencies that also offered the added bonus of currency appreciation. This so-called carry trade resulted in emerging-market currencies gaining 5% to 10% in the first six weeks of the year.

Earlier this year, a broad basket of emerging-market currencies including the real, Turkish lira, Indian rupee, and Indonesian rupiah were viewed as the best carry currencies. The purchases were funded either through the dollar or euro.

Now that central banks in many of these countries are resisting, investors are hesitant to go for the same play. After all, no one wants to bet against the central bank. Rather, they are keen on currencies like the rand and Mexican peso, whose central banks don't intervene on a daily basis in the market. Both also offer higher interest rates on local bonds.

"That story of broad risk-on, risk-off way of looking at currencies is changing," said Guillermo Felices, head of European currency strategy at Barclays Capital. "Investors have to be much more discerning in the way one picks carry. Lazy carry will be penalized."

Central banks' protectionism, of course, isn't expected to end carry trades based on the wide yield differentials. Over the medium to long term, emerging-market currencies are expected to gain against the dollar and other developed-world currencies. And as central banks in the U.S., Europe and Japan keep interest rates low and continue with their quantitative-easing policies, investors will be on the lookout for higher-yielding paper.

"There's a competitive nature to this game," said Stephen Jen, partner at SLJ Macro Partners, an investment company that also manages a hedge fund. "Money will go to places where capital flows are welcome, where policy makers are more tolerant."

For many investors that place is Mexico. The currency has gained 10.2% this year, and its central bank hasn't indicated any shift in policy to curb the appreciation. And Mexico's close trade links with the U.S. make it an automatic beneficiary of a recovery here.

In addition, Thanasis Petronikolos, head of emerging-market currency and debt at Baring Asset Management, sees opportunities in dollar-denominated bonds of Chinese companies and so-called dim sum bonds, which are listed in Hong Kong but denominated in Chinese yuan.

But he doesn't recommend backing out of Brazil or Hungary, especially if investors got in early.

"The fundamental story on the strength of the real is still there," he said. "With high-yielding local bonds, investors should be ready to cope with short-term volatility."

title: DJ UPDATE: Emerging Economies May See Repeat Of Inflationary Cycle
text:
-- LTRO expected to spur investors to buy EM assets

-- Some EM central banks, however, resist currency appreciation

-- Rising oil and commodity prices bring back inflation fears

(Updates to add details throughout) 


 
   By Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The global economy is seeing echoes of 2009 and 2010, where easy monetary policy from advanced countries created a vicious cycle in which emerging markets attracted short-term money inflows from yield-seeking investors that in turn led to currency interventions and inflationary forces.

This risk, some say, is that this cycle--in which some see the makings of a competitive depreciation "currency war"--will exacerbate the problem of imported inflation and eventually force emerging market central banks to hike interest rates. That in turn could give rise to a "hard landing" slowdown in growth for both emerging markets and the world as a whole.

On Wednesday, the European Central Bank loaned EUR529.30 billion to 800 European banks. This boost in liquidity is expected to send a fresh influx of buyers into emerging market currencies, which had already recovered more than half of their 2011 losses within the first six weeks of this year, largely in response to a similar ECB action in December.

To add to their concerns, the resumption of a rapid surge in oil and commodity prices adds to the inflation challenges facing developing economies and limits their room for maneuver.

To be sure, emerging market countries' currencies and economies benefit from the incoming foreign capital, but many of them struggle to keep pace with the rapid pace of change in currency valuation, which make life harder for their key export industries. Back in 2009 and 2010, rapid exchange rate appreciation led policymakers to impose capital controls and intervene to weaken their currencies, both of which can scare off needed long-term investors.

Many economists are sympathetic to these countries' positions--a paper released Wednesday by the traditionally hands-off International Monetary Fund even advocated "temporary" intervention as a tool for containing volatility. But it's also widely recognized that central banks run can stoke inflation if they keep their currencies too weak, mostly because it makes imports more expensive than they would otherwise be. Eventually that can prompt a countervailing response with interest rates, which in turn could stall growth in the emerging market world. This is pretty much how the cycle played out in 2010.

"There's a sense of deja vu of last year, when [such easing in developed markets] triggered emerging market economies to start currency wars," said Alessio de Longis, portfolio manager of Oppenheimer Currency Opportunities Fund.

The situation turns particularly volatile when rising oil and commodity prices are thrown into the mix, as they are now. Net oil importing countries get hit with an immediate inflation threat and although energy producer countries such as Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Russia, Colombia and Malaysia benefit from higher export receipts, the currency appreciation challenge is even bigger in these countries.

While emerging market central banks can justify intervening against speculative moves in the currency, it's harder to explain countering capital flows that finance its growth. "Central banks have to strike a fine balance resisting currency appreciation but not turning away investors," de Longis said.

Capital flows into emerging economies are an "intense challenge," especially when these countries are easing rates, said Brazilian Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini, whose country has been a magnet for foreign money inflows, at a presentation on Wednesday. Already this year, the Brazilian central bank has initiated dollar purchases to weaken the real and on Thursday the government expanded the coverage of a tax on foreign currency loans to cover those of three-year periods from the previous two year limit. Tombini also reiterated his belief that the central bank can get its benchmark Selic rate down to single digits, from its current level of 10.5%, which should make the real less attractive.

The dollar is trading at BRL1.7176, currently, and many analysts see little upside potential to the currency.

Other central banks have joined the fray. Colombia has begun interventions and South Africa is buying dollars again. Others with strengthening currencies, such as Mexico and Chile, are likely for now to stick with monetary easing rather than direct intervention.

Indeed, until now, it was thought that many central banks--including the all important People's Bank of China--would be able to recover the growth lost last year by continuing to ease monetary conditions. But if inflation rears up again, not all central banks will be able to cut rates to boost domestic growth, said Guillaume Tresca, emerging market strategist at Credit Agricole .

"Inflation has accelerated in Central Europe, and higher oil and commodity prices could lead only to higher prices," he said.

Tresca expects emerging market currencies to face a correction in the coming weeks as the focus shifts to oil prices and return of inflation concerns. While there may be some currencies that do well, emerging Europe outside of Russia is expected to retreat, he said.

--By Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires ; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com

title: Colombia 's Peso Touches Six-Month High Despite  Intervention
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's peso is trading at a six-month high Monday morning despite persistent efforts by the government and central bank over the past few weeks to stem the currency's gains.

Cautious expectations of another Greek bailout are propelling investors to add to their emerging markets bets, pushing Colombia's currency to COP1,773, its strongest level since mid August, and 0.6% stronger from Friday's close.

On Feb. 3, Colombia's central bank said it would start buying $20 million daily in the spot forex market to help soak up excess U.S. currency that's been flowing into the country's booming oil and coal sectors. The bank wants to weaken the peso because it is making Colombia's exported products less competitive.

For its part, Colombia's government said it would hold off on repatriating $1 billion worth of oil profits this year, which it hopes will also help stem the peso's gains.

While these measures have modestly slowed the pace of the peso's gains, analysts say the dollar flow toward Colombia from foreign investment is probably too great to halt or reverse the trend.

The peso's recent gains are also related to the central bank's decision last month to increase its benchmark interest rate to 5.0%, citing the need to cool down a surging economy and inflationary pressures. So-called carry traders in the forex market are taking advantage of the higher rate to borrow currencies such as the dollar at payback rates near zero to buy the peso and pick up easy yields.

title: Emerging Market Central Banks Back To Square One: Fighting  FX  Gains
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Five months later, and Brazil's central bank is back to where it was last September: buying dollars to tame the real's appreciation.

The hectic pace of the January rally in emerging markets has startled many central banks and forced some of them to take immediate measures to intervene to protect their currencies from further rapid appreciation and keep their exports competitive.

Investors who are already retooling their strategies to incorporate higher projected year-end levels now also have to factor in interventions and the effort by central banks to slow the pace of appreciation. Colombia's has already indicated that it will follow Brazil's lead and take measures to slow the Colombian peso's ascent.

Central banks, meanwhile, may feel compelled to shift from their focus on spurring growth to resuming their battle against currency gains. The announcements from Brazil's and Colombia's central banks were seen as signs of the times, with emerging market currencies now having recouped much of the losses that arose during last year's global risk fears, which saw many erase between 10% and 22% of their value against the greenback in the second half.

"In the short term, investors have to be concerned about intervention especially because of the magnitude of the recent rally," said Andres Garcia-Amaya, strategist at J.P. Morgan Funds. "It makes governments jittery as it makes exports less competitive."

The huge flow of capital into emerging markets this month--$11.3 billion into equity funds and $1.65 billion into bond funds, according to EPFR Global--was primarily stoked by liquidity measures from both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.

Still, as Guillermo Osses, head of emerging markets debt portfolio management at HSBC Global Asset Management, points out, "Investors won't indiscriminately purchase currencies," this time, unlike 2010, when a flood of buying forced many central banks to prevent further appreciation of their currencies.

Brazil, certainly, with its high interest rates, has seen a surge of foreign buyers of its local bonds, and now of its equities too as investors seek other ways to gain currency exposure. Latin America's largest economy, in a bid to keep its exports competitive and its manufacturing activity buoyant, last week purchased dollars and did so again Monday.

Colombia, the resource-rich commodities exporter, is trying to make sure that the flux of foreign capital flowing into the country consists of investments into the economy and not speculative trading. Its central bank said Friday it would start to buy a minimum of $20 million daily for at least three months in the foreign-exchange market.

But, for a while, the duo are likely to be the only countries intervening with their currency. Asian and European economies have a way to go before they start worrying about intervention, analysts and investors said.

Some investors, however, already are betting that the measures won't halt the overall appreciation trend, and are happy to hold onto currencies like the Brazilian real.

"It does not necessarily make me run to the exit," said Alexander Kozhemiakin, portfolio manager at Standish in Boston, adding that Brazil's intervention came a bit sooner than he expected, but his firm is currently long the Brazilian real against the Colombian peso. His read: central banks "are not protecting their currencies at a certain level; they're smoothing volatility."

Others are waiting for intervention to present an opportunity to go long the Colombia peso, placing bets that it will appreciate.

Alex Pigatto of Nomura Securities expects that Colombia's $400 million a month in dollar purchases would fall far short of its expected foreign inflows of $1.2 billion monthly.

"We are flat FX here, but watching for another opportunity to re-enter in long Colombia Peso [trade]," he said.

text:
(Corrects level of peso)

* Colombia central bank ends dollar option auctions

* Re-starts buying at least $20 mln daily

* Exporters suffer from strong peso currency

By Helen Murphy

BOGOTA, Feb 6 (Reuters) - The Colombian peso weakened on Monday after the central bank resumed its dollar purchasing program to curb gains in the currency that has prompted complaints from exporters.

The bank resumed buying at least $20 million daily for three months or more to boost reserves and slow gains in the peso. It also ended on Monday a plan to buy dollar options whenever the peso moved 4 percent or more from the 20-day moving average.

In foreign exchange trading, the Colombian peso eased 0.15 percent to 1,787.00 pesos per dollar on Monday, but it has strengthened more than 8 percent so far this year.

The bank intervention followed moves by some regional central banks to stem the rise in their currencies. Brazil's central bank on Friday entered its foreign exchange market, buying dollar forwards.

"The latest set of measures announced by Colombia and Brazil to curb currency strength are unlikely to have a lasting impact on foreign exchange markets," said Capital Economics in a report. "Instead, fiscal reforms hold the key to preventing excessive currency appreciation in Latin America."

Colombia has seen record foreign investment flow into the nation as security improvements lower the risk of exploring for oil, gold and other natural resources.

The flood of money, coupled with attractive yields compared with near-zero interest rates in developed nations, has bolstered the value of the peso.

Colombia's dollar purchase program previously ran through September 2011. The bank introduced a dollar option policy in October, but scrapped the program on Monday.

Policy makers last week raised the benchmark lending rate a quarter point to 5 percent to slow inflation and cool bank lending, bringing complaints from exporters of flowers and bananas that the move would attract additional capital, boost the peso and damage their business.

Luis Carlos Villegas, head of Colombia's main business group, known as Andi, said last week the bank had been "overly prudent" in raising the rate.

Exporters like flower growers have suffered from the strengthening peso because they pay costs in pesos and receive dollars for their sales. As many as 20,000 flower jobs have been lost in the last four years, most blamed on the strong currency.

In a bid to stem the peso's rise, the government said it would not bring in dollars for financing in 2012 and would keep $1 billion in dividends from state oil company Ecopetrol, and another $1.2 billion in royalties, abroad.

"We are surprised with how strong a hand the government has intervened in the foreign exchange market this year and wonder if it isn't becoming over concerned with the impact of rising interest rates on peso's relative performance given the disparity with the rest of the region and emerging markets in general," RBS said in a note.

Colombia's vote to increase the lending rate bucked the trend of other Latin American central banks that have either cut rates and kept them steady to shield their economies from the debt crisis in Europe and a global slowdown.

The government has said it would avoid imposing capital controls to prevent pressure on the currency and instead aim for long-term measures and micro-structural reforms. In 2007, it established unpopular capital controls - lifted later - to deter the entry of speculative money.

(Reporting by Helen Murphy Editing by W Simon)

title: Colombia flower, banana growers clamor for peso measures
text:
* Currency has firmed 6.2 pct so far in 2012

* Cenbank hiked key interest rate on Monday

* Sectors worry over speculative capital inflows

By Jack Kimball

BOGOTA, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Colombia's flower and banana industries pleaded with the government and the central bank on Wednesday to reign in the strengthening peso currency after the monetary authority hiked interest rates.

Colombia like other emerging markets is trying to tame inflation - the scourge of central banks worldwide - amid worries the Eurozone debt crisis and anemic U.S. growth might impact the local economy.

The Andean nation has bucked the trend in Latin America by hiking interest rates, the latest rate rise on Monday -- a move that curbs inflation but also puts upward pressure on the peso by making local assets more attractive.

Banana and flower exporters are among the biggest employers of rural Colombians and lead a lobby of exporters that have been the most vocal seeking a weaker currency.

"The rate hike (on Monday) is an invitation for speculative capital to come to the country in higher volumes, sharpening the revaluation process," the flower and banana growers industries said in a joint statement.

"Most worrying is that the measure to hike the interest rate has not even come accompanied by some exchange rate intervention given the space that exists to increase reserves."

Colombia's peso has firmed more than 6 percent so far this year, making the local unit one of the best performers of the world's 36 most-traded currencies, partly thanks to strong foreign direct investment inflows.

The complaints from the flower and banana industries will add more pressure on policy makers to fight peso appreciation. However, the central bank has been less willing in the recent past to take major steps such as capital controls and preferred structural changes and dollar purchases.

Strengthening currencies hit exporters the most since they pay costs in local currency but receive dollars for their sales. Strong exchange rates can also help ease consumer prices by making imported goods cheaper.

In a move to stem the peso's rise, the government announced on Monday it would not bring in dollars for financing in 2012 and would keep $1 billion in Ecopetrol dividends and another $1.2 billion in royalties abroad.

Billions of dollars in foreign direct investment, mainly in the oil and mining sectors, have flowed into the country since a 2002 U.S.-backed offensive pushed leftist guerrillas back to ever-remoter jungle and mountain hideouts.

Once seen as a failing state, Colombia has begun to turn its image around by improving security, reigning in stubborn fiscal deficits and recouping three investment grade credit ratings from Wall Street that were lost in a 1999 financial crisis.

While interest rates remain low in developed economies, Colombia's relatively high rates create attractive differentials for investors and could bring in more dollars and drive more appreciation of its currency.

On Wednesday, the peso currency firmed 0.85 percent to 1,794.85 versus the U.S. dollar - its highest level since September last year.

Since the start of the year, the peso has trended stronger, breaking through the 200-day moving average on a firming path after weakening to below that average from mid-September.

title: Colombia Central Bank Forex - Intervention  Free For Second Month
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's central bank, which bought an average of $411 million a month in the forex market during each of the first nine months of 2011 to limit peso strength, didn't intervene at all in October or November, it said Monday.

The bank's $3.72 billion in dollar purchases from January through September were part of a program that began last year to drain U.S. currency from the market and stem peso strength that was due to a weak U.S. currency and heavy foreign investment that's seen dollars pour into Colombia.

But the bank allowed the program to expire at the end of September, as a global financial crisis caused investors to dump the peso and other Latin American currencies, which reversed their trend toward strength. Colombia's peso is 8% weaker since the beginning of September and was trading Monday at COP1,933 for a dollar.

The central bank in October implemented a new forex volatility-prevention program in which it will buy or sell $200 million through put or call options on any day in which the peso's exchange rate moves 4% up or down from the 20-day moving average. But so far those boundaries haven't been touched.

title: UPDATE 1-Colombia restricts dollar deals to halt volatility
text:
(Adds comment from finance minister, background)

BOGOTA, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Colombia on Wednesday imposed a limit on the amount some pension funds can invest in the foreign exchange market, seeking to reduce volatility and speculation, the Finance Ministry said.

The government action follows a central bank pledge on Sept. 30 to intervene to reduce volatility when Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> moves 2 percent in either direction.

"The limit seeks to restrict trades whose intent is to make short-term bets, but not to restrict the execution of a stable investment strategy," the statement said.

Colombia's "obligated" pension funds -- those that receive contributions from the amount workers are required to pay -- cannot invest more than 2.5 percent of their holdings in the spot or forward markets over any five-day period.

Those pension funds hold assets worth a combined total of $52 billion, limiting their investment in the foreign exchange market to no more than $1.3 billion over any five-day period, the ministry said.

All Colombians must pay 4 percent of their salaries into pension funds. There is a system for those who wish to save more, but those "voluntary" funds are not subject to the new rules.

Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said the government noticed some unusual trends in trades made by pension funds that hold the retirement savings of ordinary Colombians, noting that they sold a net $880 million worth of U.S. dollars from May to June but bought a net $1.12 billion from August to September.

"Variations of nearly a billion dollars in the space of two or three months ... yes, I think you can categorize that as speculation," Echeverry told reporters.

Colombia's peso turned negative versus the dollar this year on Sept. 12, losing another 5.9 percent since then, putting the brakes on a strengthening trend that began in 2008.

Colombia's central bank said in September it would call auctions in the spot market for an amount of $200 million when the market rate deviates 2 percent or more from its 10-day moving average. But it has not had to intervene since making the announcement.

The peso closed 0.14 percent stronger on Wednesday at 1,900.3 per dollar.

(Reporting by Nelson Bocanegra; Writing by by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Leslie Adler and Andrew Hay)

title: DJ Colombia Content With Peso's Plunge, In No Hurry To Halt It
text:
--Peso has dropped 10% since Aug. 31 amid worries of global recession 
--Colombia central bank waiting two weeks before any forex intervention 
--Finance Minister Echeverry 'not unhappy' with peso's decline 
   By Dan Molinski 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's peso has plunged 10% in recent weeks but authorities say they won't consider intervening until at least the middle of October, a signal that the government is content if not outright giddy that its currency is finally falling against the perennially weak dollar.

The peso was recently trading at COP1,979 for $1, which is 10% weaker than the COP1,778 seen at the end of August, as fears of a global recession cause investors to unwind their bets on riskier assets.

Colombia's currency is 8% weaker over the past two weeks and 3% weaker over just the past two days. Such volatile moves for a currency could sometimes lead to high inflation and a host of other problems, and thus would cause many central banks to sound the alarm bells and immediately start intervening in an effort to bring the foreign-exchange market under control.

Not Colombia's central bank, however. Though it unveiled a powerful intervention plan Friday in which it will step in and buy or sell $200 million dollars if the peso bounces more than 2% up or down from its 10-day average, the bank said Monday that the program won't take effect until Oct. 14.

That delay, say analysts, shows that while central bankers in Bogota are keenly aware of the risks to forex volatility, they also know such volatility can be a good thing if it brings the peso to levels they have long been aiming for.

Government officials have said they are comfortable with the peso in the COP1,900s range, while Colombia's national industry association, known as ANDI, says a level around COP2,000 would be good.

Colombia's peso reached its strongest level of the year in July, at COP1,747 to the dollar, an exchange rate nearly 50% stronger than February 2009, when the currency was around COP2,600 per dollar. Such strength has significantly damaged Colombia's vital export sector, as many of their products have become prohibitively expensive abroad.

"The current levels around 1,960 isn't a level where you could say that the peso is actually weak. We've been there many times," said Felipe Hernandez at RBS Securities. "The peso is finally weaker and that's what the government wants. Exporters and everyone feels comfortable."

For years, the knee-jerk reaction by authorities in Latin America to a falling local currency was to intervene to try to stop the bleeding. After all, a weakening currency often created double-digit or triple-digit inflation rates, as already-expensive imported goods suddenly became exorbitantly expensive.

But in Colombia and many other Latin American countries, the years-long trend toward a stronger currency has stabilized prices for refrigerators, cars, computers and other so-called tradable goods. Flat-screen televisions in Colombia have even seen a sharp decline in prices, partly because of technological advances but also due to a stronger currency.

That's why tradable goods here have seen inflation rates near zero over the past year, a trend that's helped offset the rise in local goods such as food and transportation and has kept overall annual inflation within the central bank's 2% to 4% range.

As such, when Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry was asked last week what he thought about the peso's sharp decline, he said he was fine with it.

"It's good for exporters, with people that compete with imports, so I'm not unhappy with what has happened," said Echeverry, who is also a board member of the central bank.

Colombia's central bankers, of course, must remain vigilant of forex movements. Many local companies have a large amount of dollar-denominated debts but earn their income in pesos, so a weaker peso could make it harder to repay those debts. But government officials say most local companies hedge their dollar-denominated debts.

-By Dan Molinski, Dow Jones Newswires; 57-310-867-6542; dan.molinski@dowjones.com
