title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Colombia
text:
BOGOTA, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Election violence, on-going bloodshed caused by guerrillas and drug gangs, and sensitive ties with neighbors Venezuela and Ecuador as well as the United States are key risks to watch in Colombia.

ELECTIONS, VICTIMS AND SCANDALS

Rising violence ahead of local elections in October as armed groups jockey for control of local councils, mayoralties and governorships, and therefore control over resources and drug routes, is worrying the government. [ID:nN1E76O0VB]

The independent Electoral Observation Mission says about a fifth of the approximately 1,000 municipalities are at risk of violence or fraud. President Juan Manuel Santos' still-high popularity in opinion polls has taken a hit over perceptions of increased corruption and insecurity as well as his government's response to heavy downpours that battered the Andean nation.

Defense Minister Rodrigo Rivera resigned in late August for failing to stem attacks from Marxist guerrillas.

A "victims law" that will pay reparations to those affected by decades of armed conflict and return land to displaced peasants is aimed at pacifying rural areas. But some experts fear a violent reaction from former paramilitary groups and drug barons who took over that land. [ID:nN25183324]

Gunmen have killed more than a dozen community leaders pushing for land restitution in areas where outlawed militias, cocaine lords and rebels still fight for control of the drug trade. [ID:nN24146586] [ID:nN08227877]

Colombia's improved security and fiscal performance were cited by Standard & Poor's and Moody's for giving the country back investment grade status [ID:nN31302945] and the passage of recent reforms led to an upgrade by Fitch. [ID:nN1E75L1JH] [ID:nN08261853] [ID:nN09254206] [ID:nN14198067]

Santos has a majority in Congress and recently received support from the Green Party, bringing his backing in the legislature to more than 90 percent -- a number only matched during the National Front period between 1958 and 1974 that followed more than a decade of rural violence. That is likely to ensure his reform agenda in the second half of 2011 will go smoothly.

What to watch:

-- More attacks against victims' rights workers.

-- An increase in violence as elections draw near.

LEFTIST REBELS, DRUGS AND NEW GANGS

Santos is keeping up former President Alvaro Uribe's tough stance against left-wing rebels, ex-paramilitary gangs and cocaine traffickers. He has vowed to break up gangs linked to ex-paramilitaries, crack down on drug trafficking and improve security in the next three years. [ID:nN24118982] His government almost captured the leader of Colombia's largest guerrilla group, the FARC, earlier this year. [ID:nN1E762085]

The FARC, Latin America's oldest insurgency, says it wants talks. But Santos, a former defense minister, says the rebels must end hostilities, halt criminal activity and release hostages before any negotiations.

Colombian rebels, however, have answered that with a series of bombings, murders and kidnappings across the Andean nation.[ID:nN1E7680AK] [ID:nN1E76906A] They have also attacked energy and mining infrastructure, although the level of bombings is far below what was registered a decade before. [ID:nN1E76D0RU] [ID:nN14198897] [ID:nN04120440]

Attacks against energy infrastructure rose 18 percent in January to July this year versus 2010, and a recent spate of kidnappings and attacks against oil workers has forced the government to say it would study new ways to provide more security to oil companies. [ID:nN1E772186] [ID:nN1E7760BJ]

Colombia remains the world's No. 1 cocaine producer, and multiple illegal armed groups are engaged in the drug trade. Groups have fragmented and rebels have formed alliances with drug-trafficking gangs and ex-paramilitaries in some areas and are battling for control of others. Cocaine output, however, dropped last year due to heavy rains, crop eradication and military enforcement, according to government estimates.

New criminal bands known by their Spanish acronym "Bacrim" are widely seen as the major emerging threat. They are linked to former paramilitaries and drove a rise in massacres in 2010, the United Nations says. [ID:nN24266002] The October elections will be a test of what role the groups may play in politics.

What to watch:

-- Strikes on FARC leadership, large-scale desertions.

-- More bombings of oil, coal infrastructure.

-- Increased sway of new criminal gangs.

CURRENCY, RATES AND THE ECONOMY

With investment grade ratings from three credit agencies now under Colombia's belt and robust economic growth, authorities are keeping a watch on inflation and the peso's appreciation as investment flows increase. [ID:nN1E76B127] [ID:nN1E76715F]

Greater global economic uncertainty was cited by the central bank as its reason to keep interest rates steady at its August meeting after six straight hikes, and the strong peso currency is a major worry for policy makers. [ID:nN1E77I0ZA]

Santos said Latin America would better cope with global financial turbulence if its central banks were to coordinate foreign exchange intervention. [ID:nN1E77F1TJ]

Colombia faces more pressure to pay for repairs to infrastructure after torrential rains destroyed roads and flooded towns, killing some 400 people and disrupting the lives of 3 million people. The government estimates damages in the billions of dollars. That could fuel inflation and hit economic growth, now forecast by the central bank at between 4.5 percent and 6.5 percent for this year.

What to watch:

-- More pressure on the central bank to keep rates stable.

-- New fiscal measures to fund reconstruction.

TENSIONS WITH NEIGHBORS, U.S. TRADE DEAL

Ties with the United States, Colombia's main trade partner and for long a close ally, are strained over a stalled free trade deal and the recent expiration of trade benefits.

Colombia has proposed measures to improve labor relations with its unions, who have suffered violent attacks in the past, in an effort to overcome resistance to the trade deal in the U.S. Congress. [ID:nN1E77E098]

Tensions between Colombia and left-wing neighbors Venezuela and Ecuador have eased considerably since Santos took office last year, but ideological differences are always just below the surface.

What to watch:

-- How Santos manages any flare-ups in relations again.

-- Improving bilateral trade with Venezuela.

-- More moves to approve U.S. free trade pact.

(Editing by Daniel Wallis and Kieran Murray)

title: Colombia Peso Stable Despite Worries Of Excessive Strength
text:
--Colombia peso in tight-range trading over past 3 weeks 
--Currency just 2% stronger versus dollar since August 2010 
--Banks buying dollars at COP1,780 due to global jitters 
   By Dan Molinski 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's currency could remain bound to the tight trading ranges it has seen over the past three weeks, pleasing monetary authorities who have been working to prevent excessive strength against the weak dollar.

Despite persistent concerns that the peso is on the verge of strong gains that could spiral out of control and cause serious damage to Colombia's important export sector, the currency is a mere 2% stronger compared with 12 months ago.

During late-morning trading Tuesday in Bogota, a dollar was fetching COP1,783, making the peso 0.2% stronger on the day. Since Aug. 10, the peso's closing level has hovered in a narrow range between COP1,766 and COP1,796.

Analysts say a combination of forex intervention by Colombia's central bank and recent volatility in global markets, which reduces the peso's appeal, is likely to keep any would-be peso strength muffled for the next several weeks, if not months.

"This lateral trend we've been seeing is likely to continue," said Juan Pablo Viera, a currency trader at Colombia's biggest brokerage InterBolsa, in Medellin. "The range for the dollar, give or take a few, is between COP1,770 and COP1,800."

Viera said his brokerage has recently been seeing "important buyers of dollars" each time the peso strengthens toward the COP1,780 mark.

The buyers, he said, are mostly traders working for Colombian banks and other financial institutions. "It's because of the volatility in global markets. They cover their positions by buying U.S. Treasurys and things like that."

That's not to say there's no risk the peso could make a strong move upward, especially when and if global markets settle down. Colombia has been experiencing a huge increase in foreign investment into its oil and coal sectors, which has flooded the forex market with dollars and kept constant pressure on the peso to strengthen.

But analysts say the government's dollar-buying efforts in the forex market should continue to help quell any bursts of peso strength from foreign investment flows.

Authorities said in April they were creating a $1.2 billion fund from dollars bought locally as a way to rein in the peso's gains. Additionally, Colombia's central bank buys at least $20 million daily in the forex market.

In a report Tuesday, RBS analysts said the government has plenty of local currency with which to continue its forex intervention.

RBS noted that Colombian tax authorities brought in COP47 trillion ($26 billion) during the first six months of the year, a 33% rise year over year. Colombia's tax haul for the full year 2011 is expected to easily surpass government targets.

The increased tax revenue, RBS said, "reflect the strong cash position of the government in local currency and imply it does not need to sell dollars this year and could even use some of the excess cash to buy dollars."

-By Dan Molinski, Dow Jones Newswires; 57-310-867-6542; dan.molinski@dowjones.com [ 30-08-11 1704GMT ]

title: UPDATE 4-Colombia cbank pauses rate hikes on global worries
text:
* Cenbank board decision to hold rates was unanimous

* Move seen as pause in tightening, not end of cycle

* Monetary body did not mention any new currency measures

* Board would like to see weaker peso currency

(Recasts, adds analyst comment, details)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Eduardo Garcia

BOGOTA (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank paused its tightening cycle Friday after six straight months of interest rate hikes, citing concerns over turbulence in global financial markets and its possible impact on economic growth.

The bank held its benchmark interest rate steady at 4.50 percent in a unanimous decision after dissenting votes at its past two policy meetings.

The decision caught some analysts off guard after the bank raised growth forecasts for Colombia last month.

Economists saw it as a temporary pause to gauge the effects of recent market turmoil. Many analysts expect the bank to resume rate increases in order to keep a lid on rising inflation in Latin America's fifth largest economy.

"They're talking about a pause, a pause is not a completion of the hikes, I believe that what they're doing is taking a breath and then they'll continue (with the increases)," said Andres Pardo, head of economic research at Corficolombiana.

PRUDENT TO HALT

Colombia was one of the last countries in Latin America to start upping rates and its central bank has faced pressure from the government to hold borrowing costs steady, as Chile and Peru have done.

Still, the bank struck a pessimistic tone in its statement, saying inflation was rising above the mid-point of the central bank's 2 percent to 4 percent target.

Nineteen of 35 economists polled by Reuters this week expected the bank to raise rates 25 basis points. The remaining 16 said the bank would hold rates.

As fears grow the developed world is shifting from slow growth to stagnation, the bank said it was prudent to see what effect market turbulence might have on economic growth.

"The increased uncertainty in international financial markets and its possible effect on the growth of the global economy, that was a key element," Jose Dario Uribe, general manager of the central bank, told reporters, following the policy meeting.

From the United States and Italy to Japan and Greece, slow growth is hobbling the capacity of governments to service their debts, spooking markets and sapping confidence and so further darkening the economic outlook.

To many economists, high-growth emerging markets like Colombia appear better placed to weather the storm.

NO NEW CURRENCY MEASURES

Colombia has grappled with the dilemma of whether to raise rates to combat inflation. Higher rates have made their assets more attractive, stoked their domestic currencies and made exports less competitive.

Chile, Peru, Brazil and Colombia have been intervening in a bid to tame their strong currencies but are struggling given a weak dollar abroad and high interest rate differentials with the United States which attract capital inflows.

Colombia's monetary authority did not mention on Friday any new measures to combat the strength of the peso currency, which has firmed 7.2 percent so far this year.

The bank's current intervention of purchasing a minimum of $20 million daily is set to expire on September 30 -- the date of the board's next policy meeting.

"Definitely (the exchange rate) does not leave us calm (at the current level), and as we've said, I would say, that all members of the bank's board would like to have a more depreciated exchange rate," Uribe said.

(Writing by Jack Kimball; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: Colombia  currency  seen maintaining firm trend in 2011
text:
* Peso strength may be offset by acquisitions near yr-end

* Experts see peso between 1,700 and 1,840 for rest of yr

By Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso currency may keep its firming trend due to expansive monetary policy in the United States and Europe, but its appreciation should be stymied by local firms' foreign acquisitions.

With debt woes weighing down Europe and the United States, investors have snapped up emerging market currencies in regions like Latin America despite measures ranging from capital controls to central bank interventions.

Experts see Colombia's peso <COP=STFX> trading between the 1,700 level -- seen as the government's pain threshold -- and 1,840, which would represent a 4 percent rise from the point at which it closed in end 2010.

"The flows continue to support the (upward) pressure on the peso," said Camilo Perez, director of economic research at Banco de Bogota.

While interest rates remain low in developed economies, Colombia like other emerging markets is hiking rates, which creates attractive differentials for investors and could bring in more dollars and more appreciation to their currencies.

Wall Street economists see odds of around one-in-three the United States will slip back into recession, heightening expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will launch another round of unconventional credit easing. [ID:nN1E778212]

That could unleash another flood of dollars into economies such as Colombia that have been battling appreciation pressures on their currencies since U.S. monetary easing first began.

Colombia's attractiveness for outside investors has risen this year after three rating agencies gave the Andean country back its investment grade rating, Congress approved a raft of fiscal reforms and the economy continued growing strong.

The peso currency has been on a firming trend since 2003 thanks to improved security opening up the nation as never before to foreign investment, but it has seen the strongest appreciation since October 2008, firming more than 20 percent.

Since mid-2009, Colombia's 200-day moving average has been on a firming trend, which has also held more or less true for its short-term moving averages.

ACQUISITION IMPACT

Taking the edge off the peso's strength will be a central bank dollar buying program of at least $20 million a day, a $1.2 billion fund abroad by the government and strong imports.

Coupled with portfolio inflows, Latin America's No. 4 oil producer expects $12 billion in foreign direct investment, mainly into oil and mining, this year -- experts say there's about $4.5 billion remaining to come into the country.

High commodity prices for Colombia's coal, oil and coffee will also help push up the currency.

title: DJ UPDATE: Colombia's Echeverry: Ready To Take Steps Against 'Excessive' Peso Gain
text:
(Updates with more comments from the minister throughout, and comments on economic growth.) 


 
   By Matthew Cowley 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Colombia's government is "always ready" to take steps to stem any "excessive" appreciation of the peso caused by a "temporary, unsustainable" flood of money from advanced countries, the government's top finance official said Saturday.

"I'm not fighting the trend. I'm fighting against the temporary excessive appreciation," Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry told Dow Jones Newswires in a broad interview.

"It's difficult to anticipate. But you have to be there, the market needs to know you're present."

The central bank stepped into the currency market in September 2008, buying at least $20 million per day. Echeverry said this has been "very efficient," and the currency depreciated against the dollar.

Still, since early April, the currency has once again started to gain, prompting some calls for the government to intervene more heavily.

Echeverry said Colombia tries to avoid capital controls as much as possible, as they have been shown not to work and can introduce distortions. But the monetary policies adopted by advanced economies, including low interest rates and so-called quantitative easing, have led to a wall of cash flooding into a number of emerging markets.

"The question of capital controls depends on your pain threshold. And you never know what the threshold is until you're there," he said.

Colombia has been putting its fiscal house in order, which allows the government more ability to maneuver in the foreign-exchange market, he said.

On the one hand, having the government books in order makes it easier to allow the currency to float freely, Echeverry said. On the other hand, it also helps in these extraordinary times when the government takes steps, he said.

The government has introduced legislation to fix pensions, health care, royalties from mining and oil, which will improve the country's fiscal position.

Last year, the government saved $1.5 billion in dividends from the government-run oil company, Ecopetrol SA (EC, ECOPETROL.BO, ECP.T). Tax revenue is up sharply this year, and the government plans to save some of that money as well, Echeverry said, without saying how much would be set aside.

The government also plans to use that tax revenue to pay off about 10 trillion pesos (around $5.5 billion) in securities known as TES coming due in May, Echeverry said. It has brought forward tax deadlines from the second half of the year so as to have the money, he said.

The government's borrowing plan for the rest of the year totals some $1 billion to $1.5 billion from international markets, the minister said, adding that he doesn't expect to borrow more than that. The government is waiting until the fiscal legislation is passed by Congress, probably in June, to be able to have a better picture to present to investors, he said.

Standard and Poor's raised Colombia's sovereign credit ratings to investment-grade last month, and Echeverry said he will meet with the other two major agencies, Moody's Investors Service and Fitch Ratings, on Monday. Both still have Colombia in speculative territory.

Echeverry is expecting gross domestic product to expand by 5.5% to 6% this year, with most sectors of the economy, including oil, trade and manufacturing all showing robust expansion. Only agriculture and the financial system are lagging at the moment, he said.

Meanwhile, the government likely won't need more approvals from the legislature to spend on reconstruction efforts in parts of the country damaged by rain at the end of 2010, Echeverry said.

"We have already executed a large part of the money" for reconstruction, the minister said. "It's possible that we won't have to go to Congress to execute the resources, and that we won't have to resort to a budget amendment."

"I think we will have the resources needed to be able to cope with the winter without additional legislation," Echeverry said.

The minister said that a recent decision by Canada's Greystar Resources Ltd. (GYSLF, GLS.T) to withdraw an environmental licensing for its Angostura gold mine project in northeastern Colombia shouldn't deter mining investments.

"We need resources but not at the expense of others. There's a tradeoff," Echeverry said. "What's important in each case is to quickly tell investors whether you can or can't, or whether you can under certain conditions, but that's the same in Canada, Australia, or wherever."

Greystar ended its years-long bid to mine for gold in the highlands of Colombia following mounting opposition to the plan from environmentalists and business leaders. The company has said it will study to see whether the project is still viable.

title: DJ Colombia's Peso Extends Gains For 9th Straight Session
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--The Colombian peso nudged a slight gain against the peso Monday, extending a trend that has seen the Colombian currency strengthen against the dollar in recent days.

The peso closed at COP1,817 to the dollar from COP1,817.75 Friday, according to central bank data. It was the 9th straight session that the peso strengthened against the dollar, a tendency that could continue in the coming days.

Alianza Valores, a Bogota-based brokerage firm, said in a research note Monday that the exchange rate could dip below the COP1,800 level in the first half of the year.

A surge in exports in February, when they increased 37% from a year ago to reach $3.9 billion, is set to carry on thanks to high prices for oil and coal, Colombia's top exports. That is likely to continue fueling Colombia's economy but will also represent a strong exchange rate, said RBS Securities in a research note.

Colombia had been dogged by a strong peso, with exporters and trade unions in the past ramping up pressure on the government when the exchange rate nears the COP1,750 mark. The peso's strength has been fueled in large part by foreign investment into Colombia's commodities-rich economy.

The central bank and the government, however, have avoided placing controls on foreign investment to curb the peso's strength. Instead, the central bank has resorted to buying dollars in the spot market to the tune of $20 million daily to mop up U.S. currency, a move which also allows the monetary authority to build up its international reserves. "Colombia should continue to intervene in the market in an opportunistic way," RBS said in a research note.

Adding to the inflows of foreign investment, other factors are also pressuring the exchange rate. Colombia's foreign debt was raised to investment-grade last month by Standard & Poor's rating agency, opening the door for the institutional investors that have restrictions on investing in anything but investment-grade instruments.

The central bank also began raising interest rates in February, a move that could generate more portfolio investments into Colombia and lead to a stronger peso against the dollar.

title: Emerging-Market Debt,  Currencies  End February Little Moved
text:
-Emerging-market debt ends February with little movement

-Chinese commitment to yuan's slow appreciation allowed minor gains by Asian currencies

-Watch for key rate decisions from Brazil and Poland this week


 
   By Cynthia Lin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market assets ended February on an ambivalent note as the lingering unrest across the Middle East held currencies and credit of the developing world within a tight band, ahead of a data-heavy week.

The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index global remained flat for much of the day, but ended two basis points wider, to 303 basis points over Treasurys. Its index gained nearly 0.1% in price terms on Monday.

"Frankly there hasn't been any big drivers in terms of EM debt," said John Peta, portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management, but "inflation is clearly a theme for the coming year. People in emerging-market worlds are more impacted by inflation so leaders in these countries have to be attuned to the higher inflation, and hiking rates is one way to put a dent in that...and perhaps they will let their currencies appreciate more than people might expect."

Last Friday, Russian and Colombian policymakers' decisions to hike rates came at somewhat of a surprise, Peta added.

Grabbing much attention over the weekend, Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said in a public forum that China's 5-year growth target would be lowered to 7.0% from 7.5% for 2011-2015, marking the nation's shift away from speedy growth and toward a steadier, more value-driven role in production and domestic consumption. The Premier also reiterated his concerns about inflation, supporting the case for the yuan's gradual appreciation and further rate hikes.

In India, Finance Minister Mukherjee presented the nation's annual budget, forecast to come in at a 5.1% deficit for 2011 and pared down to 4.6% in 2012. Amid the government's attempts to slim the deficit, the budget also included a hefty increase in spending over the next year, which will likely keep demand pressures strong, leaving the battle against inflation in the hands of its monetary authorities.

Emerging-market currencies straddled the breakeven point on Monday, with Asian currencies gaining slightly against the U.S. dollar while its Latin American and Eastern European counterparts came in mixed.

The news out of China and India set the stage for broad, but minor, gains by Asian currencies. The Indian rupee ended nearly 0.3% higher against the U.S. dollar, while the Korean won and Indonesia rupiah each gained more than 0.1%.

On the Embig, Asia's regional index tipped one basis point tighter, but lost 0.11% in price terms. The notable leader was Vietnam, whose spread tighten 21 basis points, to 351 basis points over benchmark, gaining 1.21% on the day.

In Eastern Europe, the Turkish lira was slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar, being one of the more oil-import dependent nations in its region. While inflation expectation have been largely held under control, analysts will be watching this week's fresh inflation print.

Having suffered as a proxy to the spreading unrest in the Middle East, USD/TRY once again tipped above the TRY1.60 mark early Monday, before falling back to TRY1.5985 recently, according to CQG.

In contrast, the Polish zloty inched higher against the euro, up 0.55%, to PLN3.9540, according to FactSet. Despite growing price pressures, Poland's monetary policy authorities are expected to keep interest rates unchanged in a tight vote on Wednesday.

The Brazilian real edged lower ahead of its policymakers' rate decision on Wednesday. The real was recently at BRL1.6630 against the dollar, from its previous close of BRL1.6620, according to FactSet.

The Colombian and Chilean pesos slipped, with the latter nation's industrial production data rising slightly less than expected and unemployment increasing a bit more than anticipated. Chile's peso ended at CLP475.80, compared with CLP474.50 on Friday, while trading in a range of CLP474.00 to CLP476.70.

Colombia's peso fell, with authorities continuing to intervene through daily U.S. dollar purchases, even after its central bank unexpectedly hiked rates last week. On the Embig, Colombia's spread narrowed ten basis points, to 156 basis points over Treasurys, and gained 0.74%.

The South African rand was once again a top performer, strengthening more than 0.8% against the U.S. dollar on Monday, to ZAR6.9504, according to FactSet. Officials reported on Monday that exports fell 17% in January, while imports climbed 14%, pulling South Africa's trade balance back into deficit territory. South African credit was 22 basis points wider, to 178 basis points over Treasurys. It gained 0.1% on Monday.

Not far behind, the Hungarian forint advanced 0.75% against the euro. On Tuesday, Hungary's government is slated to announce its much anticipated fiscal-tightening plans, that includes reducing its debt to escape downgrades to its credit rating that would put the country's bonds in junk territory.

In the week ahead, Brazil is scheduled to release a slew of data, including fourth-quarter GDP, IPCA inflation, and details to its BRL50 billion fiscal spending cut package. Interest rate decisions are also due out of Brazil, Mexico, Poland, and Indonesia.

-By Cynthia Lin, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4403; cynthia.lin@dowjones.com

title: DJ Colombia's Peso Steadies As Rains Bring Worries Of Inflation
text:
*Colombia Central Bank Not Seen Raising Rates Until 2Q

*Bank's Intervention Program Keeps Lid On Peso Strength

*Natural Disaster Helps Tamp Down Peso Strength 


 
    By Dan Molinski 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Central bank intervention has helped keep Colombia's currency from getting too strong against the dollar, but divine intervention--in the form of torrential rainfalls--clearly deserves some of the credit.

Colombia's peso is nearly 2% weaker in February and within earshot of where it began the year, trading recently as weak as COP1,891 for $1 Thursday. This despite forecasts by many traders at the start of 2011 that by now the peso would be strengthening toward COP1,750 due to continued heavy inflows of foreign direct investment into Colombia.

Analysts say rising inflation in Colombia, a direct result of six months of lashing rains that wiped out farmers' crops and caused food prices to soar, is one of the main factors for the peso's recent stability and even modest weakness.

Consumer price inflation is up 1.56% over the past two months alone, bringing annualized inflation to a 19-month high of 3.4%. That means inflation, which weakens a currency's value, is now in the top range of the central bank's 2011 inflation target of 2% to 4%.

What's more, the bank hasn't responded to the rising inflation by raising interest rates, which remain at a historical low of 3%. Bank Chairman Jose Dario Uribe says the uptick in prices is a "temporary" supply-side problem and that once the rain goes away, so too will the higher inflation.

The bank's apparent lack of concern over the higher prices is what has some investors rattled, analysts say.

"The market is a little nervous about the inflation, specifically the 3.4% 12-month figure ... and the bank seems to be rather dovish about it all," said Win Thin, currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

In a policy statement two weeks ago, the bank said it's only going to raise interest rates if inflation remains a problem--which it doesn't expect--or if the economy continues to grow as forecast.

The government expects the economy to grow 5% this year. But third-quarter growth was a lower-than-forecast 3.6% and some analysts worry growth could continue to suffer from the rains and floods, which beyond wiping out crops also killed hundreds of people, left thousands homeless and destroyed bridges and highways.

The government says recovery and reconstruction will cost upwards of $5 billion. Coal and oil producers in Colombia have cited the rains for lower-than-expected output in recent months.

With that in mind, analysts don't expect Colombia's central bank to hike rates until sometime in the second quarter of this year.

Meantime, other factors are also keeping a lid on peso strength.

The central bank set up a policy last year, amid a surging peso, that each day through mid March it would buy $20 million in U.S. currency in the forex market to prevent peso strength.

Also, Latin American currencies in general haven't outperformed in 2011 the way they did over the past couple of years, and analysts say Colombia's peso is part of that trend.

Despite the higher inflation and the bank's daily dollar purchases, some currency strategists feel the peso's on the verge of trending upward again.

"This [modest peso weakness] isn't going to last," said Po Jeng, who analyzes currencies at Colombia's InterBolsa brokerage in Bogota. "By the end of this week or perhaps next week, the focus will once again shift to foreign investment flows into Colombia, and you're likely to see the peso gain."

She expects the peso to strengthen to around COP1,800 for $1 by the end of 2011.

Foreign direct investment shot up 37% last year to $9.4 billion and could top $10 billion in 2011 as oil companies and other big-money investors pour dollars into this Andean nation.

title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Colombia
text:
BOGOTA, Dec 1 (Reuters) - President Juan Manuel Santos' ambitious reform agenda, an uptick in the guerrilla and drugs war, measures to tame the soaring peso and still delicate relations with neighboring Venezuela and Ecuador are key issues to watch in Colombia in the next year.

SANTOS' REFORM PROGRAM

Since coming to office in August, Santos has pushed an ambitious set of reforms ranging from the management of oil royalties to overhauling the health system and a tax system adjustment. The success of the reforms are seen as essential for Colombia to tackle its fiscal deficit and regain the investment grade it lost in a 1990s fiscal crisis. Key to watch will be the royalties reform, tax overhaul and a fiscal regulation proposal that seeks to lower debt and better savings. Santos has a strong majority in Congress, but several proposals already must have to wait to a second legislative session start in March.

The royalties reform has faced resistance from lawmakers allied with government but who represent oil-producing regions. Currently Santos says royalties benefit only a few commodities-producing states and says the reform will centralize how cash is distributed.

Colombia is a crude oil producer and the world's No. 5 coal exporter thanks to a fall in guerrilla violence and an increase in foreign investment. Santos is also pushing a fiscal regulation to use surplus oil and mine revenues to cut debt. The reform envisages an overseas saving fund for commodities revenues to help shield the economy during hard times.

Local officials in producing regions are already talking about protests if their royalty share is reduced by any reforms. Two lawmakers are also proposing an increase in royalties paid by international companies.

That bill has no government backing, but with commodity prices rising it may signal the risk of latent demand for more state share of oil and mining wealth. Some communities are also now protesting by against oil companies to demand payment for infrastructure repairs, and protests may rise as investment increases in rural areas. One protest halted drilling at a Canadian oil company recently.

While Santos is adamant he will not raise taxes, some analysts believe some form of tax reform will be inevitable later in his presidency, especially if he is serious about the deficit. A current proposal would lift a tax deduction on some fixed-income investment, bringing an extra $2.6 billion to state offers from 2011.

What to watch:

-- Protests against oil or mining companies.

-- Details on how royalty reform will share out cash.

-- Splits in Santos' majority over managing the oil boom.

-- How the government handles tax adjustments.

MANAGING THE PESO

Colombia's peso currency has risen around 8 percent so far this year, hurting exporters who receive revenue in dollars and threatening to chip away at the moderate growth Colombia has seen since the global crisis.

The government and central bank have already taken several measures such as holding off bringing back dollars from overseas this year and saying they would use external financing to only pay for overseas obligations.

The central bank has left the door open for more announcements to try and tame the peso but the finance minister has dismissed the need for now of forceful intervention in the market.

In the past, Colombia has slapped capital controls on short-term portfolio investment to ease the peso's rise and exporters of coffee, oil, coal, flowers and nickel are demanding more measures.

But the government is wary of such market-unfriendly moves. Short term measures may not be enough to stem the peso as Colombia receives a boom in oil and mining dollars. But the overseas saving fund planned for oil and mining revenue would in the long term ease appreciation.

What to watch:

-- Central bank announcements to curb the peso.

-- How Latin America manage currency appreciation.

ARMED GROUPS, DRUG TRAFFICKERS

Santos has promised to keep up Uribe's tough stance against left-wing rebels, paramilitary gangs and cocaine traffickers mixed up in Colombia's long conflict. At his swearing-in ceremony, he said the door to dialogue with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, was "not locked with a key."

But his government scored a huge political and military victory in September with a bombing raid that killed top FARC commander Mono Jojoy. That strike will likely spark further desertions from FARC ranks and prompt the government to step up its offensive rather than seek out any dialogue with the FARC. The next target will be Alfonso Cano, the FARC's top commander.

The FARC says it wants talks, but Santos, a former defense minister, says rebels must end hostilities, halt criminal activity and release their hostages before any negotiations. Under intense military pressure, the FARC has settled into hit-and-run attacks. It has still shown its military capacity with a recent surge in those attacks.

Santos will continue with Uribe's security policies and manage the close alliance with Washington as the White House trims military aid. The FARC could seek to gain credibility by releasing some hostages while trying to show its force by pulling off high-profile operations. The government will try to expand a program to consolidate its military successes by bringing in social and economic development programs quicker to areas hit hardest by conflict and drug trafficking.

Colombia remains the world's No. 1 cocaine producer and multiple illegal armed groups are all engaged in the drug trade, making the government's task more complex. Armed groups have fragmented and rebels have formed alliances with drug-trafficking gangs and former paramilitaries.

Despite the demobilization of paramilitary groups who once fought the FARC, new crime groups have emerged and rights groups say they are an increasing threat to vulnerable, rural towns and some urban areas where small-time drug-trafficking is common. A car bomb in Bogota soon after Santos came to office was a reminder of risks. Markets mainly dismissed the bombing, but a sustained increase in urban attacks would unnerve investors.

What to watch:

-- Blows to FARC leadership, large-scale desertions.

-- Urban attacks by FARC to show presence.

-- Evidence of alliances between armed groups.

ANDEAN NEIGHBORS

Tensions between Colombia and its left-wing Andean neighbors, Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez and Ecuador's President Rafael Correa, have eased considerably since Santos took office after more than two years of diplomatic disputes.

The new Colombian leader has taken a very pragmatic approach. Chavez and Santos met just days after Santos was sworn in and the two promised to restore diplomatic ties, resume trade and seek payment of around $800 million that Venezuela owes to Colombian exporters. Since then, several initiatives such as cooperation against drug-traffickers and guerrilla presence in Venezuela have underscored improving relations.

Both countries could use a resumption of their $7 billion a year in bilateral trade. But Santos and Chavez have bickered in the past and underlying differences between U.S. ally Colombia and Washington adversary Venezuela remain unresolved. That may stir up tensions again. Some analysts question whether Venezuela has the cash to pay debt owed to Colombian companies, and Colombian exporters are wary of returning wholesale to the Venezuelan market after prolonged trade restrictions.

With Ecuador's Correa too Santos has made headway with the two governments announcing their intention to fully restore ties frayed two years ago over a Colombian bombing raid on a FARC rebel camp across Ecuador's border.

Colombia has helped supply Ecuador with much-needed electricity in the past and continues to do so. But FARC rebels crossing into Ecuador will likely remain a point of tension.

What to watch:

-- How Santos manages any flare-ups in relations again.

-- Stalled bilateral trade and Colombia debt payments. (Editing by Kieran Murray)

title: UPDATE 2-Colombia's  central bank  keeps key rate at 3 pct
text:
* Decision in line with unanimous poll forecast

* Inflation target set at 2 to 4 percent for 2011

* Cenbank sees inflation ending 2011 at lower target limit

* No mention of any new peso measures at meeting (Adds details, comment, analyst)

By Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank on Friday maintained its benchmark interest rate at 3 percent, in line with market expectations, and set its 2011 inflation target at between 2 percent and 4 percent.

All 45 analysts consulted by Reuters this week had forecast the bank would keep the same rate as the authority has done since April this year due to low inflation expectations and a recovery in economic growth after the 2009 financial crisis.

Colombia's monetary body said on Friday the 2011 inflation target would be the same as 2010 at between 2 percent and 4 percent.

"The available inflation projections suggest that upon ending 2011, inflation will be situated at a level near the lower limit of the target range," it said in a statement.

Last year's inflation rate was 2.0 percent.

Around Latin America this month, Chile's central bank upped its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3 percent while Peru's authority held its rate steady at 3 percent as inflation showed benign increases. [ID:nLIP002084] [ID:nN16125546] <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

For more Latin American interest rates [ID:nN14153782]

For a graphic on Colombia's battle with its currency, click on: http://r.reuters.com/kuv25q

For a graphic of Latin America inflation trends:

http://r.reuters.com/peb64q("http://r.reuters.com/peb64q") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Analysts expect the bank to keep its rate at 3 percent for at least the rest of the year.

"The central bank continues to derive significant comfort from a macro environment characterized by moderate growth taking place against a backdrop of still negative output gap and benevolent current and expected inflation dynamics," Goldman Sachs analyst Alberto Ramos said in a note.

"Furthermore, domestic currency appreciation has turned into a valuable inflation moderating force by anchoring tradable goods inflation in negative territory."

NO MENTION OF NEW PESO MEASURES

Emerging markets are bracing for a wave of investment from yield-seeking investors after the U.S. Federal Reserve said it would spend $600 billion buying bonds in a second wave of quantitative easing designed to keep down U.S. rates.

Colombia's central bank did not mention any new measures against the peso currency, and none of the analysts polled by Reuters had expected any new steps to help curb the peso.

"There are some analysts that would like us to make large interventions, massive interventions... and even give examples like the case of Brazil," bank chief Jose Dario Uribe said at a news conference. "In our case, we've seen through history that the most effective interventions are ones we're doing now."

Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry told Reuters earlier this month that Colombia would try to avoid imposing Brazil-style capital controls to curtail the strength of its currency but "nothing is ruled out." [ID:nN12127423]

The central bank is buying at least $20 million a day in a program, scheduled to last until mid-March, meant curb the local currency, which has surged 8.8 percent this year; the government has also announced mainly structural measures.

Since early October, the currency has weakened around 4.5 percent on those measures and fears of more interventions.

Uribe said earlier this month the bank had not ruled out the possibility of "big" forex interventions. [ID:nN05292894]

Colombia said on Tuesday it had not exhausted all currency measures and would only use external financing next year to meet outside obligations. [ID:nN16108112] (Writing by Jack Kimball; Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: WRAPUP 2- Colombia 's  central bank  eyes "big"  FX intervention
text:
* Central banker's first reference to "big interventions"

* Countries around the world move to control currencies (Adds context, analyst's quote)

By Hugh Bronstein

BOGOTA, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank does not rule out the possibility of "big" interventions in the foreign exchange market to control the strength of the local peso currency, central bank chief Jose Dario Uribe said on Friday.

"The fact that these interventions have not worked in the past does not mean that they might not work in the future. In fact, we do not discard the possibility of big interventions," Uribe said in televised remarks.

The central bank is buying at least $20 million per day in a program, scheduled to last until mid-March, meant to take some of the juice out of the local currency <COP=RR>. Since the year began, the peso has climbed 11 percent against the U.S. dollar to 1,821 per greenback.

Friday's comment was the first in which Uribe, usually known for using measured language, spoke of "big interventions." But local market players did not read the comment as indicating an immediate increase in dollar purchases.

"I am betting that the bank will continue relying on verbal interventions such as this one," said Daniel Velandia, chief economist at Bogota brokerage Correval.

"He is making the point that they are serious about controlling the peso and reaffirming that while $20 million per day is the minimum, that minimum could be raised, if necessary," Velandia said.

Policymakers worldwide are moving to keep their currencies from strengthening as investors -- turning their backs on low interest rates in developed economies -- pour money into higher-yielding emerging markets. The measures have been wide ranging.

The waters of the debate have been muddied by the Federal Reserve's decision, announced this week, to buy $600 billion in long-term bonds with new money in an effort to revive the flagging U.S. economy.

Brazil, warning of a "currency war," criticized the U.S. plan and has raised taxes on foreigners buying local bonds for the second time since the start of October.

INFLATION SEEN UNDER 3 PERCENT

Policymakers in Bogota have avoided imposing capital controls as they campaign for Colombia to win back the investment-grade credit rating that the country lost in an economic crisis 10 years ago.

But political pressure to ease the peso's rise remains strong. And Colombian businesses that sell their products overseas are clamoring for policymakers to do more.

Exporters who get paid in dollars while having to pay their costs in pesos say they are being forced to lay off workers as profits shrink along with the once-strong dollar.

Colombia's inflation rate has a "high probability" of being under 3 percent this year, Uribe also said on Friday.

The bank's target range for inflation this year is between 2 percent and 4 percent.

"We see a high probability that inflation will be under 3 percent this year," Uribe said. "Why will we have inflation under 3 percent? For the appreciation of the peso, because the economy has excess capacity and due to the close of trade with Venezuela."

Venezuela has shut off trade with neighboring Colombia as part of a diplomatic spat over Bogota's close military alliance with Washington. The border's closing has slowed Colombia's recovery from the 2008-09 world crisis.

Colombia expects its economy to expand 4.5 percent this year and in 2011. Uribe said Colombia's inflation rate will be within the official target range.

"Our technical team is projecting an inflation rate not very far from 2 percent in the year ahead," Uribe said.

The bank's official inflation projection for 2011 is between 1.8 percent and 3 percent. (Additional reporting by Nelson Bocanegra and Javier Mozzo; Editing by Jan Paschal)

title: UPDATE:  Colombia  Keeps Rate at 3%; Extends  Forex Intervention
text:
(Updates with analysts comments)


 
   By Darcy Crowe 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's central bank held its benchmark interest rate at 3% for a sixth straight month on Friday while also unveiling an extension of its dollar purchases in the foreign-exchange market to rein in the appreciation of the peso.

The central bank will buy a minimum of $20 million daily until at least May 15, central bank Chairman Jose Dario Uribe said.

Potential measures by the central bank had been widely expected by the market, with the peso retreating against the dollar this week after President Juan Manuel Santos said Saturday that the government would soon announce new steps to rein in the peso.

"The measures announced by the central bank came short of the market expectation," Alberto Ramos, an economist with Goldman Sachs, wrote in a note.

The central bank's buying program was previously slated to last until January 15.

The central bank started buying $20 million daily on Sept. 15 to rein in the peso's surge, a decision which Uribe said had been widely successful. The central bank has so far purchased $580 million in the second half of the year, Uribe said

Despite the September decision, a group of leading business groups asked the central bank on Oct. 11 to step up its efforts against the peso's surge, which is threatening exporters.

The peso's climb, which nears 12% this year, "puts at risk the positive economic outlook for the Colombian economy," the business groups said in an open letter. The business groups also asked the bank to consider lowering its benchmark rate in a bid to weaken the peso.

The peso has gained against the dollar this year in part fueled by foreign investments in the country's booming oil and mining industries. Foreign direct investment is expected to reach $10 billion this year.

Some economists warned that the central bank would unveil capital-control mechanisms to limit the number of dollars entering the Colombian economy and stem the peso's appreciation.

Other observers also said authorities could limit the short-term borrowing abroad by local firms to discourage them from bringing dollars into Colombia.

Uribe reiterated that the central bank had weighed the costs and benefits of capital controls and had decided they weren't currently justified.

Before the announcement on Friday the peso closed at COP1,840.00 to the dollar, weakening from 1,836.99.

Alianza Valores, a local brokerage, said that the market's initial reaction will strengthen the peso to as much as COP1,815.

The central bank was also widely expected to keep its benchmark rate unchanged at 3%. "Inflation has been in line with our expectations," Uribe said, adding that faster economic growth isn't pressuring prices. The Colombian economy will likely grow 4.5% in 2011, Uribe said.

Price increases this year have stayed within the lower range of the central bank's 2% to 4% target. Consumer prices in September declined 0.14% as a result of drops in food prices. Inflation over the 12 months through September was 2.28%.

After emerging from a slowdown last year, the Colombian economy picked up speed and grew 4.5% in the second quarter. Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry has said that the gross domestic product could expand 5% this year.

-By Darcy Crowe, Dow Jones Newswires; (57) 1 703 8953; darcy.crowe@dowjones.com [ 10-29-10 1817ET ]

title: Colombia talks peso, markets eye capital controls
text:
* Peso down 3.4 pct in two weeks on intervention fears

* Santos talks about IMF and capital controls in speech

By Jack Kimball and Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Comments by the Colombian government indicate higher chances it will use short-term capital controls to temper the country's rising peso, Colombian analysts said on Wednesday.

Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos on Wednesday said he was surprised the International Monetary Fund now saw capital controls as a way to curb sudden surges in money flowing into emerging markets.

"I didn't think I'd live to see a head of the IMF saying that suddenly there are some capital controls that should be imposed. That for me is a total paradigm shift but it's the reality," Santos said in a speech.

Economic observers say some companies are speculating in the Andean nation, taking advantage of cheap money in developed markets and making carry trades in Colombia -- a reason why the market expects some short-term capital controls.

While the government has said it would take new measures against the peso this week, Bogota has not said what the move might be and is weighing a number of options. Analysts say the signs indicate some form of short-term capital controls.

"This is simply anticipating information that could come on Friday on the side of capital controls on external debt," said Camilo Perez, head of economic research at Banco de Bogota.

A Reuters poll of analysts found the majority think the central bank will announce additional forex measures at its meeting on Friday, with the most probable move seen as a control on short-term capital inflows. [ID:nN25272647] <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

While a recent G20 meeting pledged to move towards market-determined exchange rates and called for measures to reduce excessive external imbalances, investors saw no reason to change their view of stronger emerging currencies. [ID:nTOE69K01G]

Many emerging economies are concerned that the rush of speculative inflows in recent months could create potentially destabilizing bubbles, making policymaking more difficult.

In Latin America, high commodity prices and strong growth have attracted a slew of investors. Nations in the region, such as Brazil and Peru, have moved to curb their currencies.

At the weekend, Santos said the government would announce measures this week to help mitigate the impact of the rising peso currency <COP=RR>. [ID:nN23159856]

The central bank has restarted a dollar buying program to try to stop the rise of the peso, which has surged 11 percent this year. The currency, however, has eased 3.49 percent in the last two weeks on fears of more interventions.

Colombia's markets are enjoying strong demand thanks to growing expectations it may soon regain an investment-grade rating -- net foreign portfolio inflows were $179 million, with $951 million flowing in and $772 million flowing out.

From January to September, net foreign loans of the private sector were negative $80 million, with $5.97 billion entering the nation and $6.05 billion leaving as debt repayments, according to central bank data.

"The answer isn't easy because capital movements toward the developing world are being produced globally. That's why it's necessary to have a battery of instruments," former finance minister, Jose Antonio Ocampo, wrote in a local paper.

"Without a competitive exchange rate, investment exports different from mining and hydrocarbons will not take place and some companies will go out of business," Ocampo wrote. (Editing by Frank Jack Daniel; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: PREVIEW-Colombia cenbank rate seen stable, eyes on peso
text:
WHAT: Colombia's monthly central bank policy meeting

WHEN: Friday, Oct. 29

OUTCOME: Bank seen keeping benchmark rate at 3 percent

REUTERS FORECAST:

A Reuters poll of 40 analysts found that nearly all observers expected the central bank to leave its key interest rate at 3 percent at its monthly meeting on Friday. Only two analysts saw a reduction in the rate.

Of the observers surveyed, 27 said that they expected the monetary authority to announce additional measures against the surging peso currency, with the most probable move seen as a control on capital inflows from external debt.

Looking longer term, nearly all of those polled estimated the bank would keep its benchmark interest rate stable until year end, and more than two-thirds think that the rate will close 2011 between 4 percent and 4.5 percent.

FACTORS TO WATCH:

With the interest rate likely to remain unchanged, all eyes will be on the bank's remarks on the peso and possible measures the board could announce to slow the currency's rise. For more details on possible measures, click [ID:nN15183902]

In mid-September, the monetary authority restarted a dollar purchasing program of at least $20 million daily. President Juan Manuel Santos said on Saturday that the government would announce measures this week to help mitigate the impact of the rising peso currency <COP=RR>. [ID:nN23159856]

The government and the bank have been under pressure to do more to control the strengthening currency. Other nations in the region, such as Brazil and Peru, have also moved to curb their currencies. For a Factbox on Colombia's past interventions, click [ID:nN24243857]

"Concerning foreign exchange measures, we don't rule out capital controls, especially for private external debt," said consultants EConcept in a note.

"However, to the extent that international conditions and daily interventions by the central bank are able to keep the exchange rate above 1,800 pesos per dollar, the probability of placing those controls is reduced."

MARKET IMPACT:

Maintaining the interest rate is unlikely to move the peso or local peso-denominated TES bonds as the market will have factored that into its trading options.

But there is a lot of interest in peso measures although many players have already adjusted their positions to account for likely moves by the government or central bank. (Reporting by Nelson Bocanegra; Writing by Jack Kimball; Editing by Frank Jack Daniel and Diane Craft)

text:

* Cenbank board to hold monthly policy meeting on Friday

BOGOTA, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos said on Saturday that the government would announce measures in the coming week to help mitigate the impact of the rising peso currency <COP=RR>.

Latin America's No. 4 oil producer has seen its currency strengthen due to inflows into its mining and energy sectors, dollar sales to finance government spending and a recovery from the global financial crisis.

"In the coming week we're going to take measures that we've studied well ... take measures that really have an impact on this quite complicated situation," Santos said.

Santos did not give any details.

The country's government and central bank have been under pressure from companies and unions to do more to stop the appreciating peso, which has hurt exporters' profits. (Reporting by Luis Jaime Acosta; editing by Jim Marshall)

title: UPDATE 2-Colombia eyes peso measures, firming trend remains
text:
* Santos gives no details of possible actions to curb peso

* Peso has gained 12 percent year-to-date against dollar

* Colombia can't avoid the change in dollar's value - IMF (Recasts, adds analyst, details)

By Jack Kimball and Javier Mozzo

BOGOTA, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Colombia's government vowed to act to tackle the economic impact of the country's strong peso and the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday the Andean nation could not avoid the change in the dollar's value.

Latin America's No. 4 oil producer has seen its currency strengthen due to inflows into its mining and energy sectors, dollar sales to finance government spending and a recovery from the global financial crisis.

The peso <COP=RR> has surged around 12 percent against the dollar so far this year to the chagrin of battered exporters who receive earnings in dollars but pay costs in pesos.

"We have to look out so that our economy is not affected by a stronger revaluation from which the rest of the world is (also) suffering," President Juan Manuel Santos told La Republica newspaper. "We're going to take action."

"Very soon we'll announce a package of measures to face this phenomenon in addition to what the government and the central bank have already done," he was quoted as saying.

Santos gave no details on possible measures.

The central bank announced in mid-September a dollar purchasing program of at least $20 million a day to try to contain the rising peso. For more see [ID:nN15145483].

In Latin America, high commodity prices and strong growth have attracted a slew of investors, increasing capital inflows that boost local currencies. Other nations in the region, such as Brazil and Peru, have moved to curb their currencies. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Colombia past market interventions     [ID:nN24243857]
 Steps other countries are taking       [ID:nSGE69503F]


^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

GOOD NEWS, BAD NEWS

Santos reiterated government plans to cut the costs of doing business. Bogota presented a reform bill to Congress last week including a cut in the energy surtax. [ID:nN15219226]

Colombia's monetary authority also modified its foreign exchange intervention rules last week to make it easier for the bank to enter the market. [ID:nN15189451]

The government has said it would receive two dividend payments abroad from state-controlled Ecopetrol oil company worth about $1.4 billion. [ID:nN13283686]

"The measures adopted by the authorities so far may signal that policymakers are trying to avoid more onerous administrative controls ... that's the good news," Daniel Volberg of Morgan Stanley said in a recent note.

"The bad news is that none of the measures the authorities have adopted so far appear to have broken the peso's advance," he said.

The world's No. 5 coal exporter has seen a boom in oil and mining investment since the government in 2002 launched a U.S.-backed offensive against leftist rebels which opened up areas of the country once under guerrillas control.

Colombia's largest coal exporter, Cerrejon, said on Monday that its costs have been raised by the effect of the strong domestic currency against the U.S. dollar. [ID:nLDE69H1EZ]

Colombian firms and exporters have called on the government to take more measures against the rising currency such as accumulating more international reserves. [ID:nN11111019]

Nicolas Eyzaguirre, head of the International Monetary Fund's Western Hemisphere Department, said it would be impossible for Colombia to avoid a stronger peso currency due to strong growth and investment in mining.

"Colombia finds itself in an auspicious phase, not cyclical but structural for the development of its mining sector and there are fundamental and structural factors that make this economy attractive for foreign investment," Eyzaguirre told journalists in Colombia's capital, Bogota.

"And it follows that the value of the dollar will be more moderate than what it was in recent years and trying to avoid that reality is not going to be possible." (Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: UPDATE 1- Colombia  cenbank modifies  forex intervention  rules
text:
* Peso falls on central bank's announcement

* Colombia cenbank under pressure to do more against peso (Adds background, peso details)

BOGOTA, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank said it had modified its foreign exchange intervention rules to make it easier for the bank to enter the market discretionally and help control the surging local peso currency.

Colombia's peso -- which has been strengthening this year -- closed down 0.43 percent to 1,809.10 against the dollar, with investors seeing the modifications as an indication the bank could step up interventions.

Last month, the bank started buying at least $20 million daily through auctions to help stem the rise of the peso, which has firmed more than 10 percent so far this year. The private sector has called for the government to do more.

The new rules, issued late on Thursday, made it easier for the central bank to intervene in the market at its own discretion as it can now participate in a private-initiative clearing house created for currency transactions in 2008.

The bank stopped intervening discretionally in the market in 2007, according to traders.

For a copy of the changes in Spanish, click http://www.banrep.gov.co/documentos/reglamentacion/cambiaria/2010/29.pdf("http://www.banrep.gov.co/documentos/reglamentacion/cambiaria/2010/29.pdf")

Colombia's rule change follows moves by other emerging country governments that have sought to stem the rise of currencies, stop their economies overheating and defend exporters. Authorities in Brazil and Peru have tried to curb their currencies.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Colombia's peso down on cenbank, region weak
text:
* Dollar's recovery curbs regional rally

* Colombia's peso falls on central bank's rule change

* Chilean peso flat after rates raised slightly

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Caroline Stauffer and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Friday as investors bet the dollar's recent decline was overdone and Colombia's peso fell after new rules cleared the way for more central bank intervention.

Bets the U.S. central bank will soak up safe-haven debt and drive down borrowing costs in the United States, a policy tool known as quantitative easing, have lifted demand for higher yielding assets like Latin American currencies.

But U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said on Friday policymakers were still weighing how aggressive they should be. [ID:nLDE69E1EV]

After sinking to multi-month lows against a basket of currencies on Fed expectations, the dollar recovered. The Brazilian real and the Mexican peso weakened as a result.

"The Euro's decline against the dollar indicated the forex market had already priced in a lot of quantitative easing potential - that's why Latin American currencies are adjusting to the weak side today," Robert Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital in New York said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=>shed 0.21 percent to 12.4125 while Brazil's real <BRBY> slipped 0.18 percent to 1.664.

Brazil's Finance Minister Guido Mantega told reporters on Friday the government was waiting for currency markets to stabilize before taking fresh measures to curb the real's rise. [ID:nN15201659]

The threat of more aggressive intervention in Colombia, however, prompted the country's peso to close 0.43 percent weaker to 1800.10 per dollar.

The central bank issued new rules late on Thursday, making it easier for the central bank to intervene in the foreign exchange market at its own discretion. [ID:nN15204150]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> closed flat at 478.8 per dollar, the day after the country's central bank raised the country's benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent.

The bank has slowed the pace at which it raises rates for fear that higher rates would fuel an even bigger rally in the peso, which is trading around a 29-month high.

But the threats kept coming. Chile's peso appreciation is worrying and could soon have an adverse effect on economic activity and inflation, Central Bank board member Enrique Marshall said in a presentation posted on the bank's website on Friday. [ID:nN15190638]

Mexico's central bank on Friday held its target for overnight bank lending at 4.5 percent, the lowest since policymakers began targeting the rate in January 2008.

Mexico has maintained record-low interest rates as foreign investors looking for bigger returns pour cash into Latin America.

The central bank said that "these capital inflows have contributed to the recent appreciation of the exchange rate, the accumulation of international reserves and continues reducing interest rates along the yield curve." [ID:nN15196452]

title: FOREX  VIEW: Mexico Likely To Stay Neutral In  Currency  Battles
text:
MEXICO CITY (Dow Jones)--Latin American countries fighting what some governments see as a currency war aren't likely to find an ally in Mexico.

Amid global tensions over exchange rates, Brazil has raised a tax on certain financial operations in an effort to discourage the heavy foreign capital inflows that are boosting its real, while Thailand this week removed a tax break on foreign investment in its government bonds in an attempt to slow the baht's rise, and the U.S. Federal Reserve appears poised for another round of quantitative easing that could weaken the dollar.

The Mexican peso still has room to recover from the beating it took in 2008 and 2009, despite its own recent appreciation. The peso is trading around MXN12.40 to the dollar, up 6.5% year-to-date and 26% from its all-time low in March 2009, but still nearly 20% weaker from before the 2008 crisis. Brazil's real, meanwhile, is up 5% year-to-date but 41% stronger from the end of 2008.

Mexican policy makers appear loathe to intervene to weaken the peso and give Mexican exports a competitive advantage.

During a weekend visit to Washington, Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero said his country "believes and trusts" in a free-floating currency, which has allowed Mexico to absorb external shocks in the past. Cordero said countries need to be careful when implementing "easy fixes" such as capital controls, noting that the Brazilian real continues to appreciate despite such measures. Exchange policy shouldn't be a trade policy tool, he added.

Cordero described Mexico's currency circumstance as "fortunately different" than that of some other Latin American countries, alluding to recent export gains in the U.S. market. Mexican products now represent 13% of U.S. imports compared with 10% just three years ago, Cordero said, attributing the advance to structural advantages that Mexico boasts over other countries--its geographical location, border trade infrastructure, and improving labor productivity--rather than relying on foreign exchange advantages.

"It's evident that Mexico is a stand-alone case compared with South American countries because of its greater exposure to the U.S. trade balance. We have seen that when the risk premium rises due to uncertainty about the U.S. recovery, the peso is the currency that most suffers," said Moises Junca, chief Latin America foreign exchange strategist with BBVA Securities.

Yet some see Mexico's export gains as a crutch.

"The Mexican peso has been a laggard among the region's appreciating currencies for a reason: whereas other countries can rely on some degree of domestic demand strength to cushion their economies against currency strength, the Mexican recovery remains externally driven," Luis Arcentales, an economist with Morgan Stanley, wrote in a Monday research note. "And with export-oriented industry already decelerating, Mexico seems to be the economy that can least afford significant currency strength."

Gross domestic product expanded 5.9% in the first half of the year and is expected to slow in the second half for full-year growth between 4% and 5%. Below-capacity output and low inflation have allowed the central bank to hold its benchmark overnight lending rate at 4.5% since July 2009, with no signs that it's contemplating a rate increase before the second half of 2011. Brazil's benchmark selic rate is 10.75% and expected to rise early next year.

The rebound in exports after a trade slump in 2009, rising crude prices, and remittances from Mexicans living in the U.S. are all sources of peso strength. Also this year, Mexico's Oct. 1 inclusion in Citibank's World Government Bond Index is seen attracting as much as $16 billion in fresh foreign investment, much of which has presumably already arrived.

While policy makers in countries like Brazil, Colombia and Peru are intervening to limit currency appreciation, Mexico has adhered to a comparatively subtle mechanism of selling $600 million in dollar put options each month. The Bank of Mexico uses the options to build foreign reserves when the peso is appreciating; commercial banks can exercise the options when the peso is stronger than its 20-day average.

Recent peso gains have led to some discussion on whether the central bank might opt to raise the dollar amount of the options it sells each month. RBC Capital Markets thinks that's a possibility, but adds that "the MXN is one of the least vulnerable emerging market currencies to foreign exchange intervention."

text:
* Colombia battles strengthening peso currency

 * Analysts: cenbank board of two minds on capital controls

 * Fiscal issues could limit dollar purchases-analysts  (Adds fiscal details, analyst)

 By Nelson Bocanegra and Jack Kimball

 BOGOTA, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Colombian Central Bank Governor Jose Dario Uribe said on Thursday foreign capital of the private sector had been net negative this year and more debt payments by Colombians were flowing out than loans coming in.

 The Andean nation's monetary body is under pressure by Colombian firms to do more to combat the rising peso currency, but the governor's comments suggest he thinks it may not make sense now to use capital controls, analysts said.

 "We've said that from our viewpoint, we have instruments that we use to the extent and intensity that we consider appropriate ... there are other instruments that so far we have not employed because we consider that the costs outweigh the benefits," Uribe told local Radio W.

 "External capital of the private sector, distinct from foreign direct investment, is still net negative. That means despite a growth in disbursements of foreign credit, Colombians are paying more credit in even larger amounts outward and hence what they pay outward surpasses what is entering from abroad.

 "So that's still not a factor that's weighing on what's happening with the exchange rate," he said.

 Despite calls for more intervention, neither the central

 "That reflects that there are two positions on capital

 Latin America's No. 4 oil producer has seen a five-fold

 The World Bank said Latin America should moderate fiscal

their currencies. [ID:nN24260311]

 Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said late on
Wednesday the government would ask lawmakers to eliminate a tax
deduction for investment beginning next year. [ID:nN13286688]

 The tax deduction -- which is currently 30 percent -- would

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  mixed on  intervention  fears
text:
* Brazil's real drops 0.42 pct, Mexican peso down 0.03

* Colombia's peso closes at highest since August 2008

* Chile's central bank president warns of intervention

(Updates prices, adds details on Colombia, Chile)

By Samantha Pearson and Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Brazil's real weakened sharply Wednesday after the government authorized its treasury to increase its dollar purchases on the local market as the country steps up efforts to halt appreciation.

The real was bid 0.42 percent weaker at 1.680 per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"The government is going to make an effort to adopt more measures to get control of the currency in this currency war that is going on worldwide," said Luiz Eduardo Portella, a fixed-income and currency trader at Brazil's Banco Modal.

Brazil's central bank announced Wednesday it had extended to 1,500 days its maximum period for contracts to be settled in the currency market.

That would allow the treasury to buy more dollars. But confusion over the move prompted speculation that a much bigger measure was in the works, causing the real to plunge.

Brazil has stepped up its efforts to contain the currency's appreciation recently, Tuesday raising a tax on bond purchases by foreigners. The tax did little to tame the real's recent rally.

"To me the Brazilians have signaled another step up the ladder," said Win Thin, senior currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York. "I think they may adjust the tax again."

Chile's peso strengthened 0.11 percent to 482.25 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, extended its rally. The peso has rallied nearly 13 percent since the end of July.

Chile's Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said Wednesday the bank could intervene to halt a sharp appreciation of the peso.

Colombia's peso also gained 0.69 percent to close at 1789.05, its highest level in more than two years.

In mid-September, the central bank started purchasing what it said would be at least $20 million daily for at least four months to help ease the peso's rise and investors fear additional measures will be taken.

"There's some investor caution because these are the levels that make the central bank uncomfortable," said Gustavo Sorzano, an analyst at Helm Bank in Bogota.

EYEING THE FED

Markets have been factoring in the prospect of the U.S. Federal Reserve announcing new asset purchase plans since the Bank of Japan eased monetary policy on Tuesday. A broadly weaker dollar has boosted emerging market currencies.

An unexpected fall in U.S. private sector employment on Wednesday led analysts to believe U.S. non-farm payroll reports due Friday could disappoint, which would further pressure the U.S. central bank to try to stimulate the economy.

Mexico's peso edged down 0.028 percent to 12.477 per dollar in volatile trading.

"The prospect of Fed easing is generally good for riskier assets, but if the Fed is considering quantitative easing, it shows they are really worried about economic recovery - that's the other side of the coin for Mexico," said Brown Brothers Harriman's Thin.
