title: FACTBOX-Key political risks to watch in Colombia
text:
BOGOTA, Oct 1 (Reuters) - President Juan Manuel Santos' ambitious reform agenda, an uptick in the country's guerrilla and drugs war, a soaring peso and still delicate relations with neighboring Venezuela and Ecuador are key issues to watch in Colombia in the next year.

SANTOS REFORM PROGRAM

Since taking office last month, Santos has proposed an ambitious set of reforms ranging from the management of oil and mining royalties, and agrarian land reform, to overhauling the health and justice systems.

Key for Colombia's attempts to tackle its stubborn fiscal deficit -- seen at 4.4 percent of GDP this year -- will be royalties reform [ID:nN31245717] and a fiscal regulation proposal [ID:nN07144747], which are both before Congress.

Santos has a strong majority in Congress, but the royalties reform is already facing resistance from lawmakers allied with government but who represent oil-producing regions.

Currently the Santos administration says royalties benefit only a few commodities-producing states under a system rife with mismanagement. The royalty reform will centralize how cash is distributed so that all regions benefit.

It also seeks to stamp out inefficiency and corruption as crude production grows to an estimated 1.5 million barrels per day within a few years.

Local officials in producing regions are already talking about protests if their royalty share is reduced. Investors are keen to see Colombia better manage its deficit and debt as steps to recovering investment grade with rating agencies after it lost the status during the 1990s. [ID:nN16265600]

Colombia is a significant oil producer and the world's No. 5 coal producer thanks to a sharp fall in guerrilla war violence under Santos's predecessor, Alvaro Uribe. The fiscal regulation, proposed by Uribe's government and adopted by Santos, looks to use surplus oil and mining revenues to cut debt and tackle the deficit. Later, the reform envisages an overseas saving fund for commodities revenues to help shield the economy during hard times.

Constitutional reforms also take time with eight debates required in the two-chamber Congress. While Santos is adamant he will not raise taxes, some analysts believe some form of tax reform will be inevitable later in his presidency, especially if he is serious about the deficit. [ID:nN30181910]

WHAT TO WATCH:

-- Protests in oil-producing states as reform advances.

-- Splits in Santos' majority over managing the oil boom.

-- Any shift on how to manage tax reforms.

ARMED GROUPS, DRUG TRAFFICKERS

Santos has promised to keep up Uribe's tough stance against left-wing rebels, paramilitary gangs and cocaine traffickers mixed up in Colombia's long conflict. At his swearing-in ceremony, he said the door to dialogue with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, was "not locked with a key." [ID:nWEN8602].

But his government scored a huge political and military victory in September with a bombing raid that killed top FARC commander Mono Jojoy [ID:nN23139058]. That strike will likely spark further desertions from FARC ranks and prompt the government to step up its offensive rather than seek out any dialogue with the FARC. [ID:nN24193042]. The next target will be Alfonso Cano, the FARC's top commander.

The FARC says it still wants talks, but Santos, a former defense minister, says rebels must end hostilities, halt criminal activity and release their hostages before any negotiations.

Under intense military pressure, the FARC has settled into hit-and-run attacks. It has, however, still shown its military capacity with a recent surge in those attacks. [ID:nN19273057]

Santos will continue with Uribe's security policies and manage the close alliance with Washington as the White House trims military aid. The FARC could seek to gain credibility by releasing some hostages while trying to show its force by pulling off high-profile operations.

The government will try to expand a program to consolidate its military successes by bringing in social and economic development programs quicker to areas hit hardest by conflict and drug trafficking.

But Colombia remains the world's No. 1 cocaine producer and multiple illegal armed groups are all engaged in the drug trade, making the government's task more complex. Armed groups have fragmented and rebels have formed alliances with drug-trafficking gangs and former paramilitaries.

Defense officials say that could give the FARC a short-term life-line and lead to a brief spike of violence as military pressure increases. Despite the demobilization of paramilitary groups who once fought the FARC, new crime groups have emerged and rights groups say they are an increasing threat to vulnerable, rural towns and villages.

A car bomb in Bogota soon after Santos came to office was a reminder of security risks, though authorities have yet to blame any specific group [ID:nN12273335]. Markets mainly dismissed the bombing, but a sustained increase in urban attacks would unnerve investors.

WHAT TO WATCH:

-- Further blows to the FARC's leadership, large-scale desertions.

-- Urban attacks by FARC to show presence.

-- Evidence of alliances between armed groups

MANAGING THE PESO

Colombia's peso currency has risen around 12 percent so far this year, hurting exporters who receive revenue in dollars and threatening to undermine the moderate growth Colombia has seen since the global crisis. That has worried the government, and the central bank recently began a program to purchase dollars to curb appreciation. [ID:nN15145483]. It left the door open for more measures and at a recent central bank meeting, the board said more intervention was possible alongside other mechanisms.

In the past, Colombia has slapped capital controls on short-term portfolio investment to ease the peso's rise [ID:nN24243857] and exporters of coffee, oil, coal, flowers and nickel are already demanding more measures. [ID:nN16117081].

Short term measures may not be enough to stem the peso as Colombia receives a boom in oil and mining dollars. But the overseas saving fund planned for oil and mining revenue would in the long term ease appreciation.

WHAT TO WATCH:

-- New measures from central bank or government.

-- How other countries in Latin America manage currency appreciation.

ANDEAN NEIGHBORS

Tensions between Colombia and its left-wing Andean neighbors, Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez and Ecuador's President Rafael Correa, have eased since Santos took office after more than two years of diplomatic disputes.

Chavez and Santos met just days after Santos was sworn in and the two promised to restore diplomatic ties, resume trade and seek payment of around $800 million that Venezuela owes to Colombian exporters. [ID:nN10132853]

Both countries need a resumption of their $7 billion a year in bilateral trade [ID:nN10179861]. But Santos and Chavez have bickered in the past and underlying differences between U.S. ally Colombia and Washington adversary Venezuela remain unresolved. That will likely stir up tensions again [ID:nN11231503].

Colombia has accused Venezuela of allowing FARC guerrillas safe haven on its soil. Some analysts question whether Venezuela has the cash to pay debt owed to Colombian companies, and Colombian exporters are wary of returning wholesale to the Venezuelan market after prolonged restrictions on commerce and concerns over future spats. [ID:nN11224605]

Relations with Ecuador have improved since a 2008 crisis sparked by a Colombian army raid across its border to attack a FARC rebel camp. Under Santos, the two governments have held talks, especially since Colombia has helped supply Ecuador with much-needed electricity.

A local Ecuadorean judge has also revoked an arrest warrant against Santos for ordering the 2008 raid, when he was Colombia's defense minister, opening the way for a presidential meeting.

WHAT TO WATCH:

-- How Chavez, Santos manage their fledgling detente.

-- Stalled bilateral trade and debt payments.

-- A meeting between Santos and Correa. (Editing by Kieran Murray)

By Caroline Stauffer and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's real strengthened on Thursday as capital poured into Brazil ahead of a huge stock offering, while Colombia's peso weakened ahead of a central bank meeting.

The real <BRBY> bid 0.12 percent stronger at 1.717 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market as investors prepared for a $79 billion offering by state-controlled oil company Petrobras that is expected to price later on Thursday.

But trading was very volatile. Although huge amounts of dollars are expected to enter Brazil's market over the next couple of days, traders were worried about recent threats by the government to use the sovereign wealth fund to intervene.

"Investors are still weighing up the power of the sovereign wealth fund in the short-term," said Cristiano Oliveira, chief economist for Banco Safra de Investimento in Sao Paulo. "There is a battle to contain the real's appreciation and now this other player has turned up and it's one that is heavily armed."

Brazil's government on Monday authorized the use of its sovereign wealth fund to buy U.S. dollars in the foreign exchange market as part of efforts to weaken the real. [ID:nN20102448] The central bank already intervenes in the market on a daily basis, buying dollars.

Meanwhile, the rising price of copper, Chile's main export, helped to boost the country's peso to a 2-year closing high against the dollar.

The peso <CLP=> firmed 0.9 percent to 488.50 per dollar, closing at its strongest level since June 2008.

"The only fundamental favoring the peso right now is the rebounding price of copper," said one trader in Santiago.

The peso has appreciated more than 10 percent since early July, prompting intervention warnings from the central bank, which analysts expect to step in if the peso firms past 480 per dollar. [ID:nN19249922]

COLOMBIAN PESO LAGS

Colombia's peso <COP=RR> shed 0.35 percent to 1811.25 on fears the country could take further measures to curb its currency's rally.

"Colombia's peso has been a regional star, and today it is losing a little bit of steam," Nomura Economist Benito Berber said. "My suspicion is that it might have to do with the likely announcement of additional intervention policies."

Colombia's central bank meets on Friday and some economists believe further intervention measures could be announced.

The peso has strengthened 11.77 percent this year, leading the central bank to begin purchasing dollars to help slow its ascent on Sept. 15.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> traded nearly even, shedding 0.08 percent to 12.6378 per dollar.

The currency has gained nearly 5 percent in September, boosted in part by foreign investors buying Mexico's peso ahead of the country's inclusion in October in a major global bond index run by Citigroup.

"The peso is a very good deal around 12.62 and we are seeing foreigners buying in," said Enrique Trejo, head of currency trading at brokerage IXE in Mexico City. title: Colombia exporters call for added peso measures
text:
* Central bank urged to lower key interest rate

* Coffee players hit by peso despite high bean prices

By Javier Mozzo and Diana Delgado

BOGOTA, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Colombian exporters said on Thursday the government should help lower the cost of doing business and the central bank should take more measures to help firms weather a strengthening peso currency.

Various Latin American economies have seen their currencies contend with appreciation this year due to high rates of growth and foreign investment inflows.

Regional powerhouse Brazil is aggressively buying dollars, Peru is tightening deposit requirements and Chile has warned it may have to intervene.

Colombia's peso -- one of the region's strongest-performing currencies -- has firmed around 12 percent this year, hurting exporter profits and prompting the central bank to restart dollar purchases. For details, see [ID:nN15145483]

Luis Carlos Villegas, president of the National Association of Colombian Entrepreneurs, said the bank should lower its benchmark interest rate -- currently 3 percent, down from 10 percent in 2008. He also said the central bank had scope to increase its foreign exchange reserves from the current eight months of import cover.

title: INTERVIEW-Colombia sees difficult recovery for Venezuela trade
text:
* Colombia exporters owed $800 mln in debts from Venezuela

* Room for central bank to buy $7 bln-$9 bln in reserves

By Javier Mozzo

BOGOTA, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Colombian trade with neighboring Venezuela will "never" return to its previous levels, Bogota's trade minister said, after a spat whittled billions-of-dollars-a-year in commerce down to a trickle.

Strained ties between Colombia, the U.S. top ally in Latin America, and Venezuela's socialist government have periodically ratcheted up tensions in the volatile Andean region.

Bilateral trade rose to $7 billion two years ago, but slid after Venezuelan leader Hugo Chavez partially froze commerce to protest a deal that gave Washington more access to Colombian military bases.

"Clearly commerce with Venezuela is never going to be what it was in the past," Sergio Diaz Granados, Colombia's Minister for Trade, Industry and Tourism, told Reuters in an interview.

"The Venezuela that we're going to work with in the coming years is very distinct from the one (Colombia) has worked with in the last 10 or 15 years," he said late on Tuesday.

Relations have improved since Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos took office last month -- after the former government accused Caracas of harboring leftist Colombian rebels, prompting Chavez to briefly break off diplomatic ties.

Santos and Chavez have said they will set up a commission to look into restoring bilateral commercial ties.

Colombian exports to Venezuela are expected to plummet to $1 billion this year, Bogota says, well below last year's $4 billion and $6 billion in 2008. Exports averaged around $1 billion annually between 1995 and 2000.

Granados also said Venezuelan companies had paid $72 million of an estimated $800 million owed to Colombian exporters.

PESO AND INTERVENTION

Separately, he said Colombia expected to attract more than $10 billion in foreign direct investment this year.

After the government pushes through its fiscal plans, the central bank would have room to purchase up to $9 billion and help contain the rising peso <COP=RR>, Granados said before the central bank announced that it would restart dollar purchases.

Colombia's central bank said on Wednesday it would begin purchasing at least $20 million daily for the next four months to help ease the local currency's rise. For details, see [ID:nN15145483]

"There have been other initiatives (to manage the exchange rate) such as asking the central bank for greater action once the government gets approval of its fiscal laws and it could ... ask the bank to make more effort," Granados said.

"Today the international reserves are at a maximum seven months of imports and eleven years ago they were eleven months, (so) there is room for the bank to buy at least between $7 billion and $9 billion," he said, without giving more details.

Since taking office in August, the Santos administration has proposed an ambitious set of reforms ranging from the management of oil and mining royalties, and agrarian land reform, to overhauling the health and justice systems.

Tackling a stubborn fiscal deficit is one of the main challenges for the government, especially as the country seeks to recover the investment grade rating it lost during a 1990s fiscal crisis. [ID:nN16265600] [ID:nN09190061]

"The condition (to announce the purchases of dollars) will be when the fiscal reforms are passed," Granados said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real off; Colombia peso down on  FX  plan
text:
* Colombian peso falls 1 pct on cenbank intervention plan

* Weak U.S. manufacturing data prompts regional losses

* Brazil's real down 0.4 pct; Chilean peso drops 0.2 pct

* Mexico peso strengthens 0.4 pct ahead of holiday (Adds Mexico commentary, updates prices)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Caroline Stauffer

BOGOTA/MEXICO CITY, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso fell sharply on Wednesday after authorities said they would buy dollars to curb the currency's rally while Brazil's real weakened after worse-than-expected U.S. manufacturing data.

The Colombian currency lost 0.95 percent after the country's central bank said it would start purchasing at least $20 million daily for the next four months.

"Those who were short dollars yesterday had to exit to buy at whatever price," said Camilo Perez, chief economist at Banco de Bogota in the country's capital.

Investment in Colombia's booming oil and mining sectors has led the Colombian peso to strengthen more than 10 percent this year, putting pressure on the country's exporters.

Across the rest of the region, currencies mostly sagged after a surprise drop in manufacturing activity in New York state during September. [ID:nN15143494]

Brazil's real <BRBY> shed 0.4 percent to 1.716 on the local spot market after the U.S. data, while Chile's peso <CLP=> weakened 0.18 percent to 494.60 per dollar.

Latin America, a major producer of commodities and manufactured goods, would suffer should the global economy take a turn for the worse.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.37 percent to 12.7759 per dollar ahead of a two-day holiday that begins on Thursday. The peso has been supported in recent weeks by Mexico's scheduled entry into Citigroup's WGBI World Bond Index on October 1, which could boost flows into Latin America's second largest economy.

Regarding Colombia's intervention in its exchange market, analysts at Barclays Capital expect the central bank's measures will knock up to 2 percent off the peso in the near-term.

At the same time, some analysts said the bank could not hold the currency back indefinitely.

"These types of actions can't change a currency's long-term tendency," Correval economist Daniel Velandia wrote in a report.

JAPANESE INTERVENTION

Meanwhile, Japan's decision on Wednesday to sell yen in currency markets for the first time in six years fueled debate about how the measure might affect Brazil's real.

One head currency trader at an international bank in New York said the move could prompt Japanese retail investors, who already have some of the biggest bets on the real's appreciation, to sink more money into the real.

"Retail (investors) will look at this spike as a good opportunity to add," he said.

That might put pressure on Brazil's central bank to step up its intervention efforts in the market to protect exporters.

But other market players were less convinced.

"I don't think they will add much more to the position," said Pedro Tuesta, an economist at 4Cast in Washington.

Foreigners already hold near-record bets on the future appreciation of the real, so Japan's move is unlikely to prompt a huge shift into Brazil's currency, he said. [ID:nTOE68E02W] (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: =DJ Colombian  Central Bank  Expands Arsenal To Fight Peso Surge
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's central bank appears to be expanding its arsenal to combat the appreciation of the peso, potentially making it more difficult for investors to assess the scope of the bank's presence in the currency market.

The central bank and Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry have made it known to the market that the monetary authority has an array of tools at its disposal to rein in the peso's 13% surge against the dollar so far this year. It remains to be seen, however, whether these additional weapons are sufficient to stop the peso's advance.

The central bank has traditionally purchased dollars in the spot market and then tried to neutralize the inflationary effect of putting more pesos in circulation by selling government-issued bonds, known as TES, in the secondary market to mop up liquidity. The central bank's TES portfolio served as an indicator of how long the central bank could continue buying dollars and selling TES to limit inflation, Echeverry said.

The TES held by the central bank "indicated how much fuel it had" to intervene, Echeverry said. "Some investors would see this and say that the central bank can only buy dollars for three months, so they would wait, (and) after that they would come back to the market."

"We've made that calculation very difficult," he added.

Among the possible new tools the central bank has available is the issuance of its own bonds, which along with the TES could serve to damp any excess liquidity created by the sale of pesos for dollar purchases in the spot market. Another possibility is the use of currency options or discretionary purchases in the spot market.

Echeverry, however, has declined to specify which specific tools the central bank could use.

The central bank carried out daily dollar purchases in the spot market to the tune of $1.6 billion for the first six months of 2009. That strategy will likely not be enough to stop the peso, which continues to gain against the dollar on massive inflows of direct investment into Colombia.

"The bank's intervention needs to be very smart to have any real effect on the market," said Julian Cardenas, a currency analyst with local brokerage firm Corredores Asociados. "It appears that they are examining a combination of mechanisms" to curb the peso, he added.

The central bank disappointed several economists and analysts who had expected it would announce the start of its currency intervention at its policy meeting last month. The bank's board of directors, which includes Echeverry, is slated to meet again on Sept. 23.

A potential intervention, even with additional tools, is unlikely to be sufficient to reverse the peso's gains, said Cardenas. A surge in foreign direct investment, which is expected to reach $10 billion this year, is behind the peso's strength. On Monday, the peso traded at COP1,791.3 a dollar, its strongest since October 2009.

The peso's strength has raised the specter of capital controls, which in the past has failed to curb the peso's appreciation. The risk of capital controls is climbing because of the peso's strength, currency strategist Win Thin, with Brown Brothers Harriman, wrote in a research note.

For others, however, that remains unlikely. "They have other alternatives and using capital controls could be damaging at a time when the country wants foreign investment," Cardenas said.

* Colombia's peso, Peru's sol touch new two-year highs

* Brazil's real at 2010 high after China data

* Mexican peso gains more modest 0.5 pct (Adds details, Colombia peso, commentary; changes dateline)

By Caroline Stauffer and Nelson Bocanegra

MEXICO CITY/BOGOTA, Sept 13 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies posted sharp gains on Monday, boosted by better-than-expected factory data from China, new global banking rules and increasing risk appetite.

"Fundamental factors are aligning for equity market strength and that's helping risk sentiment for Latin American currencies," said Vassili Serebriakov, currency strategist at Wells Fargo in New York.

Colombia's peso reached a new two-year high of 1,791.3 per dollar as traders said government intervention to curb the currency's appreciation looked less likely.

"People are increasingly more aware of the limited space the central bank has to intervene," said Diego Camacho, chief economist at brokerage Acciones de Colombia in Bogota.

Chile's peso traded at its strongest in eight months on Monday, bidding at 494.5 per dollar.

The country's economy has recovered much faster than expected from the effects of a devastating earthquake in February, pushing the central bank to raise interest rates to curb inflation.

Economists widely expect the bank to raise its benchmark rate by 50 basis points to 2.50 percent at its Sept. 16 policy meeting.

"Latin America is considered a commodity export region and any possibility that commodity prices will remain strong is beneficial for Latin America's currencies," said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at 4Cast.

The Peruvian sol <PEN=PE> also hit a fresh two-year high on Monday, gaining 0.36 percent to 2.7880 per dollar.

Peru may be forced to slow its pace of interest rate hikes, despite rampant growth, for fear of fueling the recent rally of its currency, said Morgan Stanley economist Daniel Volberg. [ID:nN13202817]

MEXICAN PESO TRAILS BEHIND

The Brazilian real <BRBY> strengthened for the ninth straight day on Monday to its strongest level since Dec. 4 2009, gaining 0.23 percent to 1.714 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

China overtook the United States last year to become Brazil's main trading partner. Mexico, Latin America's second largest economy, on the other hand sends roughly 80 percent of its exports to the United States.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> strengthened 0.47 percent on Monday to 12.8778 per dollar, retreating slightly from gains made earlier in the session.

The peso posted its best performance in three weeks but failed to break monthly records like its regional counterparts.

"There have been some question marks over Mexico compared to say Chile, which has been exceptionally strong," Serebriakov in New York said. "Concerns over the U.S. slowdown have weighed on Mexico and its currency has been underperforming somewhat." title: Colombian Stocks Climb 1.5% Tracking US Gains; Peso Weakens
text:
CARTAGENA, Colombia (Dow Jones)--Colombian stocks moved higher Friday, boosted by the surge in U.S. markets, while the peso weakened slightly on expectations that the central bank will intervene to curb the currency's appreciation.

The benchmark IGBC stock index rose 1.51% to 13,904 points. The index tracked the gains in New York, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average posting a midday increase of 125 points, or 1.3%, to 10,111 points on reassurances by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke that the central bank was ready to take actions to spur a faltering economic recovery.

In Colombia, shares of state oil firm Ecopetrol SA (ECOPETROL.BO) climbed 1.33% to COP3,435.

The peso, meanwhile, weakened slightly to COP1,817.4 from COP1,816 a day earlier. On Thursday, Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said the central bank was "worried" by the appreciation of the peso, which has gained 11% against the dollar this year.

The central bank didn't announce any plans last week to buy dollars in the spot market. The bank bought $1.6 billion in the first six months of the year in a bid to tame the currency's appreciation. Some analysts believe that the central bank could soon carry out similar interventions in the spot market.

The yield on Colombia's benchmark 2020 bond stood at 7.130% compared to 7.179% a day earlier.

-By Darcy Crowe, Dow Jones Newswires; (58) 314 298 3277; darcy.crowe@dowjones.com [ 08-27-10 1517ET ]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico, Colombia pesos hit by US housing data
text:
* Surprisingly large drop in U.S. housing data weighs

* Mexican peso hits seven-week low

* Weak markets ease intervention concerns in Colombia (Recasts, updates prices)

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Aug 24 (Reuters) - A surprisingly big drop in U.S. housing sales reported on Tuesday weighed on the currencies of Mexico and Colombia, the two Latin American economies that could suffer the most from slowing growth in the United States.

Sales of U.S. existing homes in July fell to their slowest pace in 15 years, AN industry group reported. For details, see [ID:nN24249810]

Mexico's peso slumped to its weakest since July 7.

"This was another disappointing number for the markets and it provides more signs that, definitely, in the United States the economy is slowing down," said Gabriel Casillas, an economist at JPMorgan in Mexico City.

The United States is the top trading partner of both Mexico and Colombia, making them the most vulnerable in the region to a decrease in U.S. demand for their exports.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> lost 0.32 percent to 12.9705 per U.S. dollar. The peso briefly traded above the psychological level of 13 per dollar before paring losses.

Colombia's peso <COP=STFX> lost 0.31 percent to bid at 1,819 per dollar. Speculation has been mounting that Colombia's central bank could wade into currency markets to stem sharp gains in the currency.

However, growing fears of a U.S. slowdown could help weaken the Colombian currency and allow the central bank to hold off on intervention plans, analysts said.

"If the markets, particularly in the United States, are preforming badly, they may be able to delay announcing something," said David Beker, head of Latin American fixed income strategy at Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch in New York.

BRAZIL, CHILE RECOVER

The Brazilian real <BRBY> firmed 0.11 percent to bid at 1.763 per dollar on the local spot market, recovering from a one-month low hit earlier in the session.

Traders in Sao Paulo said exporters had made the most of the morning's jitters to buy the Brazilian currency at cheap levels, which helped cap losses.

Foreign investors may also have been tempted to buy the Brazilian currency at that level in order to buy local bonds and take advantage of Brazil's relatively high interest rates, analysts said.

The real has also been boosted by optimism over inflows, partly due to the upcoming massive share offering by Brazil's state-run oil company, Petrobras.

"When the dollar was at a strong level, that ended up attracting inflows," said Jose Carlos Amado, a currency trader at the Renascenca brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed a slight 0.06 percent to bid at 504.20 per dollar.

The head of Chile's central bank said the peso was trading in line with current fundamentals, dampening concerns of imminent intervention following sharp gains in the Chilean currency. [ID:nN24252365]

Bond spreads indicated that investors had become more wary of the region's higher-risk assets following the U.S. data.

Yield spreads between emerging market bonds and U.S. Treasuries, a key gauge of risk aversion, widened 15 basis points to 283 basis points, according to the JPMorgan EMBI+ index <11EMJ>.

The spread on Brazilian bonds was at the widest level since late last month, rising 11 basis points to 212. (Additional reporting by Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo and Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso sinks, Colombia unit firms
text:
* Mexico peso hit by weak retail, bomb threat scare

* Colombia central bank holds trigger on intervention

* Mexico peso weakens 1.24 pct, Colombia unit adds 0.43

* Brazil's real slips 0.4 pct, tracking U.S. markets (Recasts, changes byline and dateline, updates prices)

By Jean Luis Arce and Nelson Bocanegra

MEXICO CITY/BOGOTA Aug 23 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso sank to a one-month low on Monday, hurt by surprisingly weak June retail sales data while Colombia's peso firmed in relief the central bank did not begin intervening in the currency market.

Mexico's June retail sales report undermined hopes that consumer demand will offset slowing growth in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner. [ID:nN23157622]

June retail sales fell 0.77 percent compared with May, and only grew 1.5 percent year-on-year, compared with expectations of a 4.1 percent rise.

"That's a sharp slowdown and doesn't help for consumers and it doesn't tell us a good story in terms of consumption, which is what we expect to recover in the coming months," said Italo Lombardi, a strategist at BNP Paribas in New York.

The Mexican currency extended already steep losses on reports of a bomb threat to the stock exchange in Mexico City, which officials later said was a false alarm. [ID:nN23212566]

Rising violence related to the government's battle against drug cartels has made the peso more sensitive to news related to security concerns.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> sunk to its weakest since July 20 against the dollar, losing 1.2 percent to 12.9075 per dollar.

INTERVENTION RELIEF

Colombia's peso firmed on Monday, outperforming the region's currencies, after the country's central bank surprised investors late Friday by not announcing measures to curb the peso's recent rally.

Investment in Colombia's booming oil and mining sectors has caused the peso to strengthen about 13 percent this year, putting huge pressure on the country's exporters.

The peso <COP=STFX> bid 0.43 percent stronger to 1,813.40 per dollar.

However, traders and analysts were still cautious and expected the central bank could move to intervene if the dollar-peso exchange rate fell much below 1,800 per dollar.

"The trend is moderate, since traders still expect an announcement from the central bank in the coming days," said Banco de Bogota in a report.

Venezuela's announcement late last week that it would pay Colombian companies $200 million to compensate after a trade dispute also lifted the peso, said Karen Alfonso, head of economic research at the Afin brokerage in Bogota. [ID:nN20166203]

The Chilean peso, which has also been under pressure due to intervention threats, bid down a slight 0.1 percent at 504.50 per dollar.

Analysts doubt Chile will implement major dollar purchases to keep its currency from appreciating. However, the government could slow the pace at which it repatriates dollars from copper sales.

Brazil's real <BRBY> shed 0.4 percent to bid at 1.765 per dollar.

Traders in Sao Paulo said the currency was taking its lead from Wall Street due to the absence of key U.S. economic data -- firming in the morning as U.S. stocks gained but trading weaker in the afternoon when the major U.S. equity indexes turned negative.

However, the real was trading at its strongest level against the Mexican peso <BRLMXN=R> in over a month. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson and in Sao Paulo and Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Colombia  peso up as c.bank eschews  intervention
text:
* Colombia peso gains 1 pct after central bank statement

* Mexican peso posts weekly losses due to U.S. concerns

* Slowing inflation backs bets of no more hikes in Brazil (Recasts; adds comments, byline; previous dateline SAO PAULO/BOGOTA)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Michael O'Boyle

BOGOTA/MEXICO CITY, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso firmed sharply on Friday after the central bank refrained from introducing any measures to stem the currency's strong gains as many had expected.

The Colombian peso surged 1 percent to bid at 1,803 per dollar in so-called "next day" trade, compared with its official close <COP=STFX> before the central bank decision.

The central bank left interest rates on hold on Friday. While policy-makers said they were studying possible intervention measures, they did not announce any concrete actions, as widely expected. [ID:nN20139133]

"Independent of what is happening in external markets, we are going to see a rise in the peso at the start of next week," said Santiago Melo, an analyst with brokerage Alianza Valores.

Huge inflows into the Andean country's mining and oil sectors and confidence Colombia will soon regain its investment grade credit rating have boosted the peso by around 12 percent since early May.

The strength of the Colombia peso is crimping profits from the country's exporters of goods like flowers and manufactured products.

The central bank said the peso's strength stemmed from factors like improved trade and foreign direct investment, which suggests policy-makers may not implement an aggressive intervention strategy, analysts said.

However, the bank, known as Banrep, may act if the pace of appreciation increases.

"We think that even if Banrep seems willing to tolerate an appreciation trend as long as it seems warranted by macroeconomic conditions, it seems unwilling to allow for this appreciation to be excessively fast or sharp," wrote Barclays Capital analysts Roberto Melzi and Jimena Zuniga in a note.

Melzi and Zuniga expect Colombia's peso to firm to 1700 per dollar by year end.

BRAZIL SLIPS ON PETROBRAS, INFLATION

Fears over slowing U.S. growth, following weak data on jobs and manufacturing on Thursday, weighed on Brazil's real and Mexico's peso.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> lost 0.33 percent to 12.7525 per U.S. dollar. The country's central bank also held its main lending rate at 4.5 percent as expected, in an effort to stimulate growth. [ID:nN20137407]

U.S. slowdown concerns often weigh the most weigh on Mexico, since it sends most of its exports to its northern neighbor. The Mexican peso lost 0.24 percent during the week.

Uncertainty over the timing of the upcoming share offering by Brazil's state-run oil company Petrobras, expected to bring vast amounts of dollars to Brazil, has also hit the real. [ID:nN19264213]

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said on Friday the government is maintaining a September target date for Petrobras' capitalization plan.

On the local spot market, the real <BRBY> weakened 0.17 percent to bid at 1.758 per dollar. It still gained close to 0.7 percent for the week. [ID:nN20135046]

An unexpected drop in Brazil's consumer prices in the month to mid-August added to signs that growth in Latin America's largest economy is slowing more than previously forecast. [ID:nN20125845]

Yields plunged on Brazilian interest rate futures <0#DIJ:> as investors bet the country's central bank would be less likely to raise the cost of borrowing over the coming months.

The market shows traders expect no rate hike at the conclusion of the central bank's next meeting on September 1, and are betting on no rate increases next year either.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL>, which has also been hit by recent threats of intervention, reversed early losses to firm more than 0.66 percent at a bid of 504.00 per dollar. The currency gained almost 1.1 percent during the week, boosted by prospects for solid growth and further interest rate hikes as the country rebuilds from a major earthquake. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Colombia and Chile's pesos soar, c.banks eyed
text:
* Traders test out intervention threats across region

* Colombia's peso jumps by most in three months

* Chile's peso at strongest in seven months

* Brazil's real firms 0.11 pct; Mexican peso adds 0.62 pct (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Michael O'Boyle

BOGOTA/MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Latin American currencies strengthened Tuesday after data suggested the U.S. economy will keep growing, while solid debt auctions in Europe supported bids for riskier assets.

Colombia's peso jumped by the most in three months and Chile's peso hit a seven-month high, while the currencies of Mexico and Brazil firmed to one-week highs.

A 1 percent rise in U.S. industrial output for July suggested the economy of the United States had enough strength to support economic expansion in the region. U.S. producer prices also rose last month, calming fears of deflation.

"The fact that U.S. industrial production continues to advance is good news since this is the sector behind Mexico's recovery," said Luis Flores, an economist at brokerage IXE in Mexico City.

Mexico's rebound last year from deep recession was fueled by manufacturing exports. Many of Mexico's factories supply U.S. plants.

Mexico's peso gained 0.62 percent to 12.59 per dollar, gaining ground for the fourth straight session.

The United States is also Colombia's top trading partner, and Colombia's peso bid 1.52 percent stronger at 1807.00 per dollar. The currency is heading back toward a two-year high hit last week.

One trader in New York said that the Colombian peso had been boosted in early trading by a huge inflow from a dealer based in the city.

Also lifting demand for emerging market assets, Irish and Spanish bond auctions yielded solid results, easing concerns about Europe's debt troubles.

INTERVENTION LOOMS

Investors are buying Colombian bonds based on expectations that the country will soon regain its investment grade credit rating under an ambitious reform agenda set by the country's new president, Juan Manuel Santos.

Investors have flocked to Latin America's higher-yielding debt, strengthening currencies, due to expectations that slow U.S. growth will keep returns on U.S. Treasuries at record lows.

But that is raising the specter of intervention across the region as policy-makers look to protect exporters and prevent the formation of bubbles in the market.

The Brazilian real bid 0.11 percent stronger at 1.753, paring gains after hitting the psychologically important level of 1.75 reais per U.S. dollar. Analysts think the central bank could aggressively step up intervention if this level is broken for an extended period.

"There is a certain apprehension in the market about betting against the U.S. dollar at this level, which is lending very strong support to the American currency," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist for CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo.

One way that this level might be broken, he said, is if a mass of dollars flows into the country. Weekly central bank reports on dollar flows -- the latest of which is due on Wednesday -- have shown dollars starting to flow back into Brazil after flowing out during June and most of July.

Chile's government has also threatened to intervene in markets last week following a rapid rise in the country's peso, but traders have continued to test the resolve of the authorities.

Chile's peso was bid 0.66 percent firmer at 502.00 per dollar, hitting a fresh seven-month high. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson and Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo, Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; editing by Todd Eastham)

Chilean peso hits five-month high after rate hike

* Colombian peso hurt by intervention talk

* Rise in early August U.S. consumer confidence supports

* Mexican peso firms 0.06 pct, Brazil's real up 0.17 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso weakened sharply on Friday on fears of government market intervention, while Chile's peso reversed early gains one day after an interest rate hike.

Colombia's peso sank for a second straight session on concerns local authorities will intervene in the foreign exchange markets to cool sharp currency gains that are hurting local exporters. The peso <COP=STFX> shed 0.51 percent to 1,835.70 per dollar.

The currency pulled back about 1.6 percent after hitting a two-year intraday high in the previous session after Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos met with central bank officials to discuss the peso's strong appreciation.

"The official rhetorical intervention finally pushed the Colombian peso into defensive mode," wrote Enrique Alvarez, head of research at consultancy IDEAglobal in New York.

The Colombian currency has gained about 11 percent since early May, boosted by investment flows into the country's oil and mining industries -- also drawing speculative traders.

Analysts think Colombia could reinstate daily dollar purchases that expired in June, but that would do little more than slow the pace of gains.

Chile's peso hit a five-month high Friday, a day after the country's central bank raised interest rates, but the currency gave up ground as traders locked in gains ahead of the expected rate hike.

Late Thursday, Chile's central bank raised its benchmark interest rate to 2 percent, in line with expectations as the economy bounces back from a devastating earthquake. For more, see [ID:nN12145806]

Chile's peso's <CLP=CL> opened at its strongest level since early March, but reversed early gains to bid flat at 509.50 per dollar.

The country's currency has firmed about 7 percent since the end of June. Chilean President Sebastian Pinera hinted Thursday the government could cash in less dollar revenues from copper sales to offset the flows into Chilean assets. [ID:nN12124343]

But analysts looked for the currency to firm further on expectations of more interest rate hikes by the central bank, which is seen taking its benchmark rate to 3.75 percent by year-end. [ID:nN12129420]

BOND DEMAND

U.S. consumer sentiment inched up in early August from July, providing support to Mexico's peso and Brazil's real [ID:N13180040]

The data came after another report showed retail sales rebounded in July and eased concerns about the slowdown in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner and a major influence on the region.

But analysts said the Mexican peso would be far more sensitive to any negative data, given concerns of renewed recession after more signs of a slowdown in U.S. growth.

"Private consumption is a very important issue," said Daniela Blancas, a strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City. "This is the main worry about economies, above all in the United States."

Flows into Mexican peso bonds have also been boosting the currency, following a decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve to continue buying Treasury bonds and hold down its benchmark interest rate at its near-zero level for an extended period.

Mexico's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> bid down 1 basis point to 6.32 percent trading close to a record low hit in the previous session. Mexican bonds have been posting record lows since May.

The meager yields on U.S. Treasuries are giving investors more reason to buy higher-yielding emerging market debt.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> hit a session high of 12.6825 per U.S. dollar after the U.S. consumer confidence data, but pulled back to trade at 12.7235 per U.S. dollar, 0.06 percent firmer.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.17 percent stronger at 1.769 per dollar. (Additional reporting by Simon Gardner in Santiago and Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; editing by Jeffrey Benkoe)

title: Colombia may restart dlr buys to crimp peso-experts
text:
* Foreign investment keeps upward pressure on local peso

* Currency nears highest point since October

By Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, July 6 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank may restart buying U.S. dollars sooner rather than later to put the breaks on a strengthening peso currency that has neared its highest point in nine months, analysts said on Tuesday.

Strong foreign direct investment has seen the peso <COP=RR> firm nearly 10 percent over the last 12 months, and the rise has sparked an outcry from exporters who pay their costs in the local currency but receive greenbacks from sales.

Central Bank Governor Jose Dario Uribe said last week that the entity would not renew its program to purchase $20 million a day after June 30, but the monetary boss left the door open to resume purchases in the future. For details, see [ID:nLDE66014E]

With the peso so strong, experts say the moment is right for the central bank to accumulate more international reserves, which reached highs of $26.4 billion at the end of June.

"They will buy due to exchange rate conditions and due to the announcement by the finance minister, and above all because of the conditions to accumulate international reserves," said Julian Cardenas, head of research at Corredores Asociados.

The peso neared its highest level since October on Tuesday in response to a finance ministry announcement last week that the government would borrow an additional $1 billion from foreign sources. [ID:nN02205834]

"We hope that the dollar buying mechanism is reactivated before any other (exchange rate) measures," said Camilo Perez, head of economic research at Banco de Bogota.

The Andean nation said last month it expected investment in its oil and mining sectors to be $62 billion between 2008 and 2015, 24 percent higher than its previous estimate. [ID:nN21242394]

SPACE FOR APPRECIATION?

"It's a decision that depends in part on the velocity and magnitude of the appreciation. In my opinion, there's space for an appreciation of the peso before generating the need to intervene," said Jimena Zuniga of Barclays Capital.

Colombia has seen its economy rebound this year after falling due to the global economic crisis in 2009, and has upped its 2010 growth to 3 percent from a previous estimate of 2.5 percent. [ID:nN15262841]

A main challenge for President-elect Juan Manuel Santos -- who takes office in August -- will be to manage inflows of greenbacks into extractive sectors in Latin America's No. 4 oil producer and the world's fifth largest coal exporter.

Santos says he wants to create an overseas fund to help manage revenue from oil and mining.

In the past, governments have had to give subsidies to the export sector to avoid job cuts in a nation with one of the region's highest unemployment rates.

Exporters have called on the central bank to keep buying the U.S. currency to halt the peso's rise.

"It's fundamental to maintain the intervention at least for the rest of the year and increment it to avoid a major reassessment of the existing (rate)," said Augusto Solano, president of Colombia's flowers exporters association. (Writing by Jack Kimball; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

title: Colombia  Central Bank  Threat To Buy Dollars Helped Halt Peso Rise
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia's central bank did not need to intervene in the currency markets to halt the rise of the peso--the mere threat of intervention was enough.

Colombia's central bank bought government bonds worth 3 trillion Colombian pesos (US$1.53 billion) towards the end of 2009, the bank said in a statement Tuesday.

In late October, the bank announced it would spend COP3 trillion on dollars and government bonds to meet seasonal demand for liquidity. The bank spent the entire sum on bonds.

"They didn't need to buy a single dollar," said Felipe Munoz, who manages a fund of dollar-bonds with local brokerage Corredores Asociados. "Just the threat was enough to give them all the devaluation they needed."

When the bank announced its bond and dollar purchase program, the peso was approaching COP1,800 against the dollar, provoking complaints from exporters who said the strong peso was making it difficult for them to compete. The announcement helped bring to an end a peso rally where the currency gained 41% in about six months.

Buying bonds rather than dollars had been a better use of the bank's ammunition because it helped reduce long-term interest rates, said Alberto Bernal, a Miami-based debt strategist with investment bank Bulltick Capital Markets.

"Monetarily speaking it's the same, but buying bonds has a more direct effect on the long end of the (yield) curve. So you achieve one goal which is to flatten the yield curve by buying bonds, the effect is more direct," Bernal said.

Lowering long-term yields would help the housing market, among other benefits, Bernal added.

The yield on Colombia's benchmark peso-denominated government bond maturing in 2020 fell to 8.022% by mid-November, from 8.59% when the bank made its announcement. However, it then began to rise again, and ended the year at 8.467%.

The peso closed at COP1,962.15 on Tuesday, from COP1,963.50 on January 8.

Munoz of Corredores Asociados said the peso could appreciate to COP1,850 against the dollar in the coming weeks, as the Colombian government trades dollars it raised by selling dollar-denominated bonds for pesos.

The Colombian treasury placed the equivalent of $2.5 billion in bonds on international markets in 2009, of which $2 billion will be spent in 2010. Since most government spending is in pesos, the treasury sells dollars for pesos on the foreign exchange market.

title: DJ  Colombia  Ctrl Bk Didn't  Intervene  In  Forex  Market In Sep
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--The Colombian Central Bank didn't intervene in the foreign exchange market in September, the monetary authority said in a statement.

In the first nine months of the year, the monetary authority bought a net $170.9 million, according to the statement released Tuesday.

So far this year, the central bank bought $539.4 million through put options to slow the peso's appreciation and in January and February the bank had sold $368.5 million through call options to control the peso weakness.

The peso, which had hit its strongest level in nine years in June last year, weakened after the Lehman Brothers failure prompted international investors to leave Colombia.

Since early March, though, the peso has strengthened 43% against the dollar.

The peso ended Wednesday at COP1,827.5 to the U.S. dollar.

-By Inti Landauro, Dow Jones Newswires; 571-6107044 Ext 1131; colombia@dowjones.com

title: Colombia  Ctrl Bk Didn't  Intervene  In  Forex  Mkt In November
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--The Colombian central bank didn't intervene on the foreign exchange market in November, the bank said Tuesday in a statement.

During the first ten months of the year, the monetary authority bought $2.38 billion through put options and direct purchases in the spot market in a bid to slow the peso's appreciation.

The peso hit its strongest level in nine years in June, threatening the competitiveness of the country's exporters. However, the peso has depreciated 28% since hitting its strongest level in late June.

Meanwhile, the central bank sold $235 million in October through call options to slow the peso's depreciation.

The Colombian peso weakened 8.4% in October as a result of the global financial slowdown.

-By Diana Delgado, Dow Jones Newswires; 571-6107044 ext 1132; diana.delgado@dowjones.com [ 12-09-08 1726ET ]

title: Colombia  cenbank suspends  forex interventions
text:
BOGOTA, June 26 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank said it suspended its program of foreign exchange interventions, designed to control peso volatility, starting on Thursday and continuing through August 8.

The bank issued a statement on Thursday announcing the suspension, which followed its decision on Friday to buy $20 million per day in the foreign exchange market in a bid to control the rise of the peso.

The announcement of the suspension of the anti-volatility intervention program prompted selling of the peso, which sank 3.9 percent to 1,847 to the dollar, extending deep losses for the week. (Reporting by Nelson Bocanegra, writing by Hugh Bronstein; Editing by Jonathan Oatis)

We prepare our audited financial statements on a yearly basis and quarterly unaudited financial statements, each in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("GAAP"). Currently, the non-GAAP financial measures that we disclose are Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA Margin, Adjusted Net Income and Adjusted Net Income Margin.

Adjusted EBITDA is calculated by adding net income (loss), income (loss) attributable to non-controlling interest, income taxes, interest expense, depreciation and amortization, extinguishment of debt, certain non-recurring expenses and foreign currency transaction losses (gains), as further adjusted for the other line items reflected in the reconciliation table set forth in footnote 2 of "Prospectus Supplement Summary-Summary Historical Consolidated Financial Data". Adjusted EBITDA Margin is calculated by dividing Adjusted EBITDA by our net revenues.

Adjusted Net Income is calculated by adding net income (loss), income (loss) attributable to non-controlling interest, foreign currency transaction losses (gains), cashless deferred cost of financing, loss (gain) from change in fair value of warrant liability, certain non-recurring expenses and the tax impact of adjustments at statutory rates, as further adjusted for the other line items reflected in the reconciliation table set forth in footnote 3 of "Prospectus Supplement Summary-Summary Historical Consolidated Financial Data". Adjusted Net Income Margin is calculated by dividing Adjusted Net Income by our net revenues.

Our use of Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA Margin, Adjusted Net Income, and Adjusted Net Income Margin may not be comparable to similarly titled measures reported by other companies because not all companies and analysts calculate these metrics in the same manner. Also, in the future, we may disclose different non-GAAP financial measures in order to help our investors more meaningfully evaluate and compare our future results of operations to our previously reported results of operations.

We believe that the GAAP financial measure most directly comparable to Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Net Income is net income. In calculating Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Net Income, we exclude from net income the financial items that we believe should be separately identified to provide additional analysis of the financial components of the day-to-day operation of our business. We have outlined below the type and scope of these exclusions and the material limitations on the use of these non-GAAP financial measures as a result of these exclusions. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Net Income are not measurements of financial performance under GAAP and should not be considered as a measure of liquidity, as an alternative to net income (loss), operating income, or as an indicator of any other measure of performance derived in accordance with GAAP. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Net Income are used by management to internally measure our operating and management performance and by investors as a supplemental financial measure to evaluate the performance of our business that, when viewed with our GAAP results and the accompanying reconciliation, we believe provides additional information that is useful to gain an understanding of the factors and trends affecting our business. We believe the disclosure of Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Net Income helps investors meaningfully evaluate and compare our performance from quarter to quarter and from year to year. We also believe Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Net Income are measures of our ongoing operating performance because the isolation of non-cash charges, such as depreciation and amortization, and non-operating items, such as interest and income taxes, provides additional information about our cost structure, and, over time, helps track our operating progress. DISCLOSURE REGARDING FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROLS AND EXCHANGE RATES IN COLOMBIA

Since September 1999, the Central Bank of Colombia has allowed the Colombian peso to float freely, intervening only when there are steep variations in the Colombian peso's value relative to the U.S. dollar. This intervention mechanism is only used to prevent undesirable fluctuations in the exchange rate and to accumulate or reduce the amount of the international reserves, in accordance with guidelines set forth by the Colombian Central Bank's board of directors. The Colombian Superintendence of Finance, or SFC, calculates the representative market rate based on the weighted averages of the buy/sell foreign exchange rates quoted daily by certain financial institutions for the purchase and sale of foreign currency. Although the Colombian peso is allowed to float freely, the Central Bank of Colombia is authorized to intervene in the exchange market through the following mechanisms: buying and selling foreign currencies in the spot market or through call or put options at market rates through an auction process and selling foreign currencies through swap agreements through an auction process at the rates determined by the Central Bank.

The general principles of Colombia's foreign exchange and international investment regulations are contained in Law 9 of 1991 (as amended from time to time), Decree 1068 of 2015, External Resolution 1 of 2018 from the Board of Directors of the Colombian Central Bank and External Circular DCIP - 83 of August 27, 2021, of the Central Bank. Law 9 of 1991 and External Resolution 1 of 2018 established two types of markets for foreign currency exchange: (1) the free market, which consists of all foreign currencies originated in sales of services, donations, remittances and all other inflows or outflows that do not need to be mandatorily channeled through the FX market (as defined below), and (2) the controlled market, or the FX market, which consists of (a) all foreign currencies originated in operations considered to be operations of the FX market, which may only be transacted through FX intermediaries (as defined below) or registered compensation accounts, or (b) foreign currencies voluntarily channeled through the FX market. Compensation accounts are accounts opened abroad by Colombian residents (individuals and legal entities), which are registered with the Central Bank in order to channel foreign currency originated in controlled operations of the FX market or to receive and/or pay in foreign currencies transactions between Colombian residents (individuals and legal entities).

Under Colombian foreign exchange regulations, FX intermediaries are entities authorized to enter into foreign exchange transactions to convert Colombian pesos into foreign currencies or foreign currencies into Colombian pesos. In addition, there are certain requirements and obligations established by Colombian law and by the board of directors of the Central Bank in order to transfer currency into or out of Colombia.

The Colombian government and the Central Bank of Colombia may also limit the remittance of dividends and/or investments of foreign currency received by Colombian residents whenever the international reserves fall below an amount equal to three months of imports or may impose certain mandatory deposit requirements in connection with foreign-currency denominated loans obtained by Colombian residents.

RISK FACTORS

An investment in our ordinary shares involves significant risks. Before purchasing any ordinary shares, you should carefully consider and evaluate all of the information included in this prospectus supplement and the accompanying prospectus, including the risk factors and uncertainties set forth below, as updated by annual, quarterly and other reports and documents we file with the SEC after the date of this prospectus supplement. Our business, financial position, results of operations or liquidity could be adversely affected by any of these risks. The risks and uncertainties we describe are not the only ones facing us. Additional risks and uncertainties not presently known to us, which we cannot adequately evaluate or that we currently deem immaterial, may also impair our business or operations.

Risks Related to Our Business Operations

We operate in competitive markets and our business could suffer if we are unable to adequately address potential downward pricing pressures and other factors that may reduce operating margins.

The principal markets that we serve are highly competitive. Competition is based primarily on the precision and range of achievable tolerances, quality, price and the ability to meet delivery schedules dictated by customers. Our competition comes from companies of various sizes, some of which have greater financial and other resources than we do and some of which have more established brand names in the markets that we serve. We currently compete with companies such as Viracon (a subsidiary within the Apogee Enterprises Inc. Group), PGT, Cardinal Glass and Oldcastle Glass among others in the United States and companies such as Vitro, Vitelco and others in Colombia and Latin America. Any of these competitors may foresee the course of market development more accurately than we will, develop products that are superior to ours, have the ability to produce similar products at a lower cost than us or adapt more quickly than we can to new technologies or evolving customer requirements. Increased competition could force us to lower our prices or to offer additional services at a higher cost to us, which could reduce gross profit and net income. Accordingly, we may not be able to adequately address potential downward pricing pressures and other factors, which may adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.

Failure to maintain the performance, reliability and quality standards required by our customers could have a materially negative impact on our financial condition and results of operations.

If our products or services have performance, reliability or quality problems, or products are installed with incompatible glazing materials, we may experience additional warranty and service expenses, reduced or canceled orders, diminished pricing power, higher manufacturing or installation costs or delays in the collection of accounts receivable. Additionally, performance, reliability, or quality claims from our customers, with or without merit, could result in costly and time-consuming litigation that could require significant time and attention of management and involve significant monetary damages that could negatively affect our financial results.

The volatility of the cost of raw materials used to produce our products could materially adversely affect the results of our operations in the future.

The cost of raw materials included in our products, including aluminum extrusion and polyvinyl butyral, are subject to significant fluctuations derived from changes in price or volume. A variety of factors over which we have no control, including global demand for aluminum, fluctuations in oil prices, speculation in commodities futures and the creation of new laminates or other products based on new technologies, impact the cost of raw materials which we purchase for the manufacture of our products.

We quote our prices of aluminum products based on the price of aluminum in the London Metal Exchange plus a premium, and our suppliers of glass and polyvinyl butyral provide us with price lists that are updated annually, thus reducing the risk of changing prices for orders in the short term. While we may attempt to minimize the risk from severe price fluctuations by entering into aluminum forward contracts to hedge these fluctuations in the purchase price of aluminum extrusion we use in production, substantial, prolonged upward trends in aluminum prices could significantly increase the cost of our aluminum needs and have an adverse impact on the results of our operations. If we are not able to pass on significant cost increases to our customers, our results in the future may be negatively affected including without limitation by a delay between the cost increases and price increases in our products. Accordingly, the price volatility of raw materials could adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations in the future.

We depend on third-party suppliers for our raw materials and any failure of such third-party suppliers in providing raw materials could negatively affect our ability to manufacture our products.

Our ability to offer a wide variety of products to our customers depends on our receipt of adequate material supplies from manufacturers and other suppliers. It is possible in the future that our competitors or other suppliers may create products based on new technologies that are not available to us or are more effective than our products at surviving hurricane-force winds and wind-borne debris or that they may have access to products of a similar quality at lower prices. Although in some instances we have agreements with our suppliers, these agreements are generally terminable by us or the supplier counterparties on limited notice. We have a fixed set of maximum price rates, and from those prices we negotiate with the supplier of the material depending on the project. We source raw materials and glass necessary to manufacture our products from a variety of domestic and foreign suppliers. During the year ended December 31, 2022, one supplier accounted for more than 10% of total raw material purchases, at 14% of total raw material purchases. Failures of third-party suppliers to provide raw materials to us in the future could have an adverse impact on our operating results or our ability to manufacture our products.

We rely on third-party transportation, which subjects us to risks and costs that we cannot control, and which risks and costs may materially adversely affect our operations.

We rely on third party trucking companies to transport raw materials to the manufacturing facilities used by each of our businesses and, to a lesser degree, to ship finished products to customers. These transport operations are subject to various hazards and risks, including extreme weather conditions, work stoppages and operating hazards, as well as interstate transportation regulations. In addition, the methods of transportation we utilize may be subject to additional, more stringent and more costly regulations in the future. If we are delayed or unable to ship finished products or unable to obtain raw materials as a result of any such new regulations or public policy changes related to transportation safety, or these transportation companies fail to operate properly, or if there were significant changes in the cost of these services due to new or additional regulations, or otherwise, we may not be able to arrange efficient alternatives and timely means to obtain raw materials or ship goods, which could result in a material adverse effect on our revenues and costs of operations. Transportation costs represent a significant part of our cost structure. If our transportation costs increased substantially, due to prolonged increases in fuel prices or otherwise, we may not be able to control them or pass the increased costs onto customers, and our profitability would be negatively impacted.

We may not realize the anticipated benefit through our joint venture with Saint-Gobain and the planned construction of a new plant as part of the joint venture may not be completed as planned.

On May 3, 2019, we acquired an approximately 25.8% minority interest in the float glass plant of Vidrio Andino Holdings S.A.S, or Vidrio Andino, a Colombia-based subsidiary of Compagnie de Saint-Gobain S.A., or Saint-Gobain, located in the outskirts of Bogota, Colombia in connection with our joint venture agreement with Saint-Gobain. We believe this joint venture has solidified our vertical integration strategy by providing us with an interest in the first stage of our production chain, while securing ample glass supply for our expected production needs. Although our glass supply has run smoothly through the date of this prospectus supplement, we may be unable to realize the planned synergies and fail to integrate some aspects of the facility's production capacity into our manufacturing process, which may have a negative impact on our financial condition. Additionally, the joint venture agreement includes plans to build a new plant in Galapa, Colombia that will be located approximately 20 miles from our primary manufacturing facility in which we will also have a 25.8% interest. The new plant will be funded with the original cash contribution made by us, operating cash flows from the Bogota plant, and debt incurred at the joint venture level that will not consolidate into our company.

Short sellers of our ordinary shares may be manipulative and may attempt to drive down the market price of ordinary shares. Short selling is the practice of selling securities that the seller does not own but rather has borrowed from a third party with the intention of buying identical securities back at a later date to return to the lender. The short seller hopes to profit from a decline in the value of the securities between the sale of the borrowed securities and the purchase of the replacement shares, as the short seller expects to pay less in that purchase than it received in the sale. As it is therefore in the short seller's best interests for the price of the stock to decline, many short sellers (sometime known as "disclosed shorts") publish, or arrange for the publication of, negative opinions regarding the relevant issuer and its business prospects to create negative market momentum and generate profits for themselves after selling a stock short. Although traditionally these disclosed shorts were limited in their ability to access mainstream business media or to otherwise create negative market rumors, the rise of the Internet and technological advancements regarding document creation, videotaping and publication by weblog (blogging) have allowed many disclosed shorts to publicly attack a company's credibility, strategy and veracity by means of so-called "research reports" that mimic the type of investment analysis performed by large Wall Street firms and independent research analysts. Issuers who have limited trading volumes and are susceptible to higher volatility levels than large-cap stocks, can be particularly vulnerable to such short seller attacks. EXECUTIVE AND DIRECTOR COMPENSATION

This section provides a detailed description of our executive compensation philosophy and practices, the factors considered by the compensation committee in setting the compensation of our executive officers and the compensation decisions that the compensation committee has made.

Overview

Our policies with respect to the compensation of our executive officers are administered by our board in consultation with our compensation committee. Our compensation policies are intended to provide for compensation that:

  ●   is sufficient to attract and retain executives of outstanding ability and potential; 
  ●   is tailored to the unique characteristics and needs of our company; 
  ●   considers individual value and contribution to our success; 
  ●   is designed to motivate our executive officers to achieve our annual and long-term goals by rewarding performance based on the attainment of those goals; 
  ●   is designed to appropriately take into account risk and reward in the context of our business environment; 
  ●   reflects an appropriate relationship between executive compensation and the creation of shareholder value; and 
  ●   is sensitive to market benchmarks. 


The compensation committee is in charge of recommending executive compensation packages to our board that meet these goals. In making decisions about executive compensation, the compensation committee relies on the experience of its members as well as subjective considerations of various factors, including individual and corporate performance, our strategic business goals, each executive's position, experience, level of responsibility, future potential and compensation paid by companies of similar size in our industry. The compensation committee sets specific key performance indicators, or KPIs, and benchmarks for annual fixed compensation or for allocations between different elements of compensation.

Our compensation committee is charged with performing an annual review of our executive officers' cash compensation and equity holdings to determine whether they provide adequate incentives and motivation to executive officers and whether they adequately compensate the executive officers relative to comparable officers in other companies. As part of this review, management submits recommendations to the compensation committee.

We believe it is important when making compensation-related decisions to be informed as to current practices of similarly situated publicly held companies in our industry. Our compensation committee stays appraised of the cash and equity compensation practices of publicly held companies in the glass and aluminum industries through the review of such companies' public reports and through other resources. The companies chosen for inclusion in any benchmarking group would have business characteristics comparable to our company, including revenues, financial growth metrics, stage of development, employee headcount and market capitalization. While benchmarking may not always be appropriate as a stand-alone tool for setting compensation due to the aspects of our business and objectives, we generally believe that gathering this information is an important part of our compensation-related decision-making process.

Consideration of Shareholder Advisory Votes on Executive Compensation

We also take into consideration our most recent shareholder advisory vote on executive compensation, commonly known as a "Say on Pay Advisory Vote", as required by Section 14A of the Exchange Act. In the last advisory vote, conducted at our annual general meeting on December 15, 2022, our compensation program was approved on an advisory basis by over 97% of the shareholders who submitted a vote at such meeting (with less than 3% of the votes being against approval or abstaining, collectively). We consider this to be a strong validation that our pay practices are firmly aligned with our shareholders' best interests. In accordance with the shareholder vote held at our 2019 annual general meeting, we conduct a Say on Pay Advisory Vote every three years. The next will be at our 2025 annual general meeting.
