Subsequently, such financial liabilities are carried at their amortized cost according to the effective interest rate method determined at initial recognition, and recognized in the results of the period during the time of amortization of the financial obligation.

Fair Value of Financial Instruments

ASC 820, Fair Value Measurements, establishes a fair value hierarchy which requires us to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs when measuring fair value. We primarily apply the market approach for financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis. Fair value is the price we would receive to sell and asset or pay to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction with a market participant at the measurement date. In the absence of active markets for identical assets or liabilities, such measurements involve developing assumptions based on market observable data and, in the absence of such data, internal information that is consistent with what market participants would use in a hypothetical transaction that occurs at the measurement date.

F-11

The standard describes three level of inputs that may be used to measure fair value:

Level 1: Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

Level 2: Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities; quoted prices in markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable by observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities.

Level 3: Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are significant to the fair value of the assets or liabilities.

See Note 15 - Hedging Activities and Fair Value Measurements.

Derivative Financial Instruments

The Company recognizes all derivative financial instruments as either assets or liabilities at fair value on the consolidated balance sheet. The unrealized gains or losses arising from changes in fair value of derivative instruments that are designated and qualify as cash flow hedges, are recorded in the consolidated statement of comprehensive income. Revenue Recognition

Our principal sources of revenue are derived from product sales, sometimes referred to as standard form sales, and supply and installation contracts, sometimes referred to as revenues from fixed price contracts. We identified one single performance obligation for both forms of sales. Revenue is recognized when control is transferred to our customers. For product sales, the performance obligations are satisfied at a point in time and control is deemed to be transferred.

Approximately 16% of the Company's consolidated net sales is generated by supply and installation contracts with customers that require the Company to design, develop, test, manufacture, and install windows according to the customers' specifications. These contracts are primarily multi-year contracts with real estate general contractors and are generally priced on a fixed-price basis and are invoiced based on contract progress.

To determine the proper revenue recognition method, the Company first evaluates each of its contractual arrangements to identify its performance obligations. A performance obligation is a promise in a contract to transfer a distinct good or service to the customer. All the Company's contracts have a single performance obligation because the promise to transfer the individual good or service is not separately identifiable from other promises within the contract and is, therefore, not distinct. These contractual arrangements either require the use of a highly specialized manufacturing process to provide goods according to customer specifications or represent a bundle of contracted goods and services that are integrated and together represent a combined output, which may include the delivery of multiple units.

These performance obligations are satisfied over time. Sales are recognized over time when control is continuously transferred to the customer during the contract. The continuous transfer of control to the customer is supported by contract clauses that provide for progress or performance-based payments. Generally, if a customer unilaterally terminates a contract, the Company has the right to receive payment for costs incurred plus a reasonable profit for products and services that do not have alternative use to the Company.

Sales are recorded using the cost-to-cost method on supply and installation contracts that include performance obligations satisfied over time. These sales are generally recorded at amounts equal to the ratio of actual cumulative costs incurred divided by total estimated costs at completion, multiplied by (i) the transaction price, less (ii) the cumulative sales recognized in prior periods.

F-12

Accounting for the sales and profits on performance obligations for which progress is measured using the cost-to-cost method involves the preparation of estimates of: (1) transaction price and (2) total costs at completion, which is equal to the sum of the actual incurred costs to date on the contract and the estimated costs to complete the contract's statement of work. Incurred costs include labor, material, and overhead and represent work performed, which corresponds with and thereby represents the transfer of ownership to the customer. Performance obligations are satisfied over time when the risk of ownership has been passed to the customer and/or services are performed. The estimated profit or loss at completion on a contract is equal to the difference between the transaction price and the total estimated cost at completion.

Contract modifications routinely occur to account for changes in contract specifications or requirements. In most cases, contract modifications are for goods or services that are not distinct and, therefore, are accounted for as part of the existing contract. Transaction price estimates include additional consideration for submitted contract modifications or claims when the Company believes it has an enforceable right to the modification or claim, the amount can be reliably estimated and its realization is reasonably assured. Amounts representing modifications accounted for as part of the existing contract are included in the transaction price and recognized as an adjustment to sales on a cumulative catch-up basis.

The Company's supply and installation contracts allow for progress payments to bill the customer as contract costs are incurred and the customer often retains a small portion of the contract price until satisfactory completion of the contractual statement of work, which is a retainage of approximately 10%. The Company records an asset for unbilled receivables due to completing more work than the progress payment schedule allows to collect at a point in time. For certain supply and installation contracts, the Company receives advance payments. Advanced payments are not considered a significant financing component because they are a negotiated contract term to ensure the customer meets its financial obligation, particularly when there are significant upfront working capital requirements. The Company records a liability for advance payments received in excess of sales recognized, which is presented as a contract liability on the balance sheet.

Revisions or adjustments to estimates of the transaction price, estimated costs at completion and estimated profit or loss of a performance obligation are often required as work progresses under a contract, as experience is gained, as facts and circumstances change and as new information is obtained, even though the scope of work required under the contract may not change. Revisions or adjustments may also be required if contract modifications occur. While there are various factors that can affect the accuracy of cost estimates related to the revision of the proper allocation of indirect labor and indirect material costs to each project, such estimates are made based on the most updated historical information and margins of those indirect costs over the associated revenues and on all relevant information associated with each specific project at any point in time. The impact of revisions in profit or loss estimates are recognized on a cumulative catch-up basis in the period in which the revisions are made. The revisions in contract estimates, if significant, can materially affect the Company's results of operations and cash flows, as well as reduce the valuations of contract assets and inventories, and in some cases result in liabilities to complete contracts in a loss position. The Company recognizes a liability for non-recurring obligations as situations considering that projects actual costs are usually adjusted to estimated costs. The Company did not recognize sales for performance obligations satisfied in prior periods during year ended December 31, 2021.

The Company's operations in Colombia are subject to the taxing jurisdiction of the Republic of Colombia. Tecnoglass LLC, Tecnoglass RE LLC, GM&P, Componenti USA LLC and ESW LLC are U.S. entities based in Florida are subject to the taxing jurisdiction of the United States. The Company accounts for income taxes using the asset and liability approach of accounting for income taxes (ASC 740 "Income Taxes"). Under this approach, deferred taxes represent the future tax consequences expected to occur when the reported amounts of assets and liabilities are recovered or paid. The provision for income taxes represents income taxes paid or payable for the current year plus the change in deferred taxes during the year. Deferred taxes result from differences between the financial and tax basis of the Company's assets and liabilities and are adjusted for changes in tax rates and tax laws when changes are enacted. For each tax jurisdiction in which the Company operates, deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset against one another and are presented as a single noncurrent amount within the consolidated balance sheets.

The Company presents deferred tax assets and liabilities net as either a non-current asset or liability, depending on the net deferred tax position. The Company recognizes the financial statement effects of uncertain income tax positions when it is more likely than not, based on the technical merits, that the position will be sustained upon examination. The Company accrues for other tax contingencies when it is probable that a liability to a taxing authority has been incurred and the amount of the contingency can be reasonably estimated. Interest accrued related to unrecognized tax and income tax related penalties are included in the provision for income taxes. The uncertain income taxes positions are recorded in "Taxes payable" in the consolidated balance sheets.

Hedging Activity

During the quarter ended September 30, 2019, we entered into several foreign currency non-delivery forward and collar contracts to hedge the fluctuations in the exchange rate between the Colombian Peso and the U.S. Dollar. Our contracts are designated as cash flow hedges since they are highly effective in offsetting changes in the cash flows attributable to forecasted Colombian Peso denominated costs and expenses.

Guidance under the Financial Instruments Topic 825 of the Codification requires us to record our hedge contracts at fair value and consider our credit risk for contracts in a liability position, and our counter-party's credit risk for contracts in an asset position, in determining fair value. We assess our counter-party's risk of non-performance when measuring the fair value of financial instruments in an asset position by evaluating their financial position, including cash on hand, as well as their credit ratings.

As of December 31, 2021, the fair value of foreign currency collar contracts was not measured since we currently do not have any open contracts, with the last settlements taking place in January and February 2021.

We assess the effectiveness of our foreign currency collar contracts by comparing the change in the fair value of the collar contracts to the change in the expected cash to be paid for the hedged item. The effective portion of the gain or loss on our foreign currency collar contracts is reported as a component of accumulated other comprehensive income and is reclassified into earnings in the same line item in the income statement as the hedged item in the same period or periods during which the transaction affects earnings. title: Mexico stays static as its  currency  plummets
text:
The Colombian and Mexican pesos are likely to remain the worst-performing currencies in emerging markets this year, after their central banks decided to stay out as both currencies continue to fall in oil prices.

Colombia's peso fell 6.7% this week, while Mexico's currency fell 5.1% as crude oil plummeted due to a price war between Saudi Arabia and Russia. While Chile's policymakers intervened in the derivatives market and Brazil resorted to currency swaps and the immediate market, officials in the region's two most affected countries remain optimistic.

Investors should also not count on the central bank intervening in Colombia, even when crude money accounts for nearly a third of the country's exports. (Photo: Bloomberg)Mexico's central bank extended the upper limit of its foreign exchange hedging program this week, but has chosen not to sell dollars until now. That was not enough to reassure markets, as falling oil prices undermined the nation's fiscal outlook. It also weighs on the currency the fact that it had surpassed most emerging market currencies in the first month of the year, when the oil crisis pushed investors out of the market at once.

Investors should also not count on the central bank intervening in Colombia, even when crude money accounts for nearly a third of the country's exports. On the rare occasions he intervened, the central bank used options to curb the rapid appreciation of the currency, not depreciation.

While the effectiveness of currency intervention is always questionable, investors are likely to favor currencies that receive additional boost from central banks as the coronavirus spreads further and investors expect news about the oil price war.

The weight debacle: how the Mexican star currency passed to the most losing

Until a few weeks, the Mexican peso was the star currency of emerging countries.Until a few weeks, the Mexican peso was the star currency of emerging countries.

Today, she's the most losing since. The reason? A massive peso sale by speculators to cover the losses of a record number of contracts betting on a mexican currency hike, experts said.

In financial slang, the peso suffered a "squeeze," the specialists explain, which began in February with the market nervousness about the coronavirus, and which was exacerbated on Sunday by the fall in oil prices.

The Mexican currency fell in the early hours of Monday to 14%, after the collapse in international crude oil prices, although it later reduced the losses to about 4%, to quote around 21 units per dollar.

The global volatility shock caused investors to sell the weight and take the profits earned up to that point to cover the losses they would have on derivative instruments.

title: Latin American  currencies  are no longer on the brink of collapse
text:
We can say it in a very low voice, but the worst may have already happened for Latin America's foreign exchange markets.

Currencies in Brazil, Chile and Colombia are reducing losses in December after falling to historic lows last month, following a wave of violent protests that threatened to depress already slow growth in the region.

Chile's weight rose 3.3%, Colombia's weight rose 1.8% and Brazil's real gained 0.5% in the first four days of the month. It may not seem like much, but it's Chile's longest winning streak since June and Colombia since September. The central bank's intervention in Chile and Brazil has played an important role, while Colombia is relieved as the protests did not get out of hand as many feared.

Of course, not all currencies have left their problems behind. The Argentine peso remains close to an all-time low amid strict monetary controls as Alberto Fernandez prepares to take over the presidency on December 10.

"There is a possibility that Latin America's foreign exchange market will continue to rebound to close this gap" between the rest of the currencies of developing countries, which surpassed the region in November, said Ilya Gofshteyn, senior macro market strategist Standard Chartered Bank in New York. "Lower liquidity at the end of the year creates unfavourable seasonal dynamics, but I would expect the BRL, MXN, COP and CLP currencies to start in 2020 with a stronger tone."

The entry Currencies of Latin America are no longer on the brink of collapse was first published in La Tercera.

title: They rule out  intervening  peso quote
text:
Colombia's central bank is not considering any exchange rate intervention measures to alleviate the depreciation of the peso, even though the currency fell to an all-time low last week, according to a member of the monetary policy committee.

The peso has lost 7.5% in the last three months, thus becoming the worst-performing currency among emerging markets after the Argentine peso, amid the slowdown in global growth, weak oil and coal prices and investors' concerns about the country's large current-account deficit.

On October 2, it surpassed the upper end of the range between 3,300 and 3,500 pesos per dollar that the bank of the Republic manager, Juan José Echavarría, has considered "comfortable".

The worrying thing would be that the depreciation of the currency was transferred to consumer prices, but there is no sign that it is happening significantly, said José Antonio Ocampo, co-director of the central bank.

No exchange rate intervention measures are being discussed within the board, Ocampo said in an interview. So far, we haven't seen any inflationary effects, which doesn't mean it can't be.

Ocampo's comments echo those of finance minister Alberto Carrasquilla, who said the nation's monetary authorities should be ready to act if there are signs of moving currency movements to consumer prices. Carrasquilla chairs the monetary policy committee board.

In August, annual inflation slowed for the first time in six months to 3.75%, alleviating concerns that consumer prices could exceed the upper limit of the target range between 2% and 4%.

title: UPDATE 1- Colombia  cenbank head rules out  intervening  if peso falls
text:
(adds more quotes, background)

By Karin Strohecker

LONDON, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Colombia has no plans to intervene in its currency markets even if the peso depreciates by 10-15 percent, central bank governor Juan Jose Echavarria told Reuters on Tuesday.

Like most emerging currencies, Colombia's peso has weakened this year as the dollar has strengthened amid steady rate rises by the U.S. Federal Reserve. But the peso's falls have been far less severe than peers in Argentina, Turkey, South Africa or Mexico.

While there are fears Colombia's big current account deficit makes it vulnerable to contagion, Echavarria ruled out intervention.

"Absolutely not, even if we have a devaluation of 10 or 15 percent," he said in an interview. "10 percent (devaluation) is no problem at all."

Echavarria acknowledged that Colombia ranked high up on the list of countries suffering from a large current account deficit as a share of gross domestic product, together with peers Argentina, Turkey and South Africa that have come under increasing pressure recently. However, Colombia's trend had been in the right direction, he said.

"If you had a huge shock like Colombia had two or three years ago, you need to look at both - the level and the adjustment - two years ago it was 6.5 percent of GDP, now it is 3.2 percent."

The governor said he did not at this stage envisage raising interest rates either, even next year, but added that "a lot depends on the exchange rate".

A Reuters poll last week showed analysts expected the central bank to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 4.25 percent at least until the first quarter of next year and predicted a rise to 4.75 percent by the end of 2019.

Asked if he shared the view of Finance Minister Alberto Carrasquilla - who took office at the beginning of August - that the fiscal outlook for Latin America's fourth-largest economy was worrying, Echavarria said the fiscal situation was "very manageable".

"It is a new government, and new governments always look carefully at the numbers," he said.

Echavarria also saw no reason for the U.S. Fed to be swayed in its policy decisions by the woes of emerging markets.

"They have to do their job, every country has to do their job. I don't think (Fed Chair Jerome) Powell will increase or decrease interest rates because of emerging markets. The best thing for emerging markets is that the Fed does what they need to do for inflation and growth." title: Colombia  coffee-growers ask  central bank  for  currency intervention
text:
BOGOTA, April 16 (Reuters) - Colombia's coffee federation on Monday asked the country's central bank to temporarily intervene in the exchange rate to alleviate farmer income woes caused by a strengthening peso.

Colombia is the world's top producer of washed arabica. The federation this month asked the government for aid for the more than half a million families who make their living from coffee farming and whose income from exports has fallen as the peso currency has strengthened against the dollar.

"The sustained appreciation of the peso compared to the dollar could be temporarily altered with interventions in the exchange market by the central bank, without modifying the objective inflation targets," federation head Roberto Velez said in the statement.

Internal coffee prices have fallen 10.6 percent since the start of the year, the statement said, while foreign prices for Colombian beans have dipped 6 percent during the same period.

Last week the Andean country approved the importation of robusta coffee to be used to manufacture soluble coffees. (Reporting by Julia Symmes Cobb; Editing by Sandra Maler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Colombia, Mexico pesos fall after last-minute oil price drop
text:
(Updates with closing prices)

By Bruno Federowski

SAO PAULO, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Both the Mexican and Colombian pesos dropped on Friday, hurt by fresh U.S. data that boosted the dollar and a slump in the oil price late in the session.

The two currencies, which have hit a series of record lows, had been on track to post weekly gains for a second time in a row, but in the end only the Colombian peso posted a gain for the week.

The Mexican peso ended the day down 0.88 percent at 18.289 pesos per dollar, and was down 0.35 percent for the week. The Colombian peso lost 0.95 percent on Friday, but rose 0.32 percent over the last seven days.

The late fade in oil prices prompted players to take profits on winning positions in the wake of an early rally that pushed benchmark Brent crude prices to their highest level since early January.

A stronger-than-expected revision of U.S. fourth-quarter economic growth boosted the dollar index, a measure of the greenback's value against six major currencies. The index gained 0.8 percent to post its best weekly performance since November.

Despite Friday's losses, the Mexican and Colombian pesos have shown recent signs of recovery as rebounding oil prices, talk of stimulus measures in China and stronger U.S. growth extended the currencies' bounce from recent all-time lows.

The rally was also triggered by stronger central bank intervention policies announced last week to curb inflation expectations.

"The measures were timely and forceful, as well as necessary to add two-way risk back into the currency market," wrote Morgan Stanley analysts in a client note about Mexico's central bankintervention.

The bank only used up $2 billion in dollar sales and seemed to be successful in supporting the peso, they added.

Fitch Ratings affirmed Mexico's BBB-plus ratings on Friday, and affirmed a stable outlook, citing the country's diversified economic base and track record of disciplined fiscal policies.

Meanwhile, Colombia did not even need to intervene in the foreign exchange market. Although the central bank reduced the threshold triggering automatic dollar call option sales, the bank has not held any auctions so far.

The Brazilian real underperformed, weakening over 1 percent against the dollar, as it suffered from portfolio rebalancing trades usually conducted at the end of the month. Traders often try to influence a foreign exchange rate calculated by the central bank in the last session of the month, which is used to settle futures contracts, boosting volatility.

title: INTERVIEW-Colombia  forex  measures not needed as problems short-term -Meisel
text:
(Adds quotes, background)

By Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Intervention to stem Colombia's rising inflation and the precipitous fall in the peso currency is unnecessary, central bank board member Adolfo Meisel said on Wednesday, because both reflect transitory pressures.

Meisel, one of seven members of the central bank's policy-setting board, said that although inflation will be above the bank's 2 to 4 percent target range this year, he expects it will close 2016 at between 3 and 4 percent.

The peso has depreciated 65.3 percent in the last 12 months.

"For there to be intervention in the exchange rate there would have to be liquidity problems in the foreign exchange market or speculation, which we aren't seeing at this moment," Meisel told Reuters in an interview at his office in Bogota.

"So long as much of this is temporary, prices correct themselves, the devaluation is just this once, we will not have to take measures," Meisel added.

The currency continues to reach record lows; it closed at 3,261.60 pesos to the dollar on Wednesday. Analysts say the effect of continued depreciation on inflation may hasten hikes in the benchmark interest rate, which policymakers have held steady for 12 straight months.

A weak currency compared with the dollar is key to controlling Colombia's widening current account deficit, Meisel said.

Growth outlooks for Latin America's fourth-largest economy have been curbed by falling oil revenue and accelerating inflation, which reached 4.46 percent in the 12 months to July.

The bank board's vote to keep the 4.5 percent rate unchanged at its meeting last week was divided - with some members in favor of a raise.

Board member Carlos Cano said this week that the rate should have been hiked to keep inflation within the target.

Low prices for crude, Colombia's biggest export and source of foreign exchange, explain the sharp drop in the currency, the bank board said in a statement after the vote.

Meisel said there is increased risk to economic growth and for higher inflation.

"These risks have gone up, but there is an uncertainty because if there is economic deceleration that could contribute to a lower inflation," he said, adding that he sees the economy growing close to 3 percent this year and next.

"I'm still optimistic," he said. "I think the industrial sector will help in the second half of the year, I think non-energy exports will too." (Reporting by Nelson Bocanegra; Writing by Julia Symmes Cobb; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: Colombia 's  Forex Intervention  Not Weakening Peso -- Market Talk
text:
11:34 EDT - On Wall Street, an oft-repeated line is "don't fight the Fed," as the US central bank pumps money into the economy. Colombia's central bank, though, apparently doesn't have as much pull in its markets. In late June the bank said it was doubling its official dollar purchases to $2B between July and September to force the peso weaker to help exporters. Board member Mauricio Cardenas declared: "The peso's current exchange rate is not good for the country." Three weeks later, COP not only isn't weaker as Colombia's central bank was hoping, it's 1.5% stronger at 1,857/USD as investors bet on continued heavy dollar inflows. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

11:32 EDT - Last week's Canada jobs report marked the end of a 6-year run in which the comparable Canadian unemployment rate had been below that of the US. Canadian government officials have boasted about the country's superior job-creation record after the recession. That message may no longer apply when compared to the US, says TD Bank after looking at metrics such as the participation rate among people 25-54. Labor-market slack had been more significant in the US, but that's now converging. TD adds recent strength in the Canadian dollar versus the greenback "belies the convergence" in the two countries' labor markets. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

11:29 EDT - United's (UAL) continued struggles to complete its merger integration with Continental and its lagging margin performance could spark interest from activist investors, says Stifel Nicolaus. It thinks activists could try to force management to adopt a more-aggressive strategy to restructure hubs and UAL's domestic network, a turnaround effort that would go beyond the company's current 4-year plan to boost revenue and cut costs. While Stifel has confidence in management, it does admit UAL "appears to fit the criteria of what certain activists have been looking for recently to identify opportunities" in other industries. UAL CEO Jeff Smisek said in a recent interview his board is "supportive" of management's turnaround plan. As other airplane stocks rise, UAL is down 1% after last week's 15% rebound. (susan.carey@wsj.com)

11:28 EDT - Venezuelan officials have been promising measures including an overhaul to their complex FX system to turn around a moribund economy, but delays are keeping investors guessing over what kind of political clout President Maduro has to pull off painful adjustments. Jefferies says it's looking for clues in the ruling Socialist party's convention later this month, "with pragmatic measures dependent upon a consolidation of support for President Maduro." Bond investors looking for high yields have helped support Venezuelan debt prices, but Jefferies warns further delays in implementing economic measures may force market participants to become skeptical. (kejal.vyas@wsj.com)

11:28 EDT - For central bankers, what's the difference between a risk and a vulnerability? Bank of Canada Governor Stephen Poloz, known for his use of metaphor to explain monetary policy, explained in an interview with WSJ how he and his team brainstormed different metaphors to explain the difference ahead of the bank's June financial stability report. They settled on a tree in a backyard with a crack, or a vulnerability, facing the potential of a storm strong enough to knock it down -- a risk. When BoC makes its regular policy announcement and issues its monetary policy report Wednesday, there's little doubt Poloz will hold the overnight rate at 1%. The greater suspense lies in his choice of metaphor. (elena.cherney@WSJ.com; @ElenaCherney)

11:23 EDT - Barclays expects French drug maker Sanofi (SNY) to raise EPS growth guidance when it reports 2Q earnings July 31. SNY management has been too "conservative" with its current 4%-7% EPS growth guidance at constant exchange rates, a position that's hurt SNY's share price, Barclays says. "The stock trades on a heavy discount to the sector due to growth and margin concerns that we believe are excessive. Given a sector like growth profile we believe Sanofi should be trading in line with the sector and expect quarterly earnings to drive a closing of the multiple gap." Barclays expects one key sales driver -- insulin brand Lantus -- to return to normal sales growth of about 15% after a tough 1Q. SNY up 0.9% at $52.10. (jeanne.whalen@wsj.com)

11:20 EDT - Brazil's foreign exchange policy has become increasingly controversial, given its length and intensity, Goldman Sach's economist Alberto Ramos says. Heavy intervention started in May 2013 and still taking place despite the now-benign global emerging market FX environment, helping to keep the Brazilian real increasingly overvalued. That, in turn, is "keeping the economy weak and unbalanced," Ramos says. Some economists already say Brazil's GDP may grow less than 1% in 2014. (Luciana.Magalhaes@wsj.com)

11:19 EDT - The US machine tool business remains soft. Orders for the metal-cutting equipment -- used in a wide range of manufacturing -- were down 17.5% to $351.9M in May, compared to a year-ago, according to the Association for Manufacturing Technology. So far this year, orders are down 1.4% compared to 2013. The soft order books in the early part of this year are expected to be offset by a stronger second half of the year. (tim.aeppel@wsj.com; @timaeppel)

11:18 EDT - Whiting's (WLL) $3.8B deal for fellow Williston Basin oil producer Kodiak (KOG), which valued the latter's stock at slightly below Friday's closing price, shows "there is sometimes more to M&A than just numbers," says Wells Fargo. It notes CEO Lynn Peterson has much of his net worth in KOG, and that management had tried unsuccessfully for years to sell the company. "Putting ourselves in those shoes, we would be willing to take a little less to lock in the wealth and take the risk off the table," says Wells. WLL climbs 6.2% while KOG gains 4.4% at $14.86 as both hit all-time highs. (ryan.dezember@wsj.com; @RyanDezember)

11:15 EDT - Capital Economics says the deceleration in home sales in Canada -- yearly gain of 4.4% in June vs 4.6% in May -- will likely continue, with the past decline in the existing home sales-to-listings ratio pointing to a further slowdown during 2H. The recent drop in mortgage costs might spark a pick-up in home sales during the next few months, and that could delay the onset of price weakness until next year, firm says. But it's been calling for a 25% correction in the market for more than three years, and is sticking to that. "[We] still believe that the housing market is headed for a major correction over the longer term," CapEcon says. (don.curren@wsj.com @dbcurren)

11:13 EDT - The import tariffs leveled Friday by the US on South Korean steel for the oil-and-gas industry will firm up US prices--and the bottom lines of domestic producers--but won't fundamentally alter the market, say analysts. The duties on South Korean steel pipe and tube of an average 13%, or roughly $100/ton, "can probably be absorbed somewhat by the Koreans' cost structure," says John Packard, publisher of Steel Market Update. But expect South Korea, which has a 15-20% market share, to keep exporting steel pipe and tube to the US, predicts KeyBanc. It thinks the decision should help prices be as much as $110/ton higher than early-2014 levels. (john.miller@wsj.com; @wsjmiller)

11:11 EDT - Citigroup's (C) 2Q earnings were boosted $610M by the bank's release of some of its bad-loan reserves, an amount slightly less than the $646M it released in 1Q. Citi and other big national banks have been releasing reserves every quarter for more than four years because of improvements in credit quality, and those amounts go directly into the bank's operating income. Observers have been expecting reserve releases to dwindle, since credit quality isn't improving as quickly now, but thus far the big national banks' 2Q releases are holding fairly steady compared with 1Q. (michael.rapoport@wsj.com; @rapoportwsj)

title: Zinc Prices Up on Higher Demand, Falling Supply -- Market Talk
text:
14:45 EDT - Not all mining and metals commodities are treading water. Zinc prices for example are up 22% in the past year, and shares prices in pure-play zinc companies are up 30% thanks to "continued global demand growth, higher mine production costs, and declining inventory levels," says Ignace Proot, an analyst for Bernstein. Proot says Bernstein remains "bullish on zinc", because it's used in so many consumer goods and because of a "structural shortage" due to mine depletion and closures. (john.miller@wsj.com)

14:42 EDT - More coal miners are likely on the verge of cutbacks, Sterne Agee says. Prices are so bad for metallurgic coal that likely 40% to 50% of the global export production gets produced at a loss, analyst Ray Young estimates. Recent deals have set a 3Q benchmark price of $120 a ton, which isn't enough for most US producers. The industry has recently announced production cutbacks between 15M and 20M tons and more announcements are likely to come in the weeks and months ahead, Sterne Agee says. (tim.puko@wsj.com)

14:39 EDT - Private equity firm TPG is quietly incubating an internal hedge fund, its second-ever, to run a macro strategy, WSJ reported today. TPG and its partners will put as much as $100M into the fund, with hopes to raise more next year. That's a small fraction of the commitment from Blackstone (BX), and its clients, to its multi-strategy Blackstone hedge fund that will start as soon as the fall, as WSJ reported earlier this week. Each Blackstone team, of which there could eventually be several dozen, will have about $150M to trade, sources said. If prior experience is any guide however, it'll be the investment performance that proves whether or not the efforts are successful, rather than day-one cash. (rob.copeland@wsj.com; @realrobcopeland)

14:38 EDT - Fiat Chrysler may soon be listed in New York, but its post-merger financial statements will adopt accounting standards mostly used by companies outside the U.S., according to a new regulatory filing. It's a small change but one that's likely to clear up some earlier confusion. Right now, Chrysler reports using U.S. GAAP standards, while Fiat uses IFRS, which is common for European companies. After the merger, they'll just use one method -- IFRS. (christina.rogers@wsj.com)

(dan.molinski@wsj.com)

text:
The Wall Street Journal's Daily Report on Global Central Banks for Monday, June 23, 2014:

Sign up for the newsletter .

Highlights 


   -- Hilsenrath's Take: Fed Could Face Tougher Inflation Questions In Days 
      Ahead 
 
 
   -- Citigroup Fights to Recover From 'Stress Test' Failure 
 
 
   -- IMF Girds for Market Storms Ahead 
 
 
   -- ECB Says Fixing the Fix Won't Fix FX 
 
 
   -- Mexican Central Bank Divided Over Rate Cut 

HILSENRATH'S TAKE: FED COULD FACE TOUGHER INFLATION QUESTIONS IN DAYS AHEAD

Here's a question we in the press corps should ask Janet Yellen at her next press conference, or maybe some lawmaker should try at her semiannual testimony in July: Should the Fed have a memory?

The Fed's preferred measure of inflation has run below its 2% objective for 24 straight months. When the Commerce Department releases its May reading of the personal consumption expenditure price index on Thursday, it will likely extend that streak to 25 months.

Should the central bank allow inflation to run above target for some time to make up for the long stretch it has been below target?

That's a pertinent because the inflation terrain could be shifting on the Fed. The PCE price index was up 1.6% in April from a year earlier, an uptick from gains of 1.1% in March and 0.9% in February. Fed officials expected inflation to firm to 1.5% by year end. If the March trend holds it might already be there, begging all kinds of questions.

Ms. Yellen implied last week that if inflation moves to the 2% objective more quickly than the central bank expects, then it could raise short-term interest rates sooner than planned.

"If the economy proves to be stronger than anticipated by the Committee, resulting in a more rapid convergence of employment and inflation to the FOMC's objectives, then increases in the federal funds rate target are likely to occur sooner and to be more rapid than currently envisaged," she said.

But the Fed chairwoman also has implied the Fed will be patient about inflation as it approaches or even if it exceeds the target. She seems to see the mandate for patience encoded in the "balanced approach" officials say they'll take in meeting their two objectives of low-steady inflation and maximum employment.

"If the distance from achieving an objective is particularly large, it would be consistent with the balanced approach that we would tolerate some movement in the opposite direction on the other objective," she said. TRANSLATION: The Fed might let inflation drift above 2% for a time if unemployment is very high.

Does the long run of below-target inflation give the Fed even more time to act? Ms. Yellen hasn't really addressed that question.

For now she doesn't seem to think it's a dilemma she'll need to resolve.

"The recent evidence we have seen, abstracting from the noise, suggests that we are moving back gradually over time toward our 2% objective and I see things roughly in line with where we expected inflation to be," she said.

That view could be tested Thursday.

-By Jon Hilsenrath

MORNING MINUTES: KEY DEVELOPMENTS AROUND THE WORLD

Citigroup Fights to Recover From 'Stress Test' Failure. Citigroup's direction and Chief Executive Michael Corbat's fate are, to a significant extent, in the hands of the Federal Reserve. The firm is prohibited from raising its dividend or increasing its stock buybacks, two investor-pleasing moves it was expected to make. Passing next year's stress test has become an overriding focus for Mr. Corbat.

Will Fed Tolerate Inflation Above 2%? Do You Mean CPI or PCE? One of the biggest debates right now over the outlook for inflation is whether the Fed would allow inflation to overshoot its 2% target for some period of time. But the Fed's choice of target is important. The Fed targets the personal consumption expenditures price index, not the better-known consumer price index. And PCE inflation is persistently lower than the CPI.

Fitch Report: Fed's Reverse Repos Are Reshaping the Securities-Borrowing Market. Although it's only in a testing phase, a Federal Reserve program aimed at improving central bank control over short-term interest rates is already reshaping the markets where dealers go to finance their bond-trading positions.

BOJ Says It'll be Ready When It's Time to Normalize Policy. Like the Fed, which has found that ending its extraordinary support for the U.S. economy requires patient planning and careful communication, the Bank of Japan is already preparing for the Day After.

BOJ Kuroda Sees CPI Falling Near 1% Over Summer Bank of Japan Gov. Haruhiko Kuroda said Monday that the nation's embryonic inflation may hit a bump over the summer but will rise toward 2% after that, essentially rejecting speculation that a moderation in price increases near-term could spur the central bank to action -- Dow Jones Newswires

IMF Girds for Market Storms Ahead. What's one of the International Monetary Fund's top priorities? Preparing the global economy for financial volatility as the Fed exits its easy money policies.

Euro-Zone Business Activity Slows in June. Business activity in the euro zone slowed for a second straight month in June, a sign that the recovery continued to be modest as France struggled to generate economic growth.

ECB Draghi: Need to See Deterioration of Inflation Expectations Over Medium Term Before QE. The European Central Bank needs to see inflation expectations in the euro zone deteriorate before embarking on large-scale asset purchases, its president said Saturday. Speaking in an interview with Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf, ECB President Mario Draghi said "a deterioration of inflation expectations over the medium term" would need to happen before the central bank would undertake quantitative easing.

ECB Likely to Keep Interest Rates Low Until 2016. The European Central Bank is unlikely to raise interest rates from record lows until 2016, when the euro-zone economic recovery gains pace, ECB Governing Council member Ewald Nowotny said in a newspaper interview.

Analysts Skeptical New ECB Loans Will Get to Firms in Need. Euro-zone banks are due to repay EUR12.6 billion in three-year loans this week, more than three times the EUR3.7 billion repaid last week. That banks are repaying the LTROs is noteworthy because the European Central Bank recently announced that it is unleashing an additional loan to euro-zone banks later this year. That means the ECB is providing more funds, even as banks are repaying loans early.

Nearly Third of Euro-Zone Banks May Have to Raise Capital. Nearly a third of Euro-zone banks think they may have to raise capital to weather upcoming stress tests, according to a poll by consultant Ernst & Young LLP. In an anonymous survey of 294 banks across Europe, 22 said they expect to have to raise capital following stress tests and 43 said they "may need to." According to Ernst & Young, 30% of Euro-zone lenders couldn't rule out capital raising, with 8% saying they believe they will likely have to. Banks in Germany are the most confident that they won't have to go down this route, while banks in Spain are the least confident.

ECB Will Be Ready to Oversee Banks, Chief Supervisor Says. The European Central Bank faces an enormous task preparing for its new role of overseeing the euro zone's most important lenders, but will have the new single supervisory mechanism ready by early November, chief banking supervisor Danièle Nouy said Monday.

ECB Says Fixing the Fix Won't Fix FX. Changing the way that currencies benchmarks, or "fixes," are calculated is an alluring idea for mending problems unearthed by the year-old investigation into the FX market. But the ECB says simply reforming the process used to set prices would not fix the issue.

Beijing's Overhauls Get Short Shrift. Long-term economic overhauls that China's leadership promised are taking a back seat to short-term needs as Beijing wrestles with a slowing economy and a foot-dragging bureaucracy. In the more-than-six months since the Communist Party announced the restructuring package, economic growth has slowed more quickly than leaders anticipated, prompting a series of stimulus measures.

Gauge of China's Factory Activity Hits Seven-Month High. A gauge of China's factory activity showed fresh signs of strength in June, pointing to improvement in the world's second-largest economy as export demand improves and a government stimulus program takes hold.

Economists React: China's Factories Back in Business.

U.K. Interest Rates Won't Return to Precrisis Levels, Says BOE's Haldane. Britons shouldn't expect borrowing costs to rise to the levels that prevailed before the global financial crisis, and instead should accustom themselves to a "new normal" for the Bank of England's benchmark interest rate of between 2% and 3%, the central bank's new chief economist said in an interview published Saturday.

BOE Dove Says Time to Raise Rates Near. Britain's recovery has become entrenched and the Bank of England should start to raise interest rates in the coming months to reflect the stronger economy, one of its most dovish policymakers said in The Daily Telegraph Monday.

Colombia Raises Rates, Doubles Forex Intervention. Colombia's central bank raised its key lending rate for a third straight month Friday to cool an expanding economy and said it will aggressively increase its intervention in foreign exchange markets to get its currency to weaken against the dollar.

Mexican Central Bank Divided Over Rate Cut. The Bank of Mexico's surprise decision to cut interest rates earlier this month came in a split decision, as several members of the board saw more risks than benefits to further lowering borrowing costs.

Move on Money-Market Rates Shows Philippines Intent on Tightening. The Philippine central bank's decision to pay higher interest on its special deposit accounts--a tool it uses to control liquidity in the market -- represents a change of direction for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and an intensification of recent moves to tighten policy.

title: *Colombia  Central Bank  Raises Key Rate, As Expected, 25 Basis Points to 4.0%
text:
20 Jun 2014 14:30 ET *Colombia Central Bank Says Will Buy Up to $2 Billion in Foreign Exchange Market July-September

20 Jun 2014 15:19 ET  Colombia Raises Rates, Doubles Intervention in Forex Market


 
 By Dan Molinski 
 

BOGOTA--Colombia's central bank raised its key lending rate for a third straight month Friday to cool an expanding economy and said it will aggressively increase its intervention in foreign exchange markets to get its currency to weaken against the dollar.

The bank's seven-member board said after its monthly meeting that it voted to increase its key interest rate 25 basis points to 4.0%. Economists widely expected the move, especially after the government released data Thursday that showed Colombia's economy expanded in the first quarter faster than analysts were forecasting.

In explaining its rate decision, the bank said that as the oil-driven economy picks up steam, consumer inflation is rising at a faster clip than was expected, and said that raising rates now, which can reduce consumer demand and temper inflationary pressures, will avoid the need for sharp adjustments in the future.

"Taking that into account, as well as the lag-time that occurs before monetary policy actions affect inflation and growth, the board decided to increase the intervention rate," bank President Jose Dario Uribe told reporters.

Colombia's consumer inflation last year was 1.9%, one of its lowest rate in decades. But prices have climbed steadily and the annual rate through May is now 2.9% and is expected to go even higher before the end of the year. The bank's target inflation range is 2% to 4%.

The bank also announced Friday that starting in July it will sharply increase its intervention in foreign exchange markets to force its currency to weaken against the dollar, a move that could help Colombian exporters by making their products more competitive abroad. The bank said it will buy up to $2 billion from July through September, a doubling of the $1 billion limit it set for the April thru June period.

"The peso's exchange rate, where it is right now, is not good for the country," Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas, who is also one of the central bank's seven board members, told reporters in explaining the bank's decision.

Colombia's peso ended Friday afternoon at 1,883 for a dollar, 2.6% stronger from where it began the year. Officials would like to see the peso weaken toward 2,000 for a dollar.

President Juan Manuel Santos, who was elected June 15 to another four-year term, said last week Colombia's economy may grow 5.5% this year. During the first quarter, expansion reached 6.4% versus the same quarter of last year, with the growth being led by soaring investment in construction, mainly large infrastructure projects such as highways.

title: Colombia May Not Act Despite Weakening Peso -- Market Talk
text:
10:28 EDT - The Colombian peso has been a popular trade with emerging-markets investors this year, strengthening to a 6-month high against the dollar. Colombia's central bank has a history of intervening to weaken the peso to help local exporters, but Societe Generale's Eamon Aghdasi says that's unlikely for now. He says the fact that Colombia's central bank unexpectedly hiked interest rates last week shows they're becoming more concerned about controlling inflation and less willing to maintain a weak exchange rate. For now, investors can keep piling into the peso and local currency bonds without fear of intervention, he says. USD/COP at 1902.6 from as low as 1898 earlier in the session. (nicole.hong@wsj.com)

10:11 EDT - For dollar bulls, things may get worse before they get better. The prospect of dollar strength comes from decreasing slack in the labor market, tightening monetary policy and rising rates. But "these are down the road rather than around the corner," says Citi's Steven Englander. "Before we get there we have to deal with Fed dovishness, ECB and BoJ reticence on policy ease, reserves diversification." Englander admits Citi has been hurt by overestimating how quickly dollar-strength drivers would come into play and underestimating negative near-term factors. So what's the turning point? When the ECB and BoJ pull the trigger on further easing while the Fed tightens. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

1408 GMT [Dow Jones]--Using a fair value model, TRY/ZAR is now overbought and looking at positioning it is favorable to go short, says Deutsche Bank strategist Bilal Hafeez. On the same basis, ZAR and TRY are both cheap while NZD and KRW look expensive. Elsewhere, "it may be time to revise our bearish EUR/USD forecasts. However, the case for the broader USD uptrend remains intact," he adds. (chiara.albanese@wsj.com @chiaraalbanese)

1400 GMT [Dow Jones]--The U.K. economy expanded 1.0% in the three months to the end of April and is within touching distance of its prerecession peak, says the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, a nonpartisan think tank. NIESR estimates U.K. gross domestic product was just 0.17% smaller at the end of April than it was just before the economy entered recession in early 2008, suggesting that all the ground lost in the slump will very soon be recovered. Before those champagne corks pop, NIESR reminds us this is the slowest recovery on record in the U.K. The U.S. recovered its precrisis size in 2010. (jason.douglas@wsj.com)

09:50 EDT - Economists are using adjectives such as "lousy" and "ugly" to describe Canadian employment data for April, which indicated a job decline of 28,900. Desjardins Capital Markets says with the exception of job growth in Canada's largest province, Ontario, there's "nothing too positive that can be said about the report." The firm adds that the result will raise eyebrows at the Bank of Canada, as the 30,000-plus decline in full-time employment won't be "reassuring" in the context of labor market slack in the country. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

9:49 EDT - Jefferies' Chris Bury contends "the risk of a large and fast selloff in bonds is very remote," saying higher yields would be met with "ready buyers." He cites last Friday's reaction to the jobs report--Treasurys initially dropped on the strong job number but steadily rebounded. "Many people already expected yields to rise, and they have been short." Bury says without signs of higher inflation, the Fed is going to take its time raising rates. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

1340 GMT [Dow Jones]--The bad run for Indian industry likely continued in March with the sector's output expected to have contracted for the fifth time in six months. Industrial production, which includes output of factories, mines and utilities, likely shrunk 1.4% from a year earlier, according to the median estimate in a poll of 11 economists by The Wall Street Journal. It had shrunk 1.9% in February. "Lead indicators suggest there has been no improvement in the manufacturing sector, which has been the biggest laggard," says Gautam Singh, an economist at brokerage Spark Capital. Manufacturing output makes up about 75% of industrial production. The data will be issued at 1200 GMT Monday. (anant.kala@wsj.com)

09:40 EDT - Traders say there are two factors pushing Treasury prices lower this morning. One is investors booking profit. "Bond investors need fresh triggers for another leg down in bond yields," says Dan Mulholland, head of US Treasury trading at BNY Mellon Capital Markets. He says a second factor is dealers selling bonds to lower prices in order to sell the new bonds they accrued from this week's auction to clients. The 10-year note is 5/32 lower, yielding 2.62%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

9:35 EDT - It's not just the US where the labor-force participation rate is at levels last seen in years. The number of employed and unemployed people as a percentage of the Canadian population fell to 66.1% last month, the lowest level since November 2001, while the employment rate--or proportion of working-age Canadians working--hit 61.5%, the least in 4 years. It's all an indication Canadian employers aren't creating enough jobs to keep pace with population growth, says Erin Weir, an economist with the United Steelworkers union. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

This article was corrected at 10:04 ET to fix paragraph that said Canada's employment rate has reached a 14-year low. It's at a 4-year low.

09:35 EDT - Canada posts a surprise decline of jobs in April, though the jobless rate remains unchanged at 6.9% as people left the workforce. The data agency notes that when measured using concepts employed by the US government, Canada's jobless rate was 6% in April, or down 0.2 percentage points from 12 months earlier. Economist Bill Adams from PNC says that's low enough for labor-market tightness to begin fuelling stronger wage growth in coming months. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

9:31 EDT - With Canada unexpectedly shedding about 29K jobs in April, labor trends show that the underlying employment growth is moderating, BMO's Doug Porter says. Canada's 12-month growth trend is now just up 0.8% year-over-year, about half of what the US labor sector is looking like, he notes. While that's helped to chip away at Canada's jobless rate -- currently sitting at 6.9%, the lowest since January 2009 -- that's been offset by a decline in the participation rate. Porter says the jobs data ultimately show the Bank of Canada will remain on hold. (david.george-cosh@wsj.com @itsdgc)

09:22 EDT - The greenback is pushing higher against the euro, yen, sterling and the Canadian dollar. But gains have come more from profit-taking than any notable improvement in US economic fundamentals. But it's not like stronger datapoints would help anyway, says Marc Chandler, global head of FX at Brown Brothers Harriman. USD is up 0.2% on the yen, to Y101.81, while the euro is off 0.4%, at $1.3792. The pound is off 0.4%, to $1.6865. (james.ramage@wsj.com)

title: Winter Storms Hit Christopher & Banks Traffic -- Market Talk
text:
12:41 EST - Dougherty & Company says a string of large winter storms has cut into Christopher & Banks (CBK) store traffic since Black Friday, causing the firm to lower its 4Q same-store sales estimate to flat from up 2%. Firm doesn't expect a big earnings hit as CBK hasn't run any special sales during the period, but says the major weekend storms in the Midwest, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast cap potential for an upside sales surprise during the holiday season. Dougherty says inventory levels are under control and key categories are selling well. CBK drops 7.7% to $7.89, though remains up 11% over the last three months. (patrick.sullivan@wsj.com)

12:25 EST - Arabica-coffee futures rise as money managers buy after prices dipped to near-three-week lows earlier this week; traders expect more buying ahead. Index-tracking "funds should be coming into the market (next week) and buying up about 11,000 lots over five days" as they rebalance their positions at the start of the new year, says Beto Taguchi, senior trader at Ally Brazilian Coffee Merchants. The addition of that many positions would raise open interest by about 7.7%, but Mr. Taguchi says selling from producing countries would likely cap the rally before it can reach $1.20/lb., a key technical and psychological level. Arabica for March delivery on ICE was recently 3.6% higher at $1.1545 a pound. (alexandra.wexler@wsj.com)

12:22 EST - In 2013, emerging-market bond funds saw their worst year of outflows since EPFR Global starting tracking them in 2003, with investors redeeming $31.3B. Emerging-market equity funds experienced their biggest outflows since 2011, losing $27.4B last year. But analysts say these figures are not a death knell for emerging markets. The bulk of these outflows were from retail investors, while longer-term institutional investors having been holding on or even adding holdings to emerging markets, fund managers say. Barclays notes that these hefty outflows "contrast with country/bottom-up data, which shows that foreign investors have not shifted their local equity and bond positions significantly in recent months. The divergence between bottom-up and EPFR fund flow data is probably because of the stronger representation of retail-type investors in the fund flows data." (erin.mccarthy@wsj.com; @eemccarthy)

11:52 EST - Colombia's peso often moves in step with the currency of its larger neighbor Brazil, but as the real tumbled this week on a stronger US dollar, the Colombian currency has stayed range-bound, roughly between COP1,925 and COP1,945 per dollar. Today it's at COP1,937/USD. This may indicate Colombia's central bank is taking advantage of its intervention flexibility to reduce dollar buying -- which weakens the peso -- when it's not needed. Monetary authorities will buy "up to" $1B in US currency Jan-March, a $15M daily average if maxed out. But they are free to buy less. (dan.molinski@dowjones.com)

11:45 EST - Raymond James raises Finisar (FNSR) to strong buy from outperform, saying it thinks "investors do not appreciate how the company and its business have evolved." Datacom "continues to drive growth and is benefiting from strong tailwinds including copper to optical migration, increasing contributions from Web 2.0, and healthy datacenter capex," firm says. RJ also expects telecom to improve this year, "with most growth coming from improved spending in Asia offset by muted North America carrier capex." Firm admits investors "have been burned by Finisar's lumpiness in the past and many remain skittish," but it believes FNSR's business "has matured with improved customer mix and better exposure to datacom as opposed to telecom." Shares up 2.8% at $23.90. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

11:45 EST - Because of the lateness of Thanksgiving this year, some holiday-related travel was going to fall into December for airlines, muting November results and giving an added boost to last month. Still, Delta's (DAL) 10% jump from a year earlier for a key revenue measure, which followed November's 3% drop, topped the company's 7-9% prediction and "was well ahead" of what S&P Capital IQ anticipated. It boosts its price target 1/3 to $40 and EPS views through 2014 as the firm upgrades DAL--the first to release December results--to strong buy from buy. "We see DAL as best in class among US airlines." Shares, which more than doubled last year to hit new highs, are atop the S&P 500 today with their 4.3% gain to $28.89. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

11:12 EST - The bear of all bears, United-ICAP technician Walter Zimmerman, expects 2014 to be the year of "major reversals," with long-term time cycles suggesting stocks may be in "the bubble to end all bubbles." He says the DJIA can still rise up to about 17150 before reversing lower. Zimmerman isn't expecting a flash-like crash, as he doesn't believe DJIA will hit a long-term cycle low until 2016, somewhere in the 5770-4650 range, or 65%-72% below current levels. DJIA now up 64 at 16506. Zimmerman also expects gold to turn higher, 10-year Treasury yields to turn lower and US dollar to bottom around the same the DJIA starts reversing. (tomi.kilgore@dowjones.com)

11:11 EST - Jamba Juice's (JMBA) 3Q same-store sales fell 3.4% on factors including uncooperative weather and promotions that didn't help move the needle much. Wedbush sees no reason why trends didn't continue last quarter as it downgrades the beverage chain to neutral and drops its price target $2 to $13. That contrasts with rivals who saw solid summer sales gains as some "jumped on the fresh-squeezed raw-vegetable-juice trend ahead of Jamba" and "launched other new products such as breakfast bowls, Greek yogurt smoothies and crepes." Meanwhile, competitors are speeding up their new-store growth thanks to Robek's and Smoothie King cutting franchise fees. JMBA, for its part, is also opening up lots of new locations. Shares fall 2.2% to $12.07 and have traded sideways nearly all decade. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

11:01 EST - "New Year optimism is justified this time," proclaims Capital Economics, adding that this "could be the year that the economic recovery finally kicks into a higher gear." Firm says factors that have been holding back the economy -- like the euro-zone crisis, and "the unprecedented US fiscal squeeze" -- are fading, while aspects that've boosted growth -- like a better job market, stronger housing market, and business spending -- are strengthening. Capital Economics sees the economy growing 2.5% this year, "a shade below the consensus forecast of 2.7% and the Fed's 3.0%." (john.shipman@wsj.com)

10:21 EST - The snowstorm that barreled through the Northeast had led to thinner trading. In the Treasury market, trading volume as of 10am was $56B versus a 4-week average of $90B--itself anemic due to the holiday season. Some traders expect volume to pick up in the coming week. The December jobs release is due next Friday, which could influence the pace of future tapering. Treasury yields could shoot up if job growth gathers speed, but fall if the reverse occurs. The 10-year note is 3/32 lower, yielding 2.997%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

10:17 EST - GM skunks investors with its 6% drop in December US sales, sending shares to session lows, as the company says demand was slow to start the month but gained some steam by New Year's. One good sign for GM was signs that quickly growing inventories reversed some in December. At month's end, they were 4% lower than on Nov. 30, cutting the day-supply level to a non-scary 81 from 96. Still, dealer lots have plenty of product, and GM needs to prevent running plants full blast if vehicles aren't moving terribly quickly. That's what helped get the industry into last decade's fix. text:
26 Dec 2013 10:22 EDT *Colombia Peso Gains in Correction to Tapering 'Over-Reaction'- Analyst

26 Dec 2013 10:59 EDT  Colombia Peso at 5-Week High; Fed Taper Effect Less Than Expected

By Dan Molinski

BOGOTA--Colombia's peso hit a five-week high Thursday as traders who bet heavily on the dollar in response to the Federal Reserve's decision to reduce its bond-buying program began to scale back their U.S.-currency holdings.

Early in Bogota, the peso reached COP1,915 to the dollar, its strongest since mid November. In midmorning trading, it was recently at COP1,917.90.

"Investors in the foreign exchange market moved heavy into dollars and out of pesos in the weeks leading up to, and the days just after the Fed's tapering decision," said Juan David Valencia, FX analyst at Colombian brokerage Corredores Asociados. "But this is now seen as somewhat of an overreaction. The investors feel they perhaps bought too many dollars."

Some traders felt the peso and other emerging markets currencies could fall sharply when the Fed tapered last week, following a slide by Latin American and other emerging market assets when the Fed earlier in the year started talking about cutting its stimulus program.

Despite Thursday's bounce in Colombia's currency, Mr. Valencia said the overall effect of the Fed's tapering decision could still lead to a generally weaker peso in the early months of next year. He said he expects the peso to slip to around 1,950 to the dollar during that time.

The peso is 8% weaker this year after gaining 10% in 2012. Colombia's central bank was aggressively intervening in the forex market earlier this year to weaken the peso and help exporters compete better abroad. But since October, it has reduced official dollar-buying by half to about $15 million daily, on the assumption that Fed tapering and other factors such as deterioration in Colombia's trade balance will weaken the peso naturally.

title: Colombia Stocks Climb; Peso at 2-Month High
text:
BOGOTA--Colombian stocks rose Friday, fueled by continued gains in U.S. markets, while the peso reached its strongest level against the dollar since mid-August.

The Colcap index, a benchmark for the Colombian Stock Exchange, increased 0.36% to end at 1,763.11 points. The index is 4% lower this year.

Colombia's peso closed stronger at COP1,881.78 for a dollar, from COP1,886.95 in the previous trading session, according to Set-FX. Earlier in the session it hit a two-month intra-day high of COP1,879.50 for a dollar.

Colombia's central bank has been intervening in the spot market throughout the year with dollar purchases to prevent excessive strength in the peso, but starting this month it cut its daily intervention in half to about $15 million.

0000 GMT (Dow Jones)-- U.K.'s August industrial production (fell 1.1%, well below expectation, with manufacturing production falling 1.2%) should be seen as a statistical outlier, says Daniel Vernazza, an economist with UniCredit Research in London.

He points out that the month-on-month number is very volatile, and suggests the 3-month moving average index as a better guide to the true state of affairs. The index of industrial production rose to 96.5 in August from 96.3 in July (+0.2% mom), while the index of manufacturing rose to 100.3 in August from 100.0 in July (+0.3% mom). Since last November, the trend in industrial production has been clearly positive.

Mr Vernazza also draws attention to the fact that changes in industrial production tend to lag movements in the manufacturing PMI by around 4 months. In April (4 months prior to August), the manufacturing PMI reading was just 50.6. Since then the PMI has accelerated sharply, to 57.1 in August, before easing marginally to 56.7 in September.

In summary therefore, he says: "Given the volatility of the industrial production series and the upbeat sentiment figures, we expect a strong bounce next month. We stick to our GDP growth forecast of 0.9% qoq in 3Q13, and annual growth of 1.6% in 2013 and 3.1% in 2014, which is well above consensus."

(christopher.tomkinson@wsj.com)

Also, "a Yellen-run Fed would likely place significant weight on the 2nd part of the Fed's dual mandate -- full employment -- even at the cost of a temporary rise in inflation." News that President Obama will nominate Yellen is boosting shorter-dated Treasurys, where yields are sensitive to the policy-rate outlook. Two-year notes up 1/32, yielding 0.369%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

9:54 EDT - A polarized Congress and drawn-out budget debate could eat away at investors' long-term outlook on Treasurys. Goldman Sachs says that would build up a "fiscal premium" demanded on longer maturities, not necessarily reflecting serious default concerns, but fears that political standoffs in the US will happen more frequently and risk mismanaging inflation. In that vein, Goldman recommends betting on a steeper yield curve: a lower 3-year yield as growth concerns increase and higher 30-year yield on that fiscal concern. The 3- to 30-year yield gap is currently 303bps; Goldman targets 340bps. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

9:40 EDT - Venezuela hasn't made needed changes yet to its forex system because of internal government debate and policy paralysis ahead of municipal elections in December, contends Eurasia. There's a rising perception that Venezuela risks an economic and social crisis if soaring inflation and runaway depreciation on the currency black market aren't addressed. Officials have promised a complementary FX mechanism, and there had been hope they would introduce more flexibility to strict currency controls. But an earlier devaluation likely hurt President Nicolas Maduro during his run earlier this year, and he can't risk a repeat in December, says Eurasia. (ezequiel.minaya@dowjones.com)

09:39 EDT - The US is no Greece or Argentina, so concerns about a US default isn't hammering Treasurys. Instead, investors are simply cashing out of one-month T-bills and rolling money into later maturities. That reflects Treasurys' haven status and faith that a fiscal deal will eventually emerge. title: Colombia  Peso Falls as  Central Bank  Extends  Intervention ; Stocks Rise
text:
BOGOTA--Colombia's peso fell to its weakest point in nearly two weeks Friday as the central bank extended a dollar-buying program aimed at weakening the currency, while Colombian stocks rose modestly.

The Colcap index, a benchmark for the Colombian Stock Exchange, gained 0.17% to end at 1,768.52 points.

Colombia's peso closed weaker at COP1,908.50 for a dollar, from COP1,903.50 in the previous trading session, according to Set-FX.

The central bank's seven-member board, at its monthly policy meeting Friday, decided to continue intervening in the foreign exchange market until at least the end of the year in an effort to weaken the peso and help Colombian exporters. But for the first time this year, the bank set a limit on its intervention, saying it will purchase "up to" $1 billion between October and December.

title: *DJ Colombia  Central Bank  Holds Rates for Sixth Month at 3.25%
text:
27 Sep 2013 13:45 EDT *DJ  Colombia Central Bank to Continue Intervening in Forex Market

27 Sep 2013 13:48 EDT *DJ  Colombia Central Bank to Buy 'Up to' $1 Billion for Reserves Through December

27 Sep 2013 13:48 EDT *DJ  Colombia Central Bank Puts Ceiling on Forex Intervention

27 Sep 2013 14:49 EDT DJ  Colombia Central Bank Holds Rates, Tweaks Forex Intervention

By Dan Molinski

BOGOTA--Colombia's central bank left its benchmark interest rate unchanged Friday for a sixth straight month following a better-than-forecast report on economic growth, and placed a ceiling on how much it would intervene in the foreign exchange market in light of recent weakness in the local currency.

"The economic growth report from the second quarter removed any and all doubts about the path of the economy," said Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's Finance Minister and a voting member of the central bank board. "The economy is clearly recovering."

Mr. Cardenas told a press conference he and the board's other six members were unanimous in their decision to keep its main lending rate at a near-record low of 3.25%. Such an outcome was expected in a survey of private economists conducted Thursday by Dow Jones Newswires.

The bank's decision comes after two board members last month wanted to cut interest rates, arguing Colombia's shrinking industrial sector and other struggling areas of the economy needed further monetary stimulus. But last week a government report silenced calls for rate cuts as it showed the economy grew a much-larger-than-expected 4.2% in the second quarter, on-year, far surpassing the 2.7% growth rate in the first quarter.

That report has sparked optimism among many analysts that Colombia's economy, which has been hurt by broadly lower global prices for many of the commodities Colombia produces, is bouncing back. Still, some analysts fear massive labor protests throughout the nation over the past couple months might stunt third-quarter growth rates.

Meanwhile, the bank also said it would continue a dollar-buying program aimed at preventing strength in the peso's value against the dollar, but said that it was adjusting how it intervenes given recent peso weakness that renders heavy intervention unnecessary.

Mr. Cardenas announced Friday that the new policy is to only buy "up to" $1 billion total between October and December, compared to the policy of buying around $30 million daily in the foreign exchange market so far this year.

The peso is 8% weaker this year at around COP1,915 for a dollar, after gaining 10% in 2012. The peso's fall in recent months has largely been due to announced plans by the Federal Reserve to soon start reducing the amount of government bonds it buys. The expectations have caused many investors to leave emerging markets such as Colombia for higher or less-risky yields in the U.S. and elsewhere.

Central Bank chief Jose Dario Uribe said that despite the weakening trend already seen this year, the bank still would like to see it weaken further to help exporters who had a tough time selling their goods in global markets last year due to the strong local currency.

title: Colombia 's Cardenas supports extended cenbank  FX intervention
text:
BOGOTA, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Colombia's Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said on Tuesday that under current economic conditions he would like to see the central bank maintain efforts to stem gains in the currency and extend its dollar purchasing program beyond September.

Cardenas, who represents the government on the central bank's seven-member board, also told Reuters that the 3.25 percent benchmark interest rate is the "correct level" for current circumstances.

The monetary authority has bought millions of dollars daily on the spot market for months in a bid to weaken the peso and ease problems for sectors like manufacturing, which struggles to compete with cheap imports, and exporters, which face high local costs and low dollar earnings.

Cardenas has said he wants a currency at between 1,900 and 1,950 per dollar. The peso closed at 1,922 per dollar on Tuesday.

"Under current conditions I think it's necessary to continue as we are, if everything continues as today it would be desirable to maintain the policy," Cardenas said of the dollar purchases which end on Sept. 30.

The peso has strengthened steadily over the last decade - with a respite in 2008 - from about 2,800 pesos per dollar at the end of 2003, prompting heavy lobbying by exporters and industrialists. Last year it gained 9 percent, but a potent dose of government and central bank intervention, both verbal and actual, has brought it down more than 8 percent this year.

Gains in the peso have also been tempered by expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will soon pull its stimulus program, a move that may draw investment away from emerging markets like Colombia.

The central bank has balanced a monetary policy that aimed to prevent the currency strengthening too much while also bolstering sluggish economic growth. Policymakers cut borrowing costs 200 basis points from July last year before holding them steady at the last four board meetings.

Economic growth slowed to 4 percent last year from 6.6 percent in 2011 and the central bank expects 4 percent expansion again this year. Cardenas estimates the economy will accelerate 4.5 percent in 2013.

"Under the actual conditions the interest rate is at its correct level, conditions are right to maintain rates," said Cardenas.

Investment has soared over the last decade as a military offensive against Marxist rebels and right-wing paramilitary groups improved security, making it easier and safer to do business in Colombia.

Growth began to flag last year as the side-effects from the global financial crisis hit consumer confidence and overseas sales - a double whammy for manufacturers.
