title: UPDATE 1-Colombia's  currency  tumbles as investors eye Fed policy
text:
(Adds comment, peso close)

BOGOTA, June 20 (Reuters) - Colombia's currency on Thursday declined sharply against the U.S. dollar as the greenback benefited from the U.S. Federal Reserve's indications that the U.S. economy is growing strongly enough for the central bank to start reining in its stimulus program.

The peso fell 2.3 percent against the dollar, already weakened by ongoing intervention in the foreign exchange market by the government and central bank. Including the drop so far on Thursday, the peso has fallen 9.7 percent against the dollar in 2013. On Wednesday, the peso closed at 1,939 from 1,896, its biggest one-day decline since December 2010.

Investors will now be watching for Colombian policymakers to start dismantling their program of dollar purchases. A peso that is too weak makes imports costly and creates inflationary pressure.

But even as the peso declined, the central bank bought $19.8 million on the spot market on Thursday.

On Wednesday, Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said the Fed's policy-setting committee would likely slow the pace of its stimulative bond purchases in 2013 if the U.S. economy continues to grow. Purchases could end by the middle of next year.

"Risk premiums have moved higher. The movement will be moderate but the signals from the Fed yesterday ratify that there's a new tendency toward international fixed income and that's impacting the entire domestic market," said Daniel Lozano, head of economic investigation at Bogota-based brokerage Serfinco.

Colombia has attracted record foreign direct investment in recent years, as a U.S.-backed offensive against Marxist rebels and paramilitaries made the nation a much safer place to do business. While the investment helped bolster the economy, it also pushed the currency higher against the dollar.

"What's important is that Colombian fundamentals are solid," Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas told reporters in Bogota. "It's an economy that surely won't be inconvenienced by decisions made in the United States."

FX INTERVENTION

Colombia's central has bought millions of dollars daily on the spot market for months to ease gains in the currency, which last year was among the world's strongest, but some board members have raised concerns about the impact of continuing the program for too long.

Cesar Vallejo, a board member of Colombia's central bank, said recently the bank could decide to amend, or even scrap, the program if necessary.

At last month's monetary policy meeting, the bank decided to extend the program through September and buy at least $2.5 billion.

Cardenas had made weakening the currency a priority to help manufacturers and exporters, which have struggled for years with a strong peso.

The peso has strengthened steadily over the last decade, with a respite in 2008, from about 2,800 pesos per dollar at the end of 2003, prompting heavy lobbying by industrialists.

Strong currencies hit exporters the most since salaries, pensions and health benefits are paid in local currency but overseas buyers pay in devalued dollars. (Reporting by Helen Murphy and Nelson Bocanegra; Editing by Bernadette Baum and Steve Orlofsky)

title: Colombia Peso Falls to 16-Month Low of 1,900 for a Dollar
text:
BOGOTA--Colombia's peso fell to 1,900 for a dollar Tuesday, its lowest level in 16 months, hurt by a broadly stronger dollar on rising hopes for a U.S. economic recovery.

In morning trading in Bogota, the peso fell to 1,901.95, down 1.3% from Friday's close prior to the three-day U.S. holiday weekend.

Colombia's peso was among the best-performing currencies in the world last year, rising 10% against the dollar as the local economy boomed on surging oil production and rising foreign investment that flooded the market with U.S. currency. But this year the peso has seen a sharp turnaround, and is down 7.2% against the dollar, making it among the world's worst-performing currencies.

The sudden reversal in fortunes is partly due to macroeconomic factors. As hopes build for a stronger U.S. economy, Colombia's economy has slowed down considerably on lower global prices for oil, coffee, coal and the country's other top export products. Colombia's economy grew 4% last year, down from a 6.6% expansion in 2011. This year, the economy will likely grow a bit above 4%, according to the central bank.

Also hurting the peso, Colombia's central bank has been intervening in the currency market with daily dollar purchases of $30 million, aimed at mopping up excess dollars and weakening the peso further, in an effort to help local exporters. These dollar purchases are due to end Friday, but analysts say there is a good chance the central bank will extend the intervention for more months, possibly until the end of the year.

Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas, who is a member of the bank's board, reiterated last week that he wants to see the peso weaken to at least COP1,950 for a dollar, to ensure Colombian exporters are given a fair price for their products.

BOGOTA--Colombia's peso, which in 2012 was among the world's best-performing currencies against the dollar, weakened to a 16-month low Wednesday as the U.S. currency saw broad gains and Colombian authorities continued to intervene in the market to drive the peso even lower.

The peso was recently trading at COP1,854.25 for a dollar, 0.4% lower from Tuesday and its weakest intraday level since January 2012.

The Colombian currency's weakness is derived largely from recent strength in the dollar against a host of currencies as investors bet the U.S. economy will continue to gain speed even as growth in Europe and elsewhere stalls.

Also pushing Colombia's currency lower is persistent intervention in the foreign-exchange market by the country's monetary authorities. The officials want a weaker currency so Colombian exporters can see improved profits when selling their wares abroad.

An economic boom in Colombia in recent years attracted record amounts of foreign investment into the South American country, and allowed the peso to gain 10% against the dollar last year. But this caused serious damage to Colombian exporters of everything from coffee to bananas.

To counteract that trend in 2013, Colombia's central bank has been buying $30 million daily in the forex market. Amid this, the country's currency has weakened 5% so far this year, and while the intervention policy is scheduled to end May 31, the bank has indicated it may extend it until year-end.

"The government is not satisfied [with the 5% decline] and keeps saying the currency should trade at least at COP1,900/USD," said analysts at RBS.

title: REUTERS SUMMIT-Colombia cenbank's Zarate sees gigantic risk in guaranteed peso level
text:
* For other news from Reuters Latin America Investment Summit, click on http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmerica13("http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmerica13")

By Helen Murphy and Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, May 21 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank board member Juan Pablo Zarate on Tuesday warned of the "gigantic" risks of guaranteeing a level for the country's currency and highlighted the importance of a floating currency to cushion against volatile capital flows.

Colombia, which has a free-floating currency, has battled gains in the peso for years as exporters struggle with low dollar revenue and high peso costs and manufacturers face floods of cheap imports. The government has said it wants a peso devalued to about 1,900 per dollar from 1,847 today.

"The floating rate has been very important in preventing many risks in an environment of high and volatile capital flows," Zarate told the Reuters Latin America Investment Summit.

"The devaluation that we have today, I like, but I don't have a target."

Governments and central banks in advanced economies have resorted to unconventional policies to revive growth, cutting interest rates close to zero and injecting extra liquidity to boost their economies. That has led to a surge in capital flows into emerging economies, strengthening their currencies.

Latin American governments have tackled these inflows in a variety of ways. Brazil has applied strict controls on foreign capital inflows and its central bank has intervened in the local exchange market to tame the real, while Peru has opted for periodic currency-buying measures.

In Colombia, Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas has rolled out a series of measures to help businesses cope with the "over-valued" currency, asking pension funds to diversify their portfolios overseas and buy as much as $5 billion in the foreign exchange market. The central bank has engaged in currency market intervention.

Japan's recent monetary easing may encourage some countries to step up efforts in a "currency war" to attract further investment.

"It's a big temptation that we should avoid," said Zarate, 42, a former deputy finance minister.

In the 1990's Colombia engaged in currency targeting, a policy that created an explosion in internal demand and a housing bubble, said Zarate. The peso began floating freely in 1999.

ADDITIONAL INTERVENTION?

Colombia has been the victim of its own success over the last decade, as improved security enabled foreign companies to build infrastructure and send workers to remote, once-off-limit areas.

Investment in capital markets has soared since a U.S.-backed offensive against Marxist rebels and paramilitary groups made it safer to do business in Colombia. Record foreign direct investment has flooded the economy, mostly in the oil and mining industries, and created structural flows of capital that are hard to prevent having an impact on the currency.

The peso has strengthened steadily over the last decade - with a respite in 2008 - from about 2,800 pesos per dollar at the end of 2003. Last year alone it gained 9 percent, but the potent dose of intervention has brought it down about 4 percent this year.

Zarate and his six colleagues on the bank's board will meet next week to decide whether to alter the benchmark lending rate from its current 3.25 percent. They also will be asked by Cardenas to extend its dollar purchase program from May 31 until the end of the year.

Cardenas, who represents the government on the board, will ask that policymakers continue to buy at least $30 million a day on the spot market in a bid to maintain pressure on the currency and prevent it strengthening further. The bank has bought roughly $3 billion on the spot market since February.

"I think that while we have excess installed capacity and have room to intervene in the currency we should, but without targets and without allowing it to dominate monetary policy," Zarate said.

He declined to be drawn on how he felt about Cardenas' intervention recommendation, and said any change in monetary policy or interest rate movements will depend on new economic data during the month.

"The speed depends on certain phenomena; if the recovery phenomenon is abrupt then we have to react more quickly, but with the actual data available I don't see a need to change in an accelerated way and start increasing the rate 50 basis points or 100."

"As far as today's data is concerned, if a normalization process takes place and if the second half is better we will see when we need to go for a more neutral rate, but today I don't see the need for a strong adjustment."

The central bank has cut 200 basis points from borrowing costs since July last year to help bolster economic growth.

Zarate said the biggest risk to emerging markets, including Colombia, over the medium term is developed nations like the United States shifting away from monetary easing.

Almost a quarter of those polled in a Reuters survey last month estimate the central bank will begin to increase interest rates before the end of the year to ward off future inflationary pressure.

title: *DJ Colombia  Central Bank  Meisel: More Rate Cuts May Overheat Economy
text:
15 May 2013 10:06 EDT *DJ  Colombia's Meisel Says Economy Seems 'To Be Picking Up'

15 May 2013 10:06 EDT *DJ  Colombia's Meisel: Bank to Consider Extending Forex Intervention Beyond May

15 May 2013 10:06 EDT *DJ  Colombia's Meisel Says Biggest Concern is International Economy

15 May 2013 10:11 EDT DJ  Colombia Central Bank's Meisel: More Rate Cuts May Overheat Economy

--Colombia Central Bank's Meisel, a new board member, says economy 'picking up'

--Meisel says more interest rate cuts would risk 'over-stimulating' economy

--Bank to review, possibly extend intervention policy in FX market, Meisel says 


 
   By Dan Molinski 
 

BOGOTA, Colombia--Further interest rate cuts by Colombia's central bank might provide too much of a stimulus and overheat an economy that's relatively healthy, bank co-director Adolfo Meisel said in an interview.

Colombia's central bank officials will meet on May 31 to discuss possible action on interest rates. While some key economic data including industrial production continues to disappoint, most analysts believe the bank will leave its key rate steady for a second straight month at 3.25%, which is the lowest benchmark interest rate this South American country has seen since early 2011.

Speaking at his office in downtown Bogota on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Meisel suggested further rate reductions might not be necessary because of some "good signs" regarding Colombia's economy, which will probably grow around 4.3% this year after expanding 4% in 2012 and 6.6% in 2011. He pointed to consumer expectations data that he said shows consumers are regaining confidence. An economic stimulus plan announced last month by the government is also expected to help spur growth.

"Things seem to be picking up," Mr. Meisel said in an interview. "Still, the data is not easy to read; one day you see positive information, but the next day other data is negative."

The central bank lowered borrowing costs for five straight months starting in November, including a hefty 50-basis-point rate reduction in March. Most private banks have passed these lower rates on to consumers, but the cheaper borrowing costs have so far done little to help the overall economy amid a drop in consumer spending and lower global prices for oil and coal, the country's main exports.

Mr. Meisel, one of two new members appointed in March to Colombia's seven-person central bank board, said no decision has yet been made in terms of what the bank might do with interest rates, but any possible rate reduction would carry risks.

"What might happen ahead if we are over-stimulating the economy? This is the main concern," said Mr. Meisel, 59 years old, an economist with degrees from Yale and the University of Illinois, as well as Colombia's Universidad de Los Andes.

His concerns about cutting rates too much comes after neighboring Brazil's central bank brought interest rates to historic lows, only to reverse course and begin raising interest rates last month as inflation took off. Critics say Brazil's central bank had become too focused on spurring economic growth and didn't pay enough attention to inflation, which is now at the high end of the bank's target range of 2.5% to 6.5%.

Unlike Brazil, Colombia is not facing inflationary pressures. Annual consumer inflation is running at the low end of the central bank's 2% to 4% target. Mr. Meisel said inflation probably won't return to the bank's mid-range 3% target until the end of 2014. Some analysts argue that Colombia's low inflation gives it the room to reduce interest rates at least one more time this year to spur consumer spending and help drive the economy higher.

While expressing confidence that Colombia's oil-driven economy is starting to regain its footing, Mr. Meisel said the global economy continues to be a risk for Colombia.

"What most concerns me is what's happening in the international economy, things can change dramatically from one day to the next," said Mr. Meisel, who headed the bank's office in his hometown of Cartagena before moving to Bogota this year to become a board member. "And whatever we do has to take into account the international economy."

The interest rate decision, Mr. Meisel said, will take into consideration "how exports are evolving, and employment statistics, and in general the perspectives of the economy in the near future."

At the central bank's meeting this month, the board will also consider whether to extend a policy of buying at least $30 million daily in the foreign exchange market in an effort to prevent the peso from becoming too strong against the dollar. The peso rose 10% versus the dollar last year, hurting Colombian exporters' profits. But so far in 2013, the peso is 4% weaker at COP1,839 for a dollar.

The daily intervention policy expires May 31, the same day as the meeting. Mr. Meisel wouldn't comment on whether the intervention would be renewed, but he said the bank is committed to preventing strong gains in the peso against the dollar. He also said the government's efforts at forcing the peso weaker, which include trying to convince private pension funds to buy more dollars, is not seen as a "substitute" for the bank's daily dollar purchases, which he said have a more direct effect on the exchange rate than the government's efforts with pension funds.

title: FACTBOX-Actions by Mexico's  foreign exchange  commission
text:
MEXICO CITY, April 8 (Reuters) - Mexico's foreign exchange commission said on Monday it will suspend a process of offering dollars to the market on days of sharp moves in the peso currency.

Mexico has a much more hands-off approach toward its currency than many of its peers, largely eschewing the direct market intervention practiced by countries such as Brazil and Colombia.

Policy on the peso is set by the foreign exchange commission, a joint effort of the Finance Ministry, the central bank and other state agencies.

The following is a list of some of board's key decisions in past years:

October 2008 - Mexico's central bank says it will auction $2.5 billion to stop the peso's most dramatic slide since the so-called Tequila Crisis in the mid-1990s.

The central bank, which ends up selling $998 million in the market, also announces it will offer $400 million whenever the peso declines by at least 2 percent during a single session.

The amount of the daily dollar auction was trimmed to $300 million in March 2009 and to $250 million in May 2009. The auction mechanism was suspended in April 2010.

March 2009 - The foreign exchange board says it will sell $100 million daily, irrespective of peso levels, in a new mechanism to stop the peso's decline.

April 2009 - The central bank gets a swap line from the U.S. Federal Reserve to sell dollars among local financial institutions.

May 2009 - Daily dollar auction cut to $50 million.

October 2009 - Daily dollar auctions suspended.

February 2010 - The board resumes monthly dollar "put" option auctions to add to the country's federal reserves as a measure to cushion the economy from external turmoil. By using this mechanism, the central bank purchased $600 million between 1996 and 2001.

November 2011 - Mexico says it will halt monthly put option auctions and reinstate daily offers of $400 million whenever the peso declines by at least 2 percent against the dollar during a single session.

March 2013 - The foreign exchange commission suspends the daily offers triggered by 2 percent falls in the peso, saying volatility in currency markets has decreased.

(Reporting by Krista Hughes; Editing by Richard Chang)

Early in Bogota, the peso was at COP1,819 for a dollar, 0.3% weaker from Monday's close and 1.2% weaker from Friday. So far in 2013, the peso is nearly 3% weaker, making it one of the weakest in the region.

The peso gained 10% last year, significantly hurting Colombian exporters' profits and leading to widespread calls for monetary authorities to do more to force the currency weaker. Exporters of products such as coffee, bananas and cut flowers are among Colombia's biggest employers.

When the peso began to rise again in the early days of 2013, the central bank responded by saying that from February through May it is increasing its daily dollar purchases in the spot market by 50% to at least $30 million. The Colombian government's Treasury said it too would be buying dollars to offset the peso's tendency to rise.

"What we're seeing, with the peso now weakening, is the result of the rush by authorities in increasing its intervention," said Francisco Chaves, currency analyst at Corredores Asociados in Bogota.

He said less foreign investment in Colombia's oil sector compared with 2012's record year is also pushing the peso lower.

title: ANALYSIS-Latin America lays out defenses in  currency  war
text:
* Colombia joins Peru and Costa Rica in flows defense

* Pundits predict bumper year for emerging market assets

* Brazil seen on sidelines this time as inflation flares

By Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Latin American policymakers are manning their defenses ahead of what could be a new battle in the "currency wars" as flows of hot money put unwelcome upward pressure on their currencies.

Economists and investors predict that an easing in the euro zone's debt crisis, new economic stimulus measures in Japan and a return of risk appetite will fuel bumper investment flows into Latin America and other emerging markets in 2013.

Some policymakers are already at the barricades.

Colombia cut interest rates on Monday and said it would ramp up dollar purchases. Peru plans to pre-pay up to $1.5 billion in foreign debt this year and is intervening aggressively to curb currency gains. And tiny Costa Rica unveiled a steep hike in taxes on foreign investments this month.

Even Mexico, which has a hands-off approach to currency market intervention, is considering an interest rate cut that some economists believe reflects as much a desire for a weaker peso as it does concerns about growth.

"Much of the region is once again dealing with the impacts of currency wars and QE in the developed world," said Standard Chartered senior strategist Bret Rosen, referring to the extraordinary monetary easing measures undertaken by central banks known as quantitative easing.

Low interest rates in developed economies encourage investors to look for yield elsewhere, pushing up the currencies of countries at the receiving end of their attentions. Stronger currencies make exports less competitive, hurting economic growth.

It is a problem that has battered Brazilian manufacturers for several years. The government pushed back by slashing interest rates and intervening in the currency market to weaken the real, introducing capital controls and offering tax breaks for several industries.

But Brazil has less room for maneuver than other leading Latin American economies this year as policymakers are concerned about inflation, which rose above an annualized rate of 6 percent this month.

Latin American finance ministers complained last month about the impact of stimulus policies in developed economies, and Group of 20 economic policymakers are set to address the impact of monetary policy on currency valuations next month at a meeting in Russia.

Tools to combat appreciating currencies include buying dollars, as Colombia and Peru are doing; capital controls as in Costa Rica; and macroprudential measures, such as Peru's move to raise deposit requirements on dollar bank accounts.

Mark Mobius, who helps oversee $51 billion in emerging market assets at fund manager Franklin Templeton, expects a huge influx of funds into emerging markets this year as investors tire of low-yielding government bonds.

"I think it's going to be enormous, terrific, hundreds of billions. Investors have been penalized with so low rates that they are not making anywhere near what they need," he said.

Global stock markets are up 4 percent already this year, and fund tracker EPFR said it noted a clear preference for emerging market equities over bonds, which attracted most money in 2012. The VIX index, a gauge of investor stress, fell this month to its lowest levels since 2007.

The Institute of International Finance banking group predicts capital flows to Latin America will jump 5.6 percent this year from 2012 to a record $321 billion.

Inflows to the region in 2012, including foreign direct investment as well as stock and bond investment, were already estimated to be about 30 percent higher than the "hot money" period immediately before the global financial crisis in 2008.

WHAT'S HOT?

Brazil and Mexico, as the region's two biggest economies, are likely to attract the bulk of inflows in 2013, although Brazil has managed to deter a lot of speculative investors with capital controls introduced during 2010-2011, when a rush of capital pushed the real up 12 percent against the dollar.

Foreign portfolio inflows into Brazilian stocks and bonds totaled $16.5 billion last year, down from $67.8 billion in 2010.

In its January fund managers' survey, Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch said Brazil had the biggest share of "underweight" ratings in the history of the survey.

Mobius likes small to mid-cap companies in the region and firms exposed to the consumer sector, such as banks. Citigroup, which raised its stock ratings for Latin America to "overweight" as it cut back other emerging markets, likes industrials.

Mexico, for its part, is benefiting from optimism about tax and energy reforms being promised by its new government. That has helped propel stocks and bonds to record high levels.

Pacific Investment Management Co, the California-based firm known as PIMCO that operates the world's largest bond fund, sees opportunities to make money if Mexico's central bank cuts interest rates later this year, pushing up the price of bonds.

Mexico's central bank has made a U-turn from warning of rate hikes to warning of rate cuts, prompting many to suspect it is worried about the peso. The peso hit a 10-month high the day central bankers met to discuss rates, and it only came off those highs when policymakers warned the following morning that they could cut rates. Lower rates would make the peso less attractive to foreign investors.

"It's no surprise that with the peso being weaker in the second half of (last) year that they were a little bit more hawkish, and now we have had a very nice run in the peso year-to-date perhaps they would be more dovish," said Michael Gomez, co-head of emerging markets at PIMCO.

London-based Capital Economics sees Mexico's peso as the currency with the most upside this year, due mainly to the lower risk of intervention by laissez-faire policymakers, in contrast to the record $13.9 billion bought by Peru's central bank in 2012 as the sol hit a 16-year high.

Chile is likely to join Peru and Colombia in intervening to check gains in the peso while shunning capital controls, said Capital's Neal Shearing, while Brazil is in the unusual position of trying to strengthen its currency to fend off rising inflation. A stronger currency cuts the cost of imported goods.

"Inflation concerns are starting to creep back in Brazil, which now marks it out from Colombia, Chile and Peru who seem to be more worried about the strength of the currency and its impact on competitiveness," he said.

The central bank had intervened in the market in recent months to keep the real weaker than 2 per dollar, but this week rolled over currency swaps that mimic the sale of dollars in the futures market - a move with the opposite effect.

The real strengthened past the 2-per-dollar mark on Tuesday for the first time since July, and analysts said they believed policymakers would allow it to firm further if needed.

(Additional reporting by Jack Kimball in Bogota and Mitra Taj in Lima; Editing by Kieran Murray and Leslie Adler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Colombia  peso slumps on  intervention

* Brazil traders eye renewed intervention

* Mexican peso gains 0.34 pct, Brazil real firms 0.14 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Danielle Fonseca

BOGOTA/SAO PAULO, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso fell on Monday as the country's central bank bought dollars to stem recent gains while Brazil's real edged back toward a level that could trigger intervention by its central bank.

Colombia's peso weakened by the most in more than two months, shedding 0.53 percent against the dollar, after the central bank bought $30.6 million in the local market.

"The Colombian peso was the currency in the region with the biggest losses, due to these strong interventions since last week by the central bank," said Diana Guiza, an analyst at brokerage Corredores Asociados.

Last week, Colombia's central bank stepped up dollar purchases to an average of $35 million per day compared to a previous plan to buy $20 million a day.

Colombia, Brazil and Peru are trying to contain gains in their currencies as easy money policies in the United States, Europe and Japan push investors to seek out gains in higher-yielding emerging market assets.

Stronger local currencies hurt domestic manufacturers as they suffer from competition with cheaper imports while making less profit on their exports.

In Brazil, the real was up 0.14 percent at 2.0244 per dollar.

Investors expected the Brazilian central bank to soon roll over some $3 billion in reverse currency swaps that expire on Nov. 1.

The contracts, which mimic the purchase of dollars in the futures market, were sold by the central bank in early September to stop the real from strengthening past 2 per dollar - a level the bank has been defending since early July to support Brazilian exporters.

Traders expect the country's central bank or its government to take further measures if the real rises much more.

"We think that the dollar will remain around this level and within a narrow range," Joao Medeiros, head of currency trading at brokerage Pioneer.

The Mexican peso rose on renewed hopes that Spain would request financial aid.

Mexican policymakers are not expected to step up intervention efforts anytime soon. Gains in the peso are helping curb a spike in inflation by cheapening imports.

The Mexican currency gained 0.34 percent after the outcome of Spain's regional elections was seen as a boost to Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy's austerity drive.

The results rekindled hopes Madrid would soon request a sovereign bailout, seen by investors as crucial to mitigate the region's debt crisis.

Mexico's peso has been supported by signs of faster growth in its top trading partner, the United States, and data on Monday showed Mexican retail sales in August were stronger than expected.

Mexico's peso has been one of the top performing emerging market currencies this year, but gains have flagged in recent weeks as investors cashed in on the strong run-up in the currency. The peso has gained nearly 9 percent against the dollar this year.

Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission showed on Friday that the number of investors betting on a stronger peso dipped in the latest week of data, but still hovered near a record high.

Chile's peso slipped 0.5 percent as prices for copper, the country's top export, hit a more than one-month low.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso slumps on  intervention  concerns
text:

* Colombia says will keep up dollar purchases

* Mexican peso falls 0.31 pct; Brazil real up 0.28 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Moises Avila and Jean Arce

SANTIAGO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Chile's peso slumped by the most in seven weeks on Friday after the central bank warned it could act to curb currency gains, while Colombia pledged to keep buying dollars in its market to fight peso strength.

The Chilean peso lost nearly 0.8 percent to change hands at 474.60 per U.S. dollar after central bank chief Rodrigo Vergara said policymakers may intervene during "exceptional periods" in which the exchange rate is significantly out of line with fundamentals.

The move by Chile pushed it closer to the stance of policymakers in Brazil, Colombia and Peru who have been intervening in markets to fight dollar inflows that have lifted their currencies and hurt exporters.

"The central bank's comments weakened the peso because they leave the door open for a possible intervention. The market isn't just speculating about the possibility of dollar purchases, but also bank deposit requirements," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

The peso has gained more than 9 percent so far this year, making it the second strongest performer among the 152 currencies tracked by Reuters.

Stimulus measures announced by the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank boosted Latin American currencies this quarter. The measures are expected to drive down yields on U.S. and European fixed-income instruments, making emerging market assets more attractive.

The Chilean peso gained 5.5 percent against the dollar in the third quarter, while Mexico's peso firmed 4.5 percent. Brazil's real shed 0.8 percent against the greenback in the quarter after Brazil's central bankintervened.

Colombia's central bank held its benchmark interest rate steady on Friday, and it pledged to extend daily dollar purchases to keep a lid on the peso.

The central bank said it would buy at least $3 billion in the foreign exchange market via auctions from Oct. 1 through March 29, 2013, to take pressure off the peso currency.

The Colombia peso slipped 0.1 percent on Friday, bringing its decline for the quarter to 0.9 percent, hurt by central bank dollar purchases.

The Mexican peso lost a modest 0.31 percent to trade at 12.8660 per dollar as concerns about Spain made investors cautious about taking risks in emerging markets.

A stress test on Spanish banks showed the institutions need a total of 59.3 billion euros in extra capital, but uncertainty persisted about whether Spain will ask for a bailout that would let the European Central Bank begin buying its bonds.

"We could see a whole to wave of pressure related to Spain," said Jorge Gordillo, an analyst at CI Banco in Mexico City, saying that concerns about Spain could weigh on the peso in the coming week. "We think that it will be in October when Spain will ask (for a bailout), and if this happens the peso and stock markets are going to take it well."

Barclays analysts said the Mexican peso could outperform its emerging market peers in Latin America and Asia because its central bank is unlikely to intervene.

Banco de Mexico research published on Friday said emerging market attempts to stem capital inflows during the last round of Fed easing had a limited effect in the longer term.

Steps pursued by countries such as Brazil, Chile and Colombia, including new taxes on investment, higher bank reserve requirements and tariff reforms, may even make investors see them as a riskier bet, the research paper said.

The Brazilian real decoupled from the rest of the market, rising 0.28 percent to 2.0255 per dollar, as investors tried to influence the currency's closing rate at the end of the month.

Brazilian policymakers have pledged to move aggressively to offset expected capital inflows from the easy monetary conditions in the developed world.

A senior government official recently told Reuters that Brazil will defend the level of 2 reais per dollar "like a wall."

title: WRAPUP 1-Fed's QE3 stirs LatAm differences over  currency
text:
* Brazil restarts currency intervention after Fed

 * Speculation that Chile, Colombia could follow

 * Mexico's QE3 enthusiasm stands out from crowd 

 By Krista Hughes and Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Reserve's latest round of stimulus spotlights  a gulf between Mexico and its Latin American neighbors as the region girds itself for a likely revival of the "currency war."

 While Mexico embraced the Fed's decision to start a third round of bond-buying, Brazil vowed to unleash an arsenal of new measures to combat what it fears could be a sharp appreciation in its currency. 

 A stronger real could not come at a worse time for Brazil, which is battling slowing growth with a raft of measures to boost the domestic economy. This contrasts with Mexico, which is growing roughly twice as quickly as its rival and has been fretting about a weak peso pushing up prices. Close links to the United States give it a big stake in stronger U.S. growth.

 "Mexico is clearly one of the few countries in Latin America where you don't have any resistance to peso strength, and you are unlikely to do so, because the central bank prefers a hands-off attitude," said Clyde Wardle, a strategist at HSBC in New York. "That does set Mexico apart."

 Latin American currencies surged to new highs after the Fed's news, with Chile's peso hitting a one-year high against the U.S. dollar and Mexico's rising to a five-month peak on bets that yield-seeking investors will flood to the region, driving asset prices higher.

 During the Fed's second round of bond buying in late 2010 and the first half of 2011, a rush of capital pushed the Brazilian real up 12 percent against the dollar while the Mexican and Chilean pesos both gained 8 percent.

 Economists said a fresh round of currency intervention was in the cards, with Brazil kicking off o n F riday with two central bank interventions in two hours. Speculation is mounting about increased efforts in Chile and Colombia as well.

 South American officials, worried that a rise in their currencies will price their exports out of the market and drag on growth, have a history of intervening to limit currency gains.

 But in Mexico, policymakers face a different dynamic as the peso - one of the most liquid emerging market currencies and often used as a hedge for emerging market risk - has weakened about 30 percent since before the financial crisis.

 Mexican central bank Governor Agustin Carstens told Reuters the Fed's new bond buying program, dubbed QE3, would help the economy, giving no sign policymakers would try to stem the peso's rise. 

 In fact, Carstens said the stronger peso would help limit inflation by making imported goods cheaper - a much-needed break for the Banco de Mexico, which is confronting a spike in inflation to its highest level in more than two years due to fresh food prices. 

 MEXICO AT ODDS

 Mexico's laissez-faire stance will put it in a different class from Latin American counterparts that intervene to cap currency gains, like Brazil, which also fears competition from Asian powerhouse China and its yuan.

 Countries that keep their currencies cheap will face higher prices for imported goods at the same time a flush of cheap money probably drives commodity prices higher, economists said.

 Although price pressures are subdued in Chile, Colombia and Peru - meaning their central banks may not worry too much about the downside of intervention - inflation accelerated to 5.24 percent in Brazil last month.

 "QE3 will end up having two different kinds of effects on inflation," said BNP Paribas economist Nader Nazmi. 

 "In countries that fight against appreciation... the price of commodities will increase. This could lead to higher inflation in countries that do not allow their exchange rate to appreciate."

 Reacting to higher inflation by raising interest rates would make currencies even more expensive, a policy Catch-22 that the region faced during the Fed's previous stimulus, when Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega coined the term "currency war."

 The phrase has been adopted by officials in Colombia, whose peso has been the fourth-biggest gainer worldwide this year, firming 7 percent since January despite back-to-back interest rate cuts. The peso rose 0.4 percent on Friday.  

 "This shows that we should not remain silent in Colombia and that we will have to respond to these kinds of decisions from the United States," Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said.

 Chile's Finance Minister Felipe Larrain had said even before the Fed's Thursday announcement that the country was worried about another round of stimulus, and the peso is approaching levels that have sparked intervention in the past. 

 "These levels for the peso are a concern for authorities. Although we don't expect imminent action, such as an outright intervention, we do expect to see in the short-term, over the next 30 days, verbal interventions or announcements that try to contain the currency's appreciation," said Ruben Catalan, senior analyst at Bci in Santiago.     

(Additional reporting by Anthony Esposito in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: UPDATE 2-INTERVIEW-Colombia cenbank director sees maximum 25 bps cut in 2012
text:
* Dollar purchases have limited impact on currency

* Santos seeks more intervention to ease peso

* FARC peace "psychologically" good for investors

(Adds comment, details)

By Helen Murphy and Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Colombia's economy is showing signs of improvement, central bank board member Juan Jose Echavarria said, leading him to expect policymakers will hold the benchmark lending rate steady for the rest of the year or cut it by no more than a quarter percentage point.

Recent data suggests the economy will grow between 4 percent and 4.3 percent this year and register an expansion of as much as 4.3 percent in the third quarter, Echavarria said in an interview on Friday at the bank's headquarters in Bogota.

Giving his own opinion and not that of the board, Echavarria said that two months ago he would have been more pessimistic about growth in Latin America's fourth-biggest economy, but recent data like consumer confidence and energy consumption have changed his tone.

"Just two months ago we were on track for growth of 3.8 percent, but in the last (month) data gives room to be less pessimistic," he said.

Fellow board member Carlos Gustavo Cano, however, on Friday forecast growth of 3.8 percent for this year. He sees two rate cuts by year-end of 25 basis points each.

The board has already lowered its official estimate for 2012 gross domestic product growth to between 3 and 5 percent.

It views next year's economic outlook with more uncertainty as the global financial crisis hits the Andean nation's exports and industrial output, forecasting growth of between 2 and 5 percent.

"I think Europe remains an unknown and will continue that way in 2013," Echavarria said.

"And if Europe impacts China, that will cause a lot of trouble because some of the capital flows to Colombia have to do with oil. If China is complicated by Europe we will be complicated in Latin America and above all in Colombia."

The bank lowered its benchmark interest rate to 4.75 percent at its last monetary policy meeting in August in a bid to bolster the economy as the global slowdown crimps overseas sales and weak sentiment slows consumer spending.

FARC PEACE TALKS

Colombia has attracted record foreign investment in the last few years as a military offensive against insurgent groups like the Marxist FARC makes once off-limits mountains and plains accessible to international oil and mining companies.

The $330 billion economy could attract as much as $17 billion in foreign direct investment this year, the government has said, up from about $2 billion in 2000.

President Juan Manuel Santos' bid to bring an end to five decades of war with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, would have a positive impact on the economy, Echavarria said, boosting growth by about two percentage points and allowing the bank to cut interest rates further.

While international companies in the booming oil and mining sector have largely ignored the rebel threat in the last several years - investing in previously no-go areas - peace with the rebels would bring a respite of attacks on wells and other economic infrastructure, helping them expand operations.

Echavarria said the economy would not feel the peace dividend immediately and could be affected if there is "a lot of trouble over the next year" but in the long term peace would bring "a lot of positives."

"Right now there is a lot of good news out of Colombia; the macro(economic) side has been well managed and I think psychologically, for an international investor, it will help a lot if peace is also reached," Echavarria said.

BANK INTERVENTION

The flood of foreign investment into Colombia has helped make its peso currency one of the strongest worldwide, prompting the government to pile pressure on the bank to prevent the firming currency from damaging the economy.

A strong peso hurts exporters and also some manufacturers who earn in dollars but pay costs and wages in pesos.

Echavarria said there was a limit to what the bank could do to ease gains in the currency, the fourth-biggest gainer worldwide this year, firming 7.1 percent so far this year.

Board members are "more or less in agreement" that intervention programs, like the current dollar purchase program of at least $20 million daily, are not that effective in managing movements in the currency, he said.

"Almost all international and Colombian studies demonstrate that they have a limited impact," said Echavarria, one of seven policymakers on the bank's board.

Santos on Friday reiterated a call for the bank to boost the level of intervention in the currency market.

"I think the bank could increase a little more its daily dollar purchases, it has the room and the reserves to do it," Santos told a conference of exporters in Medellin.

"The government too will continue buying dollars; we will use the excess we have in the Treasury for the purchases and we'll continue with the policy of keeping our savings overseas," said Santos, a former finance minister.

The central bank has been buying as much as $20 million a day since February and last month it said it would purchase $700 million in the foreign exchange market from the end of August through September in an effort to stem gains by the peso.

The government has bolstered efforts of the bank, buying at least $800 million over the past few weeks.

title: GLOBAL YIELD: Emerging Mkt  Currencies  Steal Bonds' Thunder
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Bond investors, be aware: if you want to boost returns in emerging markets, stay away from government debt and go for pure plays in currencies.

Surging food, energy and raw material prices have spurred rising inflation worldwide, forcing central banks from Asia and Europe to Latin America to raise interest rates, while allowing local currencies to appreciate to keep price pressures from running out of control.

The policies have prompted a switch in investment strategies as rising interest rates push up bond yields, reducing the value of fixed income securities. Bond prices fall when yields rise. Bonds are also less attractive amid concerns over inflation, which eats into their fixed interest payments over time.

"A strengthening currency probably is one of the more popular policy tools central banks are going to utilize, along with higher interest rates, over the next year or two," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

Chamie said some of the best destinations for currency bets are Brazil, Russia, Mexico and Colombia where economic fundamentals are sound, central banks are hawkish and expected to rapidly tackle inflation. On the other hand, he recommended investors shun currencies in South Africa, South Korea, India and Argentina.

Brazil stands out as a popular choice. The local central bank has tightened interest rates by 100 basis points this year, pushing up its key rate to 12.25%, among the highest in the world. Brazil began to hike rates in April, after being on hold since September.

The rate increases came as inflation in May stood at 5.58%, well above the central bank's target of 4.5%. There is growing concern that food-led price pressures will spill over into wages and other sectors if left unattended.

"Brazil's real is still attractive," said Igor Arsenin, an emerging-market fixed-income strategist at Credit Suisse Group in New York. "I expect interest rates to rise significantly further in Brazil."


 
   Rising Ruble 
 

Arsenin said he expected Brazil's central bank to boost the key rate to 14.25% by the end of the year and the Brazil real, which traded at BRL1.6151 to the dollar Monday, to strengthen below BRL1.6 against the dollar over the same period.

The real has risen 9.35% against the dollar so far this year, while the Mexican peso, Russian ruble and the Colombian peso have gained 5.96%, 4.05%, and 18.1%, respectively, over the same period.

Monday, Brazil's 10-year government debt yielded 5.578%, higher than the 4.16% on offer on 10-year Treasurys.

Dario Pedrajo, who manages $100 million at Kapax Investment Advisers LLC in Miami, targeted the Russian ruble, whose value has been artificially held back by the local government.

With the Russian government shifting its attention to the fight against inflation, it may allow greater appreciation in the ruble against the dollar, making this a good time to bet on the currency's gains, he said. The ruble was trading at RUB23.6607 to the dollar Monday.

Pedrajo also noted that the Russian ruble is a better bet than the Chinese yuan because he doesn't expect a significant appreciation in the yuan in the foreseeable future.

The yuan, which traded at CNY6.8740 to the dollar Monday, has gained 5.05% this year and has risen more than 20% since a dollar peg was removed in July 2005.


 
   Risks 
 

Still, such currency bets aren't without risks - as seen in the past month with the dollar's rebound against its major rivals amid the shifting interest rate outlook.

The market is now betting on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by the end of the year, a sharp reversal from several months ago when rate futures markets were discounting additional rate cuts.

Bets on higher rates, however, were moderated last week after The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times reported that Fed officials were divided on tightening and a rate hike may not be a sure thing.

The swings in Fed rate expectations fueled fluctuations in bonds and currency markets, adding to the risks of currency bets.

"Investors need to be aware of the fact that markets remain extremely nervous," said Chamie. "Currency bets need to be a very selective process."

Investors also need to be mindful that some emerging market governments may intervene to limit the appreciation of their currencies to protect their exporters. Rising currencies make local products less competitive in international markets.

In Latin America, governments in Chile and Colombia are looking to contain gains in their currencies by intervening in foreign exchange markets. Since April, Chile has been buying $50 million a day to reverse the Chilean peso's appreciation. Colombia Friday said it plans to buy $20 million a day in currency markets.

(Min Zeng writes about Treasurys markets for Dow Jones Newswires.)

title: Colombian cenbank faces struggle in curbing peso
text:
BOGOTA, June 5 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank will find it increasingly tough to curb the peso's appreciation with currency market interventions without threatening the inflation target for this year, a bank official said on Tuesday.   

Fernando Tenjo, one of the seven central bank board members, noted the conflict between the bank snapping up dollars to slow the peso's surge against the U.S. currency while also attracting foreign capital by hiking interest rates to ease inflationary pressures.   

Short-term foreign capital is flowing into Colombia attracted by interest rates but at the same time pressuring the local currency, which has appreciated around 17 percent so far this year against the greenback.   

"To step into the currency market at the same time we are bringing up the interest rates in Colombia along with the rest of the world could practically become suicide," Tenjo said at a conference. "This works against us and against Colombians."   

Colombia's central bank has raised its key interest rate 2.75 percentage points since April last year to the current 8.75 percent. But Tenjo did not say whether the bank had considered abandoning its current policy of hiking rates.   

The central bank has also purchased around $4.9 billion in the currency market this year directly or through auctions, but has failed to arrest a 19.25 percent climb in the peso <COP=RR> over the last 12 months.   

Central bank director Jose Dario Uribe recently told Congress that compared with Colombia's gross domestic product, the recent currency purchases could be considered the largest intervention of any such institution in the world.   

Colombia's 12-month inflation had reached 6.23 percent by May, and analysts forecast that it will now be difficult for Colombia to reach its consumer price target for the year of between 3.5 percent and 4.5 percent.   

Most experts estimate that the central bank will keep hiking its interest rate to 9 percent or more.   

"We intervene in the currency market only when we do not put in danger the inflation target and it is more difficult now to make these two objectives compatible and still combat inflationary pressures," Tenjo said.   

Colombia's economy is growing rapidly, driven by domestic demand and the flow of foreign investment. The gross domestic product expanded 6.8 percent last year, and the government expects growth of between 5 percent and 5.5 percent this year.

title: DJ  Colombia  Peso Weakens A Bit As Treasury  Intervenes ,Stocks Dn
text:
BOGOTA, May 29, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

Colombia's peso Tuesday weakened slightly as the Treasury intervened in the spot market to stop the rapid appreciation of the local currency amid an active session.   

The Colombian peso closed at COP1,917.00 to the U.S. dollar, but that was after it hit COP1,900.00 in midmorning from the COP1,916.25 closing mark Monday.   

Total trading volume reached $1.21 billion, the fourth highest volume so far this year. That compares with a daily average of $694 million in April.   

Investment bank Corficolombiana said in a report the peso appreciated earlier in the session tracking other currencies such as the Mexican peso and the Brazilian real.   

"However, when the local currency reached COP1,900 the Treasury intervened driving the currency to a maximum of COP1,933," Corficolombiana said.   

The Colombian peso has appreciated 16.8% so far this year even though the government last week announced capital controls on foreign portfolio investment and even as the central bank bought $4.52 billion in the spot market in the first four months of the year.   

On Friday, Finance Minister Oscar Ivan Zuluaga said the government is open to introducing new measures in an effort to stop the strong appreciation of the peso.   

The government will also evaluate whether to extend a measure introduced Wednesday forcing foreign portfolio holders to deposit 40% of their investments in an account at the central bank for six months without interest.   

The measure complements two measures announced more than three weeks ago designed to discourage capital inflows.   

In the equity market, the Colombian benchmark stock index retreated 0.1% to 10,139.10 points, the fourth consecutive decline following the capital controls measure.   

The stock market increased at the opening of the session, but retreated, tracking the U.S. stock market's early decline Tuesday, Corficolombiana added.   

The sharpest drop came from textile company Fabricato (FABRICATO.OB), which retreated 2.5% to COP57.50. Fabricato was the most heavily traded stock with about a third of Tuesday's total trading volume ot COP64.20 billion.   

Preferred shares of the country's largest bank Bancolombia (BCOLOMBIA.BO) decreased 0.8% to COP13,500.   

In the debt market, the yield on the benchmark peso denominated TES maturing in 2020 fell 0.019 percentage point to 9.855%.

title: Emerging Mkt Debt Flat; Turkey Stable On Early Vote Prospects
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market bonds were confined to narrow ranges on Wednesday, with Turkish assets hanging onto the previous session's gains as the country geared up for potential early general elections.   

Spreads on  JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus were unchanged at 162 basis points over Treasurys, with lightly positive returns of 0.01%. Brazil's Global 2040, a benchmark for the asset class, dropped 1/8 to 135 13/16 bid, according to Reuters, while its EMBI+ spread was flat at 153 basis points over Treasurys.   

Turkey's Global 2030 fell 5/8 to 154 11/16 bid and its EMBI+ spread widened one basis point to 206 basis points over Treasurys. But returns were 0.06% on the day. A parliamentary committee approved Wednesday a proposal to hold general elections on July 22. The general assembly could approve the date as early as Thursday.   

Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan had called for early elections on June 24, but Turkey's electoral board proposed July 22 instead. Turkish markets rebounded Wednesday as investors saw early elections as a way to relieve tensions between the ruling moderate Islamist AK Party and the military-backed secularists.   

Turkey is facing an "intense situation," said George Estes of GMO, which has $5.5 billion in emerging market debt under management, but he's "not convinced that it will affect the economy or the credit."   

JPMorgan said Wednesday it has cut Turkey to marketweight in its EMBI Global model portfolio on "heightened political uncertainty." The investment house also downgraded Ukraine. On the EMBI Global, Ukraine's risk premium tightened four basis points to 155 basis points over Treasurys.   

Venezuela's Global 2027 tumbled 3/8 to 122 3/8 bid and its EMBI+ spread widened two basis points to 224 basis points over Treasurys. President Hugo Chavez has declared his intention to pull out of the International Monetary Fund. Analysts note, however, that Venezuela's sovereign bonds carry a convenant that characterizes withdrawal from the IMF as an event of default. Bear Stearns downgraded Venezuelan sovereign debt to underperform on Wednesday on these "technical default" concerns, but acknowledged that the practical implications are unclear because most Venezuelan bonds trade above par.   

Colombia's Global 2033 rose 1/4 to 148 3/4 bid and its EMBI+ spread tightened two basis points to 135 basis points over Treasurys. President Alvaro Uribe has called on his economic team and the central bank to slow the peso's appreciation and curb speculative inflows. Given that inflation is rising in Colombia, the central bank has limited ability to intervene in the foreign exchange market to weaken the peso,  Goldman Sachs noted Wednesday.   

"This should then rekindle fears that the (government) could adopt other types of less market friendly measures to deal with (peso) strengthening," Goldman said.   

On the EMBI Global, the Dominican Republic tightened one basis point to 174 basis points over Treasurys. Moody's Investors Service upgraded the country's sovereign credit rating to B2 from B3 on Wednesday. The move brings Moody's in line with  Standard & Poor's and Fitch Ratings, both of which rate the Dominican Republic single-B - equivalent to Moody's B2.

title: DJ  Colombia  Peso Weakens Sharply On Ctrl Bk Measure, Intervention
text:
BOGOTA, Mar 30, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

Colombia's peso weakened sharply after the central bank introduced a measure to stop the galloping peso. The foreign exchange market recorded its highest trading volume since 1997 when the central bank began tracking the data.   

The Colombian peso closed at 2,202.30 to the dollar, compared with COP2,147.80 on Thursday. Total trading volume jumped to $1.50 billion on Friday, compared with a daily volume of $903.7 million in February.   

The peso weakened after the central bank introduced a measure under which it aims to reduce the amount of pesos in the financial system by offering to pay interest to commercial banks that hand over their excess cash.

title: Colombia's Jan-Aug Trade Surplus $1.029 Bln -DANE
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia posted a trade surplus of $1.029 billion during the first eight months of the year, widening from a surplus of $621.9 million in the same year-earlier period, according to official data published late Thursday.  

The larger surplus is attributed to a surge in exports, which were up 30% in the period to $13.72 billion, government statistics department DANE said.  

DANE said coal exports rose 55% between January and August to $1.706 billion as the country benefitted from rising commodity prices. Oil exports rose 32% between January and August to $3.46 billion.  

In August alone, Colombian exports totaled $1.87 billion, up 24% from August 2004, due to a surge of traditional exports, especially higher revenues from coal and oil exports and to non-traditional exports. Non-traditional exports rose 6% to $929.4 million.  

Colombia posted its largest bilateral surplus in the first eight months of the year - $1.683 billion - with the U.S. The strong surplus with the U.S. is partly due to the Andean Trade Preferences and Drug Eradication Act, or ATPDEA, an accord that gives tariff-free access on goods to the U.S. market in exchange for cooperation in clamping down on illegal drugs. Colombian exports of leather goods, textiles and clothing, among others, have skyrocketed, due to the ATPDEA.  

The second-largest trade surplus was with neighboring Venezuela, where an economic recovery has been taking place.  

Market participants were particularly pleased with the export figure, which rose despite the strengthening of the peso. A stronger currency would normally erode the competitiveness of non-traditional exports and spur imports. The peso has appreciated 4.7% so far this year, despite constant central bank intervention.  

-By Diana Delgado, Dow Jones Newswires; 573153088934; colombia@dowjones.com [ 03-11-05 2250GMT ]

Strong portfolio and foreign direct investment inflows, remittances from Colombians living overseas and trade-related flows should also boost the peso.

title: Colombia  Fin Min: To Continue  Intervening  In  Forex  Mkts
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Colombia's Finance Minister Alberto Carrasquilla said Sunday that Colombian authorities will continue intervening in the foreign exchange market to stem the peso's rise against the dollar.  

"As long as inflation keeps coming down, as long as interest rates don't give us the sense that there is turmoil in the future...as long as we keep meeting fiscal targets, we will continue to intervene," he said in an interview with reporters.  

Asked if he saw any fiscal or monetary clouds on the horizon that would make the Colombian authorities stop intervening, Carrasquilla said: "Not at all...I don't see interest rates going up, I don't see inflationary expectations going up, I don't see models showing us that inflation should be a concern."  

Colombia's peso gained to its strongest level since August 2002 on Friday to COP2,288.75 against the U.S. dollar. It has appreciated nearly 4% against the dollar this year on heavy portfolio inflows, foreign direct investment, strong export revenue and remittances from Colombians living abroad.  

The peso has gained despite interventions worth $2.8 billion so far from the central bank. In August alone, the central bank bought a net $999.6 million in the local foreign exchange market in what was considered its strongest intervention ever in a single month. [ 09-25-05 1731ET ]  

Carrasquilla said that the Colombian government will continue to work toward better debt liability management, and is interested in repurchasing more debt that it issued overseas if market conditions remain favorable.  

Responding to a question on whether he plans more debt buybacks, such as the transaction Colombia conducted earlier this month, Carrasquilla said: "Yes I do."  

Earlier in September, the Colombian government bought back around $1.1 billion in overseas debt and issued $500 million in longer-dated paper to improve its debt profile and remove less liquid bonds from the market, he said.  

"We reduced the external exposure of our debt by $600 million," he said. "We are always looking for the opportunity to improve the characteristics of our debt, in size, composition, duration, rollover risk, currency risk - all of the dimensions."  

He said the Colombian government doesn't need to go to the market to fund its budget needs for 2006 as it has already raised the money. "But that doesn't mean we won't do trades. As long as conditions are good, we will do it in terms of enhancing our curve, or even going for more prefinancing."  

He said that tapping the international capital markets for its 2007 financing needs this year is a "possibility."  

There is currently a lot of enthusiasm among investors for emerging market paper and the risk premium on bonds from those issuers is currently trading at historic lows.  

Carrasquilla also said the government may issue more peso-denominated bonds in the overseas market, just as it did at the end of 2004. Earlier this month, Brazil also issued its first-ever real denominated bond in the external debt market in a placement that was highly successful.  

"We are certainly interested in issuing more" peso-denominated bonds overseas, he said. But he noted that the existing peso-denominated overseas bond has some liquidity problems. Carrasquilla said that he can't say whether issuing peso-denominated debt is better than dollar-denominated bonds.  

The finance minister said his economy continues to sustain a growth rate in the 4% area. He said that foreign direct investment in Colombia is likely to exceed earlier expectations of $3 billion this year. Carrasquilla forecasts FDI this year at $3.5 billion, a 40% jump from 2004.

title: UPDATE 2- Colombia  to continue "aggressive"  FX intervention
text:

BOGOTA, Colombia, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Colombia will continue "aggressive" intervention in the foreign exchange market to stop the peso appreciating against the dollar and plans to help businesses hurt by the currency's strength, Finance Minister Alberto Carrasquilla said on Thursday.  

The government now expects the peso <COP=> to be stronger next year than it had originally thought and has altered its forecast for the average 2006 exchange rate to 2,400 per dollar from 2,498, the minister told reporters.  

"We are going to continue supporting intervention in the foreign exchange market. They have been particularly aggressive and will continue to be so. We support them, we back them and we are united with the central bank on that issue," Carrasquilla said.  

Asked how long the authorities would continue buying dollars in the foreign exchange market, Carrasquilla replied: "Until the limits of fiscal and monetary prudence, which are a long way off at the moment."  

Carrasquilla on Wednesday described the effect of the high peso, which makes it harder for Colombian exports to compete, as a "foreign exchange hurricane". He said the government was preparing measures to assist businesses hurt by the strength of the peso, but gave no details.  

The peso has risen by almost 10 percent against the U.S. dollar over the past 12 months, due to factors including high interest rates offered by Colombian government bonds, foreign direct investment, a trade surplus and remittances from Colombians working abroad.  

The rise has come despite dollar purchases by the central bank totaling $5.75 billion since the beginning of 2004 and purchases by the government of at least an additional $700 million.  

The purchases have been accompanied by large government bond sales to make sure the excess pesos do not cause inflation, in a process known as "sterilization".  

But eventually continued dollar purchases could cause inflation, warned Alberto Ramos, a senior economist at Goldman Sachs in New York.  

"So far the heavy partially sterilized intervention has not conflicted with the inflation target due to the significant increase in the demand for pesos, by both residents and non-residents, at the positive impact of FX appreciation on tradable inflation. However, such a conflict is bound to arise at a later stage if intervention flows of the magnitude we have seen recently continue," Ramos said in a research note.  

The peso was slightly weaker on Thursday at 2,298 per dollar, after closing at 2,292 on Wednesday.  

This minor depreciation was caused partly by suspicions the central bank could announce interest rate cuts at its board meeting on Friday, traders said.

title: Colombia peso closes strongly as inflows rise

Foreign capital inflows to Colombia grew by 16.7 percent in the first seven months of this year compared with the same 2004 period, the central bank said.  

But the growth rate of inflows in the first seven months of 2005 marked a slowdown from the 19.6 percent recorded in the first six months of the year, the bank said.  

The stronger the peso, the more expensive Colombia's exports are overseas.  

Many Colombian exporters are expected to earn record revenue this year thanks to high global prices for coal, oil and coffee. Other exporters, such as those in the Andean country's huge flower business, are not benefiting from high international prices and say the strong peso threatens to put them out of business.  

In the first seven months of 2005, foreign capital inflows totaled $7.896 billion, compared with $6.785 billion from January though July 2004.  

Inflows during the first seven months of the year from exports of commodities and industrial goods totaled $2.582 billion, an expansion of 29.7 percent. The gain marked a slowdown from 36.2 percent in the first half.  

Remittances from Colombians working overseas totaled $1.969 billion in the January though July period, up 8.66 percent from the 2004 period, but under the 10-percent growth in the first half of the year.

title: UPDATE 2-Colombia  central bank  cuts rates by 25 bps.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank on Friday cut its money market intervention rates by 25 basis points and heeded a call from President Alvaro Uribe who expressed hope lower rates would stem a rise in the peso.   

Analysts had not expected the bank to follow Uribe's advice, although the bank said it was justified by low inflationary pressures. The president has said he fears a stronger peso will reduce Colombia's export earnings.   

"The decision was taken after analyzing medium-and long-term inflation projections," the bank said in a news release to announce the cuts after a board meeting.   

Colombian consumer prices rose by 5.82 percent in the 12 months to the end of November, putting the country on course to meet its 2004 inflation target of 5.0-6.0 percent.   

The bank's general manager Miguel Urrutia added at a news conference: "We take what has happened recently with the exchange rate into account when we analyze future inflation."   

The bank cut its minimum repurchase agreement rate to 6.5 percent. The repo rate is the one at which the bank lends short term to commercial banks.   

The minimum repo rate is only available in quotas. The bank also cut its "lombard" repo rate, for which loans have no fixed limit, to 10.25 percent.   

The bank cut its minimum reverse repo rate to 5.5 percent and its lombard reverse repo rate to 4.5 percent.   

Lower interest rates should weaken the peso by reducing returns for foreigners investing in Colombian assets, such as TES treasury bonds.   

But relatively high interest rates attracting dollars to Colombia are only part of the reason for the strength of the peso, which has risen by more than 15 percent over the past 12 months.   

The peso has also been bolstered by improving security after 40 years of guerrilla war, and by rising exports and remittances from Colombian workers abroad.   

The rate cut came three days after Uribe announced restrictions on short-term foreign investment in treasury bonds and stocks, another measure meant to restrain the local currency.   

The bank's first rate reduction since March, when it also made a 25-basis-point cut, did not phase the peso , which closed 10.5 pesos higher per greenback at 2,353 on Friday.   

The bank also said it would continue intervening in foreign exchange markets in 2005. So far this year, it has together with the government bought about $3 billion in U.S. currency in a bid to hold back the peso.   

The bank also said it would complete this year its planned sale of $180 million in foreign reserves to the government, which wants to use them to pay off foreign debt.   

It has also agreed with the government to study the possibility of more such sales in 2005. The bank's reserves currently stand at more than $13 billion.   

As of next year, the bank said it will begin to pay interest to local financial institutions which deposit pesos in central bank vaults. The measure is aimed at reducing the inflationary impact of dollar purchases.

title: INTERVIEW-Colombia needs fiscal reforms for surplus-minister.
text:
NEW YORK, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Colombia's economy is recovering but tax and pension reforms are needed to improve the government's fiscal situation, Finance Minister Alberto Carrasquilla told Reuters on Thursday.    

 "The most important issue for us is to reduce the ratio of debt to GDP, and among the six reform bills in Congress, the pension system reform is the most important," Carrasquilla said in an interview.    

 Currently, the government uses 3.14 percent of its income to pay pensions, but pension expenditures are up 5 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP).    

 If the constitutional amendment is passed, then pension expenditures would likely go down to 3.8 percent of GDP, Carrasquilla said.    

 In addition, if the tax reform is passed, the government would earn an extra 0.66 percent of GDP and be able to cover the pension expenditures to 3.8 percent.    

 "But the pension problem is one of liquidity," he said.    

 Colombia's public debt should fall to 52 percent of gross domestic product this year, the International Monetary Fund said early this month.    

 PENSIONS AND TAXES    

 Colombia might struggle to persuade international markets to buy 30 year bonds right now, though a temporary tax surcharge to service the debt might be an inducement.    

 The second possibility would be to charge temporary taxes that would be given back later.    

 But the country's best bet to solve its liquidity problem, after passing the pension and tax bills, would be to issue a 20-year bond to Colombia's private pension funds, which are flooded with money as many contributors are young.    

 "We would issue bonds to the funds as they don't need the amount of liquidity that they have right now, and in 20 years, when they start needing that cash, we will give it back," Carrasquilla said. "But they will not negotiate with us until we have passed those amendments in Congress."    

 The tax reform, which proposes expanding Colombia's value-added tax, or VAT, to basics like milk and medical services, faces tough opposition in Congress.    

 Santiago Castro, chairman of the Lower House Economic Affairs Committee, said on Wednesday he would have to water down the proposal to ensure passage.    

 Supporters say the bill is key to ensuring Colombia's long-term solvency, while the government tries to end a costly four-decade-old guerrilla war that kills thousands every year.    

 But with 60 percent of Colombians living in poverty and many struggling to eat, it will be difficult to convince lawmakers who want to be reelected in 2006.    

 Carrasquilla said the tax taken from the poor would be given back - possibly in the form of food coupons - but the tax taken from the well-off would be used half for social policies for the poor and the other half for fiscal adjustments.    

 "Public expenditure has always been the way to do social justice. If there is a Value Aggregate Tax there has to be social policies in place," the minister said.    

CURRENCY, ENERGY AND IMF    

 However, Colombia's economy is growing by 4 percent or more a year, supported by market confidence.    

 Colombia's currency  has been rising, pushed up by capital inflows, a rise in stocks, real estate and private investment, Carrasquilla said.    

Colombia has intervened in the currency market by around $2 billion or 2 percent of GDP, and by the end of the year the Central Bank would have bought US$3 billion.    

 In terms of exploration and production in the oil sector, Carrasquilla said contractual conditions and security issues have substantially improved.    

 "In order to recuperate production levels of 700,000 barrels a day we need to explore 60 wells per year taking into account probability of success and our geography," he said.    

 In 1999 only 6 wells were explored due to lack of funds and unappealing contracts.    

 "The 'State Take', or the portion that the country takes from the venture, was worse than in Cuba," the minister said. "There was no incentive for private companies."    

 This year Colombia is to have explored 35 new wells.    

 Also, with a strong economic recovery, Colombia is looking to graduate from the International Monetary Fund loan program soon. "We want to graduate. We are not in a crisis anymore. We don't need that backing, and we can do it taking half a step," he said.    

 The current agreement is a stand-by of two years with 100 percent of the quota, but Colombia would want an agreement of one year or less-than two years, with 50 percent of the quota.    

 The current quota is $2.2 billion. (Reporting by Manuela Badawy, editing by Toni Reinhold; Reuters Messaging: manuela.badawy.reuters.com@reuters.net; Tel +1 646 223 6055)).
