title: UPDATE 2-Colombia Cenbank cuts rates by 25 basis points.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank cut all of its intervention rates by 25 basis points on Friday, aiming to add fuel to the country's economic recovery with the first easing of monetary policy in well over a year.  

Analysts surveyed by Reuters had widely expected monetary policy to be left unchanged, saying they thought a February rate cut would be premature given uncertainty on the year's inflation outlook.  

Colombia has agreed to meet a 2004 inflation target of 5-6 percent, plus or minus two percentage points, under a $2.1 billion loan accord with the International Monetary Fund.  

But acting bank manager, Jose Dario Uribe, said the low-inflationary environment - despite a brightening outlook for economic growth - made it an opportune time to cut rates.  

"The decision was taken after analyzing the inflation forecasts in the medium-and long-term, the low trend of basic inflation and inflation forecasts, and the situation in the foreign exchange market," he said, reading a statement.  

The bank cut its minimum repurchase agreement to 7.00 percent, its Lombard repo rate to 10.75 percent, its minimum reverse repo rate to 6.00 percent, and its Lombard reverse repo rate to 5.00 percent.  

The move follows a recent appreciation of the peso , which has gained more than 8 percent against the U.S. dollar in 12 months to Feb. 20.  

The government, worried the appreciating currency could hurt exports and sap growth, is actively trying to tighten supply of greenbacks to restrain the local currency. President Alvaro Uribe has been publicly calling for lower interest rates since last year.  

The Colombian economy expanded by 3.5 percent in 2003, its fastest rate in six years, according to preliminary government figures. The government forecasts growth of 3.8 percent in 2004.  

Finance Minister Alberto Carrasquilla told reporters that he hoped the rate cut would translate into cheaper consumer credit, and stimulate demand for pesos.  

The last adjustment to rates was on April 28, 2003, when they were raised across-the-board by 1 percentage point.  

Colombia Central Bank has not cut rates since 2002. That year, monetary policy makers slashed intervention rates by an across-the-board 325 basis points.  

The Andean nation met its 2003 IMF inflation target. But its 6.49 percent rise in consumer prices slightly breached a voluntary Central Bank target of 6.0 percent.

title: UPDATE 3-Colombia's Uribe asks cenbank to halt peso rise.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, May 14 (Reuters) - Colombian President Alvaro Uribe Wednesday called for the Central Bank to halt the strengthening of the peso, and the currency dropped against the U.S. dollar after his statement. 

 "We trust that the Bank of the Republic (Central Bank) will take all the measures to comply with what we said in January - keep the exchange rate in the levels it was at in January, keep it stable in real terms and at a competitive level for economic recovery," Uribe told reporters. 

 Uribe's call was the latest volley in a so-far unsuccessful campaign to pressure the Central Bank to moderate interest rates. On April 28 the bank raised intervention rates by one percentage point to ensure Colombia meets inflation targets, snubbing earlier government calls to hold rates unchanged to protect growth. 

 The Central Bank's board is next due to meet on Friday. 

 Traders expect it will leave rates unchanged. 

 Colombian 2012 TES bonds are yielding 14.14 percent, a return attractive enough to lure investors into pesos. 

 The peso slipped sharply following the president's remarks, falling 1.66 percent to close at 2,843 per U.S. dollar. On Tuesday, it had closed up 1.08 percent at 2,796 - its highest level against the greenback since Dec. 5. 

 At Wednesday's opening price, the peso was up 3.8 percent against the dollar over the past month. It started January at 2,865 per dollar. 

 The peso lost 25 percent of its value against the dollar in 2002, far outpacing depreciation forecasts from both the government and the private sector. 

 The Central Bank frets that the peso fall increased inflationary expectations and pushed up debt servicing costs for both government and companies. 

 The bank's interest rate rise last month was a bid to keep 2003 inflation at the maximum 5.5 percent agreed under the terms of a $2.1 billion loan accord with the International Monetary Fund. 

 But the government wants a competitive peso to ensure the health of Colombia's export sector, which has been hit by a sharp economic contraction and draconian currency controls in former number two market Venezuela. 

 Solid economic growth and cutting a 17 percent unemployment rate are vital to Uribe's hopes of eradicating the poverty which feeds Colombia's four-decade-old war and its massive cocaine industry. He also needs a robust economy to keep fiscal accounts in order as he boosts military spending by a third. 

 The government expects Latin America's fifth-largest economy to expand by 2 percent this year, after anemic 1.5 percent growth in 2002. 

 "During this government, we are not going to go back to the revaluations that did so much damage to the country, which affected employment and production so much," Uribe said. 

 The bank had no plans to respond to Uribe, a spokesman said. 

 Analysts doubted the president's call would have much influence on the seven-member board, over which Finance Minister Roberto Junguito presides. 

 "Its decisions are always based on the long-term and we think this rise in the peso is transitory," said one Bogota analyst, asking not to be named.

title: Colombia Ctrl Bk Keeps Inflation Goal Despite Peso Slide
text:
BOGOTA -(Dow Jones)- Colombia's central bank doesn't think a recent slide by the country's peso ($1=COP2664) endangers the official 6.0% inflation projection for 2002, bank governor Miguel Urrutia told a news conference Friday. 

 Urrutia told Dow Jones Newswires after the press conference that year-to-date depreciation is close to 15%. 

 "We believe 15% isn't enough to have effects for the inflation target," he said. "It's manageable, although what we don't know is how much the year's depreciation will end up at." 

 He added that an exchange rate at around the current level is probably good for the economy, as it helps exporters without putting too much pressure on local prices. 

 But he added that sharp movements and volatility in the exchange rate are not desirable, "and that's why we intervene sometimes," he said. 

Colombia's central bank this week sold $266 million to the market, through the exercise of dollar call options, to support the sagging peso. 

 The peso has floated freely since 1999, but anti-volatility rules - triggered for the first time Monday - require the bank to intervene by selling call options whenever a day's average exchange rate is 4.0% above the 20-day moving average. 

 Analysts say the effect of currency erosion on inflation is muted by the relatively low weighting imports have in the basket of goods and services used for Colombia's consumer price index. 

 Most food - the heaviest weighted group, with 30% of the total - is produced locally. And while international oil prices influence gasoline costs, Colombia's government intervenes to smooth these locally. 

 A Dow Jones Newswires survey of seven analysts Friday produced an average inflation projection of 6.05% for 2002 as a whole.

title: UPDATE 2- Colombia intervenes  in  forex  market to buoy peso.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, Aug 1 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank said on Thursday it sold $180 million in dollar-purchase options to support the country's sinking peso , but the bank's second intervention in a week failed to halt the currency's slide. 

 Nervous markets have slashed nearly 9 percent off the peso's value in the past week, partly over worries about Colombia's swelling public debt and debt load. 

 But the pummeling is also due to fallout from regional financial crisis spreading northward from Brazil and Argentina. Risk-weary investors are selling off the peso, and banks are buying dollars after seeing their stocks of greenbacks cut in half since December. 

 The Central Bank said $69 million, or about 38 percent, of the dollar-purchase options sold on Thursday were exercised later in the day. The options were valid through Aug. 30 and carried a rate of 2,636 per dollar. 

 The peso, meanwhile, lost a slight 0.05 percent of its value on Thursday, closing at 2,639 per dollar. It opened stronger against Wednesday at 2,627 pesos per dollar. 

 The peso has lost about 13 percent of its value so far this year. Its accentuated slide against the greenback compares with a Central Bank forecast of an 8 percent depreciation for all of 2002 and a loss of just 2.7 percent against the dollar last year. 

 Until this week, the Central Bank had not intervened in the currency market since floating the peso in 1999. 

 But the Central Bank on Wednesday relaxed guidelines on future foreign exchange interventions to give itself more leeway to support the currency. 

 The bank said that, after Thursday, it was scrapping the $180 million limit on future forex option auctions as well as a rule stopping it from intervening again until all options are exercised. 

 The Central Bank said on Tuesday that the country's banking system had seen its stock of dollars fall by 50 percent since December to $200 million. 

Central Bank General Manager Miguel Urrutia said on Friday there was no liquidity crisis or need for the government to raise foreign reserves, which early this week hovering near a record high with $10.81 billion. 

 The bank is forecasting that foreign reserves will total $10.48 billion at the end of 2002. 

 The war-torn Andean nation, fighting Marxist rebels for 38 years, ended 2001 with record high foreign reserves of $10.16 billion, surpassing an IMF-agreed minimum of $9.14 billion for the year.

title: Colombia 's  Central Bank  Tweaks  Forex Intervention  Rules
text:
BOGOTA -(Dow Jones)- Colombia's central bank board late Wednesday altered the conditions under which it must intervene to stabilize the local peso (COP). 

 The basic rule is unchanged. The bank must auction call options, through which it can sell $180 million to financial  institutions, whenever the benchmark Representative Market Rate, or TRM, is 4.0% above or below its 20-day moving average. The TRM is a weighted average exchange rate of the previous session's trades. 

 But the bank said in a statement that it has eliminated the additional requirement that all outstanding options be used. 

 The institution devised the antivolatility rules in 1999, when it scrapped the peso's fixed trading band against  the dollar and allowed the peso to float freely. 

Intervention was not triggered until Monday, when the bank held its first auction of call options. 

 The bank's second sale - covering $180 million - is Thursday. 

 The day's TRM is COP2636.30 to the dollar, which is above the COP2628.16 trigger level. The bank said all Monday's options have been exercised. 

 The peso strengthened slightly Wednesday, as financial institutions closed positions for the end of the month.

 But the currency is still down 12% against the dollar since the start of June, and has fallen 14% for 2002 to date. 

 Traders blame a shortage of dollar liquidity among local  financial institutions, jitters about Brazil's falling real  and anticipatory demand for dollars from nervous international companies.

title: UPDATE 1-Colombian peso slides despite Cenbank  intervention .
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, July 30 (Reuters) - Colombia's embattled peso closed sharply lower on Tuesday as concern over the country's growing debt load and Latin America's simmering financial crisis outweighed the effects of Monday's Central Bank intervention to support the currency, traders said. 

 The peso closed down 1.63 percent at a new historic low of 2,645 per U.S. dollar, in the seventh straight session of depreciation against the greenback. Trade, at $475 million, was healthy as financial institutions and companies bought U.S. currency to meet end-of-month financial obligations. 

 The peso had earlier touched 2,654 per dollar before pulling back. Local banks have been squeezed by reductions in their foreign credit lines over the past month over fears of regional economic contagion. 

 Colombian debt also suffered, both abroad and at home. The spread on Colombia's global bonds has now broadened to 801 points over U.S. Treasuries, up from 618 points on May 30. 

 The Central Bank sold $180 million in dollar options to local financial institutions on Monday in its first forex market intervention since the peso was floated in 1999. 

 The move, triggered automatically by a 4 percent decline over a 20-day period, was designed to halt a decline which has lopped more than 13 percent off the currency's value so far this year and has far outstripped a forecast by Central Bank officials of an 8 percent depreciation over all of 2002. 

 "The speculation continues. They (the Central Bank) haven't put out the fire, there is still demand for dollars," said Eduardo Reyes of brokerage Afin, citing regional woes as contributors to the peso's decline. 

 The peso fell a slight 2.7 percent against the dollar in 2001. 

 BRAZILIAN TREMOR SHAKES COLOMBIA 

 On top of Argentina's seemingly endless crisis, the market has been unnerved by signs that South American giant Brazil is staggering into election-year trouble. 

 The Brazilian real sank to a new record low of 3.305 per U.S. dollar before recouping to 3.260 at midday, down 7.5 centavos from Monday's close. It is almost 30 percent weaker than where it began the year. 

 In another Latin American financial trouble zone, Uruguay's peso plunged by nearly a quarter of its value after the Central Bank declared a bank holiday. 

 Markets are also increasingly worried over Colombia's rising debt levels, with its debt-to-GDP ratio at nearly 60 percent as of March, according to Central Bank data. 

 On Colombia's local debt market, domestic TES 2012 bonds spiked to 15.78 percent on the secondary market, after opening at 15 percent. 

 "This is very ugly. It's all because of the regional crisis. We're losing a lot of ground and lots of people are buying dollars and bailing out of TES because no one wants Colombian debt," a broker said. 

 Bogota currency traders were not overly concerned about the details of the 2003 budget bill, which was sent to Congress on Monday and must be approved this year. The proposed budget would push the fiscal deficit to 3.0 percent from an expected 2.6 percent this year, as the new government of President-elect Alvaro Uribe boosts defense and social spending to tackle a 38-year-old guerrilla war. 

 Uribe's designated finance minister, Roberto Junguito, told reporters in Washington he plans spending cuts in other areas and tax increases to help pay for the government's plans. Junguito, who plans to work closely with the International Monetary Fund, promised "fiscal stability in the mid-term". 

 He saw economic growth at a sluggish 1.0 percent in 2002 - below current government forecasts of 1.5 percent - but picking up to 2.5 percent next year.

title: UPDATE 3- Colombia  to make peso  intervention  Monday.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, July 26 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank will sell $180 million in dollar options on Monday to support the peso after the currency breached a 4-percent limit of depreciation over 20 days, the Central Bank said on Friday. 

 The intervention will be the first to buoy the peso - which has lost 12 percent against the U.S. dollar this year - since the currency was floated in September 1999. 

 "On Monday, the Central Bank will sell $180 million in dollar options," Miguel Urrutia, the bank's manager told reporters. 

 Earlier on Friday, the peso hit a new historic low, closing at 2,600 pesos per dollar, down 0.33 from Thursday. The Banking Superintendency later calculated the average exchange rate for Monday at 2,596 per dollar - enough to trigger an automatic intervention. 

 Under the Central Bank's rules, the institution is obliged to intervene in currency markets if the peso's average exchange rate in the last 20 day varies by more than 4 percent against the daily average exchange rate. 

 Urrutia said there was "no need" to raise foreign currency reserves - now at a record high - and added there was no dollar liquidity problem in the domestic market. 

 Colombia's foreign reserves stood at $10.86 billion in the week ended July 17 and the Central Bank is forecasting that foreign reserves will total $10.48 billion at the end of 2002. 

 Speaking to reporters after attending a government ceremony at the Presidential Palace, Urrutia said the exchange rate is "consistent" with a government forecast of current account deficit of 2 percent of gross domestic product for 2002. 

 Colombia posted a current account deficit of $384 million for the first quarter of 2002 - equivalent to about 1.8 percent of gross domestic product. In all of 2001, Colombia ran up a current account shortfall of $1.69 billion, equivalent to about 2 percent of GDP. 

 Although the country has no official target for the current account deficit with the International Monetary Fund, the IMF does monitor the figure as part of a $2.7-billion loan accord with the Andean nation. 

 PHLEGMATIC ABOUT DEPRECIATION 

 The government has been remarkably phlegmatic about the currency's depreciation - fueled by Colombia's foreign debt load and regional jitters spreading from Argentina and Brazil - saying it is not worried and that it should help exporters. 

 Local analysts have been taken by surprise by this year's fall and many are unsure about the currency's behavior over the rest of the year. 

 The currency of Latin America's fifth-largest economy - which benefits from large but hard to quantify illegal cash flows from cocaine sales - defied forecasts in 2001, when it hardly budged against the greenback. 

 Some analysts say that the peso could bounce back in 2002, buoyed by the lack of serious weaknesses in an economy that may be sluggish - the government is forecasting a growth of 1.5 percent in 2002 - but has not set off alarm bells. 

 Colombia's debt load - at about 60 percent of gross domestic product - has some economists concerned, especially since President-elect Alvaro Uribe plans big increases in military and social spending in a country gripped by a 38-year-old guerrilla war. Uribe takes office Aug. 7.

title: UPDATE 2- Colombia  peso hits new low amid  intervention  fears.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, July 26 (Reuters) - The Colombian peso fell to an historic low on Friday, prompting fears among local analysts that the Central Bank might intervene on Monday to support the currency. 

 The government, meanwhile, pegged a nominal depreciation for the peso at eight percent and a depreciation in real terms of 2 percent for all 2002, in line with previous estimates. 

 "We have not changed our goal of a nominal devaluation of 8 percent and 2 percent in real terms, and it should remain that way at year's end," Finance vice minister Federico Rengifo told reporters at the end of a Central Bank meeting. 

 The currency, which was floated in September 1999, has lost 12 percent against the U.S. dollar this year, fueled by Colombia's foreign debt load and regional jitters spreading from Argentina and Brazil. 

 On Friday, the peso slipped to an historic low, closing at 2,600 pesos per dollar. 

 Under the Central Bank's rules, the institution is obliged to intervene in currency markets if the peso's average exchange rate in the last 20 day varies by more than 4 percent against the daily average exchange rate. 

 The Banking Superintendency was set to calculate later on Friday the average exchange rate for Monday. According to local analysts, an average exchange rate of 2,596 pesos per greenback would prompt an auction of dollar-sale options for Monday. The Central Bank has not pronounced itself. 

 PHLEGMATIC GOVERNMENT 

 Although the peso came within a whisker of intervention two weeks ago, the government has been remarkably phlegmatic about the currency's depreciation, saying it is not worried and that it should help exporters. 

 Local analysts have been taken by surprise by this year's fall and many are unsure about the currency's behavior over the rest of the year. 

 The currency of Latin America's fifth-largest economy - which benefits from large but hard to quantify illegal cash flows from cocaine sales - defied forecasts in 2001, when it hardly budged against the greenback. 

 Some analysts say that the peso could bounce back in 2002, buoyed by the lack of serious weaknesses in an economy that may be sluggish - the government is forecasting a growth of 1.5 percent in 2002 - but has not set off alarm bells. 

 Colombia's debt load - at about 60 percent of gross domestic product - has some economists concerned, especially since President-elect Alvaro Uribe plans big increases in military and social spending in a country gripped by a 38-year-old guerrilla war. Uribe takes office Aug. 7. 

 On Friday, Rengifo also announced the government will auction in August $50 million in put options to bolster its foreign reserves. Colombia's foreign currency reserves are at a record high - they rose rose $43.6 million, or 0.4 percent, to $10.86 billion in the week ended July 17. 

 The Central Bank is forecasting that foreign reserves will total $10.48 billion at the end of 2002.

title: UPDATE 1- Colombia  peso weakens, but no Cenbank  intervention .
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, July 11 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso fell tantalizingly close to a four-percent limit for depreciation over 20 days on Thursday but the Central Bank said that it had not reached a key level which would trigger automatic intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 The peso was calculated at 2,506.84 per U.S. dollar on Thursday, just above the 2,507.66 limit which would have meant it had lost 4.0 percent over 20 days, the Banking Superintendency said. 

 According to data earlier in the afternoon from Colombia's electronic trading system, the peso had lost 0.38 percent to close at 2,509 per dollar on Thursday. This level would have been easily enough to trigger intervention by the Central Bank, which had said it was prepared to sell $180 million in options to sell dollars on Friday. 

 Thursday's market data showed the peso plumbing a new historic minimum for the 12th consecutive session in a slump fueled by Colombia's foreign debt load and regional jitters spreading northwards from Argentina and Brazil. 

 Any intervention would have been the first to buoy up the currency - which has lost 9.88 percent against the U.S. dollar this year - since before it was floated in September 1999. 

 Under Central Bank rules, the institution is obliged to intervene in the currency markets if the peso varies by at least 4 percent over 20 days. 

 Finance Minister Juan Manuel Santos earlier said the currency's depreciation was not worrying and should help exporters. 

 "If you look at the devaluation year-on-year, or for the year so far, it is a very modest depreciation and there is no reason for us to worry at all," Santos told reporters. 

 The currency of Latin America's fifth-largest economy - which benefits from large but hard to quantify illegal cash flows from cocaine sales - defied forecasts in 2001, when it hardly budged against the greenback. 

 The government's official estimate was for a depreciation of only 8.0 percent for all of this year. Local analysts have been taken by surprise by this year's fall and many are unsure about the currency's behavior over the rest of the year. 

 Some say that the peso could bounce back, buoyed by the lack of serious weaknesses in an economy that may be sluggish but has not set off alarm bells. 

 SANTOS SAYS A WEAKER PESO IS GOOD 

 "A devaluation is welcome, because it helps exporters regain lost competitiveness," Santos said. 

 Colombia's exports were down in the first four months of this year, at $3.87 billion compared to the $4.03 billion recorded from January to April of last year, although this was still enough to record a $207 million surplus. 

 Most of the country's exports come from areas like oil, coal and coffee, whose prices depend on international markets, but sales of products such as flowers, textiles and leather have grown strongly this year. 

 Some economists are concerned Colombia's debt load is getting too heavy - especially as President-elect Alvaro Uribe plans big increases in military and social spending in a country gripped by a 38-year-old guerrilla war. Gross public debt is at about 60 percent of gross domestic product. 

 But Colombia's foreign reserves are at a record high, at about $10.8 billion - well above targets agreed to under the three-year $2.7-billion loan accord with the International Monetary Fund.

title: UPDATE 1-Colombia cuts rates, pegs 2001 GDP growth 1.5 pct.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, Jan 18 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank cut its money market intervention rates on Friday, most by 50 basis points, in an effort to speed economic growth the finance ministry said exceeded 1.5 percent last year. 

 "We took this decision to fuel greater economic growth, and because we are doing well on the issue of inflation," said Finance Minister Juan Manuel Santos, who sits on the bank's weekly rate-setting meetings. 

 Under the terms of a three-year, $2.7 billion IMF loan agreement which expires at the end of this year, Colombia must meet an inflation target of 6 percent or less in 2002. It met all IMF-agreed targets last year, including key ceilings on inflation and the fiscal deficit. 

 "All of the models (for inflation) show that we will meet this 6 percent inflation target this year," Santos told reporters. 

 Analysts branded the Central Bank's decision on rates "aggressive." Friday's rate cut marked the first relaxation in monetary policy this year, and followed a 350 basis point reduction in intervention rates in 2001. 

 "It is aggressive. I don't know if the government and the Central Bank took this decision to nudge the economy and business, or if it is to (weaken the peso)," said Alexander Cardenas, an analyst at Bogota-based Acciones y Valores. 

 Colombia's peso has climbed in value against the dollar by 1.14 percent since the beginning of the year, following a much lower-than-expected 2 percent devaluation in the currency in 2001. 

 Santos said Colombia's economy grew by more than 1.5 percent last year, the same figure published by the government on Dec. 21. 

 With Friday's cut, Colombia's one-day reverse repurchase agreement rate now stands at 7.0 percent, down from 7.50 percent, while repos are at 8.0 percent, against 8.50 percent previously. 

 The "Lombard contraction rate," or the rate for reverse-repo outside-auction bank loans to the Central Bank, fell by 25 basis points to 6.0 percent. 

 The "Lombard expansion rate," or the rate for repo, outside-auction Central Bank loans to the financial system, were cut 50 basis points to 11.75 percent.

title: Colombian Cenbank more ready to  intervene  in peso.
text:
BOGOTA, Dec 26 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank said on Wednesday that it was modifying its foreign exchange market guidelines to allow it to intervene more strongly, even when faced with a smaller range of peso volatility. 

 Analysts said that the move was probably aimed at keeping a tight lid on Colombia's currency - which has been relatively stable over the past year - ahead of the presidential election in May. 

 The Bank will now permit itself to intervene in the foreign exchange market if the peso's average value shifts by more than 4.0 percent over a period of 20 working days, compared to a previous limit of 5.0 percent, it said in a news release. 

 The Bank also said it could now spend up to $180 million in a single day's intervention, compared to the previous limit of $120 million in a market which usually only sees daily trade of about $170 million. 

 Even though it is giving itself more leeway, the Central Bank has never needed to utilize its intervention mechanisms since it floated the peso in September 1999. 

Colombia's peso closed 0.52 percent lower against the U.S. dollar at 2,303 pesos on Wednesday, hit by what local traders said were government dollar purchases. But the peso has performed more strongly than expected in 2001, and has only retreated about 4 percent against the greenback over the year, compared to a fall of 19 percent in 2000. 

 Latin America's fifth-largest economy is wracked by a 37-year-old guerrilla war and will see economic growth of little more than 1.0 percent this year, but its government has had little trouble meeting its financing needs. 

 Next year's election of a successor to President Andres Pastrana could generate uncertainty, particularly regarding the fate of difficult and slow-moving peace talks with leftist rebels - which have been criticized by major candidates.

title: UPDATE 3-Colombia Cenbank cuts rates by 50 basis points.
text:
(Updates with market closing, Cenbank statement, paras 7-9,12,13) 

 BOGOTA, Colombia, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank on Friday cut its money market intervention rates by 50 basis points, slightly above market expectations, the bank's sixth rate reduction this year. 

 With the cut, Colombia's one-day reverse repurchase agreement rate stands at 7.75 percent, and repos are at 8.75 percent. 

 Of 27 analysts surveyed on Thursday by Reuters, 17 had forecast a rate cut of 25 basis points and six forecast a 50 basis point reduction. 

 Economists cheered the bank's decision, saying the move was justified by a declining inflation rate, a still sluggish Colombian economy and rate cuts this week by the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. 

 "I was expecting 25 (basis points), so this was a good surprise," said Alberto Bernal, a Colombia analyst at IDEA Global in New York. 

 "We are seeing significant coordination between world central banks ... I personally think there is room for further cuts if world interest rates continue doing what they're doing," he added. 

 Colombia's stock index rallied on the news to close 1.53 percent higher, as investors saw cheaper credit for indebted companies and likely more available cash to invest in shares. 

 "Since the drop was larger than expected, some investors may begin to seek higher yields and eventually that will be in the stock market," said one trader. 

 The peso currency ended virtually unchanged at 2,302 per dollar. 

 INFLATION TAME 

 Colombia, Latin America's fifth largest economy, is widely expected to meet an 8 percent ceiling for consumer inflation in 2001 as agreed with the IMF. Last week, it reported inflation of 0.19 percent in October, bringing consumer price increases to 7.16 percent for the first 10 months of the year. 

Intervention rates have fallen by 325 basis points since the beginning of the year. The bank last cut rates by a lower-than-expected 25 basis points on Oct. 12. 

 The Central Bank said in a statement the rate cut would not jeopardize its targets and forecast declining rates of inflation next year. 

 "Medium-term projections for inflation forecast a decline in this variable, consistent with achieving the 6 percent inflation target for the end of 2002," the bank said. 

 Although economists said that the rate reductions could put pressure on Colombia's ambitious 2002 inflation target, they said the cuts were crucial to reactivate the economy. 

 Colombia's $87 billion economy has been hit this year by Marxist-rebel bombings of key oil infrastructure, plunging coffee prices and a world economic slowdown which has weakened the market for the war-torn Andean nation's exports. 

 The country's 37-year-old guerrilla war has claimed 40,000 lives in the past decade alone, and the government has said the conflict annually shaves off about 25 percent from gross domestic product. 

 The government currently forecasts 2001 growth at between 2.2 percent and 2.4 percent, down from from 3.8 percent originally. 

 Colombia's peso has depreciated by 3.38 percent since the beginning of the year, far less than in other South American nations, including Brazil where the real has weakened by almost 23 percent.

title: INTERVIEW-Colombia's exports seen unchanged in 2001.
text:
CARTAGENA, Colombia, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Hopes of robust growth in Colombian exports for 2001 have been dashed by a strong peso and global economic slowdown, an industry leader said on Thursday. 

 Instead of a government forecast of 19 percent export growth to $15.50 billion this year, Colombian industry merely hopes to eke out the same level of exports posted in 2000. 

 "We hope to end the year with exports similar to last year, that is $13.1 billion," Javier Diaz, president of the Colombian Association of Exporters (Analdex), told Reuters. 

 Hit by a world economic slowdown, exports by Latin America's fifth-largest economy in the first six months of 2001 totaled $6.11 billion, down 3 percent from the $6.3 billion exported in the same period in 2000. In June, exports totaled $990.5 million, down 13.9 percent from the $1.15 billion exported in June of 2000. 

 Colombia's oil production - the country's top foreign currency earner - has suffered badly this year from guerrilla bomb attacks while coffee sales have plummeted due to the collapse in world coffee bean prices. 

 The government cut its growth forecast for 2001 in late July, pegging growth this year at 2.4 percent, down from a previous estimate of 3.8 percent. In 2000, Colombia's economy, boosted by strong exports, grew 2.8 percent. 

 A stronger peso has meant weaker exports, Diaz said. 

 Colombia's peso currency has only weakened 2.79 percent this year, well below inflation of 6.29 percent and a depreciation of 14 percent by the same time last year. 

 The drop of sales in oil and coffee has been offset by a strong performance in exports of nontraditional products including bananas, flowers and leather. Sales from such exports were 15.1 percent higher in the first half at $3.38 billion. 

 "We expect that during the second half of the year, the nontraditional exports will continue showing the same dynamism as they did in the first half so they compensate for the fall in traditional exports," Diaz said. 

 Speaking on the sidelines of a meeting by the National Association of Industrialists (ANDI) in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, Diaz said lower interest rates would jump start economic activity. 

 Coincidentally, Colombia's Central Bank slashed its money market intervention rates on Thursday by a higher-than-expected 100 basis points, citing a June economic slowdown and relative isolation from Argentina's debt default fears.

title: UPDATE 1-Colombia cuts rates 100 bps, shrugs off Argentina.
text:
(Updates throughout with analyst quotes, bank statement, background, market reaction) 

 BOGOTA, Colombia, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank slashed its money market intervention rates on Thursday by a higher-than-expected 100 basis points, citing a June economic slowdown and relative isolation from Argentina's debt default fears. 

 The Central Bank said in a statement that Colombia's peso was "relatively stable" even as fallout from Argentina punished currencies in Brazil and Chile, and added the rate cut would not affect 2001 and 2002 inflation targets. 

 The move surprised economists, who had forecast a much more conservative rate cut of between 20 and 50 basis points. Economists cheered the decision, however, saying it was sound and would help jump-start Latin America's fifth largest economy. 

 "Having really no direct links to Argentina, the economy is trading more in tune with the global economy. There's a slowdown, so the Central Bank is cutting rates," said Siobhan Manning, emerging market strategist at Italian investment bank Caboto. 

 Colombia peso currency strengthened on the news, rising to 2,285 per dollar, up from Thursday's open of 2,290. On the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Plus (EMBI+), Colombia's portion of the index widened 4 basis points over safe-haven U.S. Treasuries. 

 Despite a 37-year guerrilla war, Colombia has long enjoyed relative isolation in the face of debt woes ravaging neighboring economies. It has never defaulted on its debt, unlike Latin America's three biggest economies of Brazil, Mexico and Argentina. 

 Indeed, Colombia has been the second best emerging market performer on the EMBI+ this year, ranking only behind Russia. 

 It raised $325 million on Tuesday by reopening its 2020 global bond, tapping demand from regional investors who were seeking to diversify their exposure away from cash-strapped Argentina - the region's No. 3 economy and its biggest foreign borrower. 

 Colombia's peso currency has only weakened 2.79 percent this year, well below inflation of 6.29 percent and a depreciation of 14 percent by the same time last year. 

 "Uncertainty generated by the situation in Argentina has not had large influence over the Colombian currency market, judging by the relative stability of the exchange rate," the bank said. 

 But the economy has been hit by the world economic slowdown. The the government slashed it growth forecasts for 2001 and 2002 in late July, pegging growth at this year at 2.4 percent - down from it previous estimate of 3.8 percent. 

 The government revised its 2002 growth forecast to 4.0 percent from 4.0 percent previously. 

 "New indicators like industrial production show a deterioration in productive activity in June. Additionally, demand for money has been below reference lines, and there is room to increase (the supply)," the bank said. 

 With Thursday's rate cut, the third of the year, the Central Bank has reduced money market intervention rates by 200 basis points in 2001.

title: Colombia cuts rates 100 bps, shrugs off Argentina.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank slashed its money market intervention rates on Thursday by a higher-than-expected 100 basis points, shrugging off worries over Argentina that have forced neighbors to hike rates. 

 The Central Bank said in a statement it decided on the rate cut after new data, including industrial production data, showed a "deterioration" in economic activity in June. 

 Local economists had forecast a rate cut of between 20 and 50 basis points. With Thursday's rate cut, the third of the year, the Central Bank has reduced money market intervention rates by 200 basis points in 2001. 

 The bank said the rate cut was "compatible" with Colombia's IMF-agreed inflation target of 8 percent in 2001 and 6 percent in 2002. 

 It added Colombia's peso was "relatively stable" despite fears of an Argentine debt default that have eroded currencies such as Brazil and Chile.

title: Colombia peso bounces back as Argentina fears ease.
text:

title: UPDATE 1-Colombia holds rates steady on Argentina worries.
text:
BOGOTA, Colombia, July 13 (Reuters) - Colombia's Central Bank held its money market intervention rates steady on Friday to guard against fallout from economic troubles in Argentina, Finance Minister Juan Manuel Santos said. 

 "In the meeting (of Central Bank directors) we were going to lower rates, but given the situation in Argentina we decided not to lower them," Santos told reporters as he exited the meeting. 

 Fears that Argentina could default on its mountain of debt have rattled markets across the world, battering Latin American currencies, as investors fretted over a potential 1998-style emerging market meltdown. 

 Colombia's Central Bank has not lowered rates since March 12 - when it cut all money market intervention rates by 50 basis points. Analysts had said a rate cut would have helped spur growth in Latin America's fifth largest economy. 

 But Santos said that the decision against a rate cut was only a precaution and added that Colombia was well prepared to withstand a ripple-effect from Argentina's economic woes. 

 "Fortunately, the situation (in Argentina) has not affected us, due to the reforms we have implemented and our policy of prefinancing," he said. 

 Colombia has foreign reserves of $9.37 billion and has already secured enough financing to meet its debt payments through the beginning of next year. 

 The government issued a flurry of debt earlier in 2001, including $1 billion of World Bank-backed bonds, a series of smaller euro-denominated issues, and 30 billion yen in four-year "Samurai" bonds in April. 

 ARGENTINA ALSO SLOWS BOND SWAP 

 Colombia has also secured U.S. regulatory approval to issue $2.5 billion of fresh U.S. dollar-denominated debt in a swap for existing U.S. dollar bonds. But Santos said the government would monitor market sentiment, especially with regards to Argentina, before forging ahead with the foreign bond swap. 

 "We don't have any urgency for the swap," Santos told Reuters on Thursday. "We have said many times the swap could be tomorrow, or in a month, or in a year. We will decide this at the moment we see it as convenient." 

 Argentina, Latin America's third-largest economy, is struggling amid a recessionary climate to service its debt - which equals about half of its gross domestic product. 

 The country has received debt rating downgrades from three agencies in as many days, with Moody's Investors Service on Friday cutting Argentina's foreign currency country ceiling rating to B3 from B2, and lowering the foreign currency bank deposit ceiling to Caa1 to B3. It said the risk of default was high and President Fernando de la Rua's proposed spending cuts would only further weaken the economy. 

 Colombia, which has never defaulted on its debt, has considerably higher credit ratings than Argentina. Moody's rates Colombia's foreign currency country ceiling at Ba2, while its foreign currency bank deposit ceiling ranking is Ba3.

title: Colombia's cenbank to boost foreign reserves.
text:
BOGOTA, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank announced plans Friday to intervene sporadically in the local foreign exchange market to boost its net foreign reserves and smooth out any abrupt changes in the peso/dollar exchange rate. 

 The bank's net foreign reserves stood at just under $8 billion as of Nov. 10, the last date for which official figures are available, compared to more than $9 billion in March. 

 Rebuilding the reserve position was one of the commitments Colombia made under a recent loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund, the central bank said in a statement. 

 To accumulate reserves, it said it would auction off special drawing rights, under which banks and other financial intermediaries would be entitled to sell the central bank $200 million in December and a total of $960 million next year. The central bank said it would only buy the U.S. currency a month after each auction, however, and at an exchange rate below the market average over the previous 20 trading sessions. 

 Additionally, the central bank said it would hold special auctions giving market players the option to sell or buy dollars from its coffers, whenever the peso traded 5 percent above or below its average trading level against the dollar over the previous 20 trading sessions. 

 The central bank eliminated its closely managed currency regime on Sept. 25, allowing the peso to float freely against other currencies. But Friday's measures will give it more leeway - aside from undeclared forex interventions through its financial intermediaries - to limit any exchange rate volatility going forward. 

 The peso closed at 1,928 to the dollar Friday, well up from its low of 2,017 on Sept. 27. That was the first day of trading after the central bank scrapped the trading band under which the currency had moved against set limits against the dollar since 1994.

title: Colombia's New Floating Peso Regime: Dirty Or Clean?
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Colombia on Monday launched its new free-floating currency regime with a promise to let market forces set the peso's value, but analysts doubt its central bank will take a completely hands-off approach. 

 Traders and analysts said Colombia's central bank has still not clarified just how "clean" or "dirty" the exchange system will be, but early signs are that there will be a fair amount of intervention. 

 "In principle, they've said the market will be clean, but I think they're going to continue with dirty interventions when they deem it necessary," predicted Juan Fernando Reseo, foreign exchange manager with Banco Sudameris in Colombia. 

 In a "clean" floating system, the value of the currency is determined solely by market forces, while in a "dirty" system the central bank uses various mechanisms to influence the currency's value at given times, but not to keep it at a preset range or value against the dollar. 

 Colombia's central bank announced Saturday that it had scrapped its five-year-old crawling currency trading band, which had obliged the bank to buy or sell dollars if needed to keep the peso within a preset range against the dollar. 


In the week before the decision to scrap the band, the central bank
had been forced to spend $401 million of its reserves to defend the
peso.
     Central Bank Says Peso To Be Set By Market



"From today on, the peso-dollar exchange rate will be determined by
the market," central bank Governor Miguel Urrutia said in a Saturday
night news conference to announce the elimination of the band.



But he added that the bank "will intervene if there are temporary or
seasonal situations of excess supply or demand in the foreign exchange
market."



The central bank then said it would auction $100 million in
dollar-denominated TES bonds on Tuesday to boost the peso during the
system's startup.



The auction of the bonds will reduce demand for dollars and represents
an attempt by the bank to head off a possible initial plunge in the
peso, according to analysts.



It is not the only tool the bank has taken to head off a peso
devaluation under the free-float system.



The central bank two weeks ago cut the maximum size of banks' dollar
spot holdings to 20% from 50% as a proportion of technical assets in a
move to block speculation against the peso.



"This measure is still in place. It means financial institutions do
not have the same capacity to buy dollars as before and it limits their
ability to put pressure on the dollar," said Erica Montanez, currency
analyst at Colombian brokerage Corredores Asociados.



"I also think the central bank will continue to sell dollars from its
reserves at given moments. Some of my sources told me the bank could
have even been selling dollars surreptitiously" Monday to support the
peso, she said.



A spokeswoman at the central bank would not confirm whether the bank
had sold any dollars.



The spokeswoman also said the degree of intervention the bank will
take in the market has still not been decided.
   How Bank Will Influence Market Still Not Clear



This lack of definition of Colombia's peso policy worries some
bankers.



"There remain many unanswered questions about what forms of
intervention in the foreign exchange market the central bank will
adopt," Armando Montenegro, President of Colombia's National Association
of Financial Institutions, wrote in a briefing.



Montenegro said it was urgent that the central bank define what
intervention measures it will take and that these measures be
"competitive, general and transparent."



A complete free-float in a small market like Colombia could generate
instability, which is why most floats in Latin America are "dirty,"
Montenegro wrote.



He cited Peru and Brazil as floating regimes with widespread "dirty"
intervention by the central banks. In Brazil's case, he said the bank
has influenced the currency through the sale of dollar-denominated
bonds, similar to Colombia's TES bonds.
     Peso Survives First Day Under New Regime



The peso closed 1.1% weaker against the dollar in Monday's trading,
easing fears of a large devaluation on the first day of the new currency
regime.



Some analysts have predicted an initial downward overshoot of the peso
against the dollar, followed by a gradual recovery since the currency is
not overvalued.



The peso had lost about 30% of its value over the past 12 months.



"Fortunately, the market was calm. This shows that there was no reason
for an overreaction or macrodevaluation. This is a favorable piece of
news and shows that the decision was made at the correct moment,"
Finance Minister Juan Camilo Restrepo told reporters Monday in
Washington, where he was meeting with officials from the Inernational
Monetary Fund.



Restrepo wouldn't comment on whether the central bank will set aside
funds to intervene in the exchange market.


Colombia was one of the few remaining countries with currency trading
bands. Chile had been the most recent Latin American country to scrap
its band, following in the footsteps of Brazil and Ecuador earlier this
year.

title: FOCUS- Colombia  peso slides despite  intervention .
text:
BOGOTA, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Traders in Colombia's currency markets wondered aloud on Thursday just how long the country's fragile exchange-rate trading band could survive as the Central Bank added up the cost of one of its most expensive bids ever to defend the peso. 

 Even as the bank burned $142.4 million in precious foreign reserves during the day, the peso crashed to the floor of its daily exchange band for the third consecutive session to close at 1,993.97 against the dollar. Since Sept. 10, the bank has spent an estimated $290 million from net foreign reserves of some $8.24 billion to shore up the currency. 

 "We're holding a minute's silence for the trading band," said Juan Carlos Gonzalez, head of research for Bogota-based brokerage Corredores Asociados. 

 A slew of unfavourable economic news sent industry as well as commercial banks rushing for greenbacks. Just this week, New York-based Standard & Poor's stripped Colombia of its prized investment-grade credit rating and the government released worse-than-expected growth figures, showing the economy contracted more than 6 percent in the first half. 

 Gonzalez did not say when he expected the "funeral" of the so-called crawling-peg regime, introduced in 1994. Under the system, the central bank sets daily upper and lower fluctuation limits for the peso in a bid to control the rate of its depreciation. 

 But most Colombian dealers and independent analysts believe it could be just a matter of days before the bank is forced to scrap the system, one of three of its kind surviving in Latin America. 

 They are convinced the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will insist that Colombia agree to end foreign exchange controls as part of a deal for a potential $3 billion extended fund facility. A final accord is expected within days, IMF chief Michel Camdessus said Thursday. 

 One of Gonzalez's colleagues at Corredores Asociados estimated that the central bank would only be able to afford intervening at the current rate for two more days. 

 "Of course, the central bank is going to say until the last minute that it's not going to scrap the band. It depends how stubborn the bank is. But if it continues selling at this level I think the band can only survive two more days," economic researcher Erika Montanez said. 

 The bank on Wednesday spent $70 million in a total volume of $97.1 million, and went on to plough in $142.4 million more on Thursday - 93 percent of the day's total trade of $149.9 million. The bank conceded it was one of its heaviest interventions ever. 

 The central bank has twice modified the exchange rate band in the last year. In the three days before the de facto peso devaluation last September, it sold about $217 million in currency markets. In the two days before the June 27 devaluation, it sold about $284 million. 

 In contrast with local analysts, Wall Street believed Colombia's trading band would not necessarily be scrapped any time soon. 

 A group of Wall Street analysts consulted by Reuters said they expected the central bank to continue defending the peso until at least the announcement of a final deal with the IMF. 

 Still, U.S. and Colombian analysts appeared to concur that the peso could drop as low as 2,200 or even 2,300 if the band is eliminated. 

 But any decline seems likely to be short term, they say, with few suggesting the peso is fundamentally overvalued. Most believe the currency is likely to return to around current levels in the mid-term. 

 Adding to pressure on Colombia's peso is the sense that trading bands have passed their prime in Latin America. Chile allowed its peso to float freely early this month, following similar moves earlier in the year by Brazil and Ecuador. 

 Colombia, like many other emerging markets, saw a currency control regime in 1994 as a way of controlling the rate of depreciation against the dollar and providing exporters with predictable exchange rates. It was also seen as a mechanism to control inflation, which averaged well above 20 percent in 1994. Inflation has now slowed and seems likely to end 1999 at around 12 percent. 

 In contrast with many of his counterparts in Colombia, Juan Jose Echavarria, head of independent economic think-tank Fedesarrollo, argued against any swift end to the peso trading band. 

 "Now is not the time to do it. It would be tantamount to rewarding all those who were betting on the casino economy," he said. "These markets have been like a betting casino with both sides seeing how much money the other has."

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Polish cbank rattles markets.
text:
LONDON, June 28 (Reuters) - Emerging market currency traders all but ignored Colombia's de facto peso devaluation over the weekend, but intervention by the Polish central bank rattled the markets, traders said. 

 The Polish central bank intervened for the first time in a year and then issued a statement saying its activities were aimed at smoothing out volatility. 

 "It was a bit of an odd thing to say. There was very little volatility and their timing was a bit out," said one trader. 

 The central bank bought euros at 4.0780 to the zloty and then sold euros at 4.0790. 

 The zloty was trading at 4.0813 bid to the euro by 1005 GMT. 

 The Polish central bank said its action was not aimed at setting a target for the zloty. 

 "This should not be called an intervention, these are normal activities of buying and selling on the forex market which are not aimed at influencing the present exchange rate level whatsoever," Monetary Policy Council member Boguslaw Grabowski said. 

 In a knock on effect, the Czech crown - which has been appreciating rapidly - weakened somewhat to 36.83 to the euro, before bouncing back to trade at 36.90. It was trading at 36.883 bid by 1055 GMT. 

 "The crown reacted on the back of that and the Czech National Bank does not want to see a stronger crown," said the trader. 

 However, the effects of central bank intervention were hard to gauge, he said. 

 "The market might be a little nervous of long zloty, stemming the buy-zloty-regardless tendency," he said.

title: Colombia  peso extends losses, despite  intervention .
text:
BOGOTA, June 25 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso continued its downward slide Friday, as the market shrugged off massive efforts by the central bank to lend the currency support. 

 The central bank reported, moments after the market closed, that it sold $174.4 million from its reserves in a bid to lift the peso off the lower or weak end of its daily floating rate exchange band. But the embattled currency, which opened at the "floor" of the band, remained stuck there all day and closed at a new all-time low of 1,737.72. 

 Dealers said the central bank's intervention in the local foreign exchange market was believed to be its biggest ever. And it followed the bank's sale of $110.4 million from its reserves Thursday, in the first major intervention since September of last year. 

 But the thinly-traded market, which handled just 93 transactions for a total of $193.6 million - including the central bank's dollar sales - failed to react to the seemingly futile effort to defend the peso from speculative attacks by banks and other financial intermediaries. 

 At least two transactions were carried out below the weak end of the trading band, including one shortly before the close in which someone purchased about $3 million at an exchange rate of 1,741.50 pesos to the dollar, dealers said. 

 "Demand (for dollars) was even more intense than yesterday," said one trader, who added that the market was clearly betting on an imminent change in Colombia's foreign exchange policy and a possible elimination of its crawling peg currency regime. 

 The peso lost just 58 centavos on the day but it slumped by more than 2.7 percent against the dollar this week and by more than 13.1 percent so far this year.

title: Colombia  peso ends at new low despite  intervention .

The central bank said it sold $110.4 million from its reserves in a bid to lift the peso off the weak end of its daily floating rate exchange band, which was set for the day at 1,737.14.


 But the peso, which slumped to the 1,737.14 level in midday trade after testing a session high of 1,730, stayed stuck there throughout the rest of the trading session amid strong demand for dollars from banks and the corporate sector, dealers said. 

 The central bank's dollar sales, as it intervened openly in the local forex market, were the largest since Sept. 1 of last year, a day before the bank was forced to modify the exchange band in a de facto devaluation. 

 Dealers reported 106 transactions in Thursday's trade for a total of $141.6 million, including the $110.4 million from the central bank's reserves.

title: Colombia cenbank says will limit  forex  volatility.
text:
BOGOTA, April 9 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank said Friday that it will intervene in the local foreign exchange market as often as necessary to limit volatility in trading of the country's peso currency. 

 In a statement issued after the central bank's regular weekly policy meeting, its seven-member board said the peso would continue trading within the parameters of the exchange rate band set for it in September of last year, effectively ruling out any change in foreign exchange policy. 

 The peso fell to a three-month low Thursday, on recent statements by government officials, including President Andres Pastrana, who said its recent appreciation against the dollar was "unacceptable" because it was hurting the beleaguered export sector. 

 But the central bank, which was widely reported to have sold dollars Thursday to curb the local currency's fall, said its board members had reiterated their "confidence" in the peso's current trading band and would keep the peso firmly within its limits. 

 "As it has done for several years, the Bank of the Republic (central bank) will continue intervening within the band, buying or selling foreign currency, to avoid extreme volatility in the exchange rate," the bank statement said. 

 The peso, which slumped to a record low of 1,605 against the dollar in early trading Friday, had firmed in late trade to 1,580, up eight pesos from Thursday's close at 1,586.

title: Colombia  cenbank  intervened  in  forex  mkt Thurs,Fri.
text:
BOGOTA, March 23 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank said Tuesday it had intervened in foreign exchange markets last Thursday and Friday to prevent the peso currency from rising amid recent wafer-thin volume. 

 Salomon Kalmanovitz, central bank co-director, said in La Republica newspaper the bank was responsible for about half the turnover in last Thursday's session and for about one-third Friday - which would amount to about $30 million. 

 Volume in Colombia's foreign exchange market has been extremely thin lately in the wake of a controversial hike in a financial transactions tax. The paucity of trade has exagerrated even slight movements in the currency. 

 Foreign currency dealers consulted said the bank had purchased dollars on those days to maintain its depreciation rate on the peso. Colombia weakens its currency - this year the target is for a 17.1 percent depreciation - to offset the impact of huge dollar inflows on the peso. 

 The currency is allowed to trade within very wide bands set daily by the central bank. In last week's trade, the peso was nowhere near the outer limits of the band, and the bank appeared to be defending the middle of the range, traders said. 

 On Friday, for instance, the peso closed at 1,548 to the dollar, while the daily band was a billowing 1,461 to 1,681. 

 Kalmanovitz said the central bank had not intervened directly, but had carried out transactions through commercial banks. 

 "The (central) bank has had to intervene all too frequently because there is high exchange rate volatility. We made up half the volume in Thursday's trade and more than one-third Friday," Kalmanovitz said. 

 Overall volume in Colombia's currency has been low for more than two weeks since the Constitutional Court increased an emergency levy on financial transactions. 

 A preferential 0.00012 percent levy had been applied to interbank deals since last November, but the court ruling upped that rate to bring it into line with the 0.002 percent levy on all general bank transactions. 

 The peso opened Tuesday at 1,547 against the dollar, up 1.7 pesos compared to Friday's close. The market was closed Monday in observance of St. Joseph's Day.

title: Colombia peso ends weaker but well off lows.
text:

 The currency - which has remained under pressure ever since its de facto devaluation last month - tumbled 11.73 pesos against the dollar Monday to close at a new record low of 1,591.23. 

 The session marked the first time the currency dropped to the lower limit of its exchange rate band since the band was raised by 9 percentage points on September 2. 

 The central bank said it sold the $4.5 million from its reserves when the peso dropped to an intraday low of 1,591.24, the lower end of its exchange rate or intervention band. 

 But traders on the interbank or foreign exchange market said the central bank was actually seen selling dollars all day, through financial intermediaries. 

 The $4.5 million was just the small part of the bank's dollar sales that it did in its own name, the traders said.

title: Colombian Peso Closes Weaker; Central Bk  Intervenes  Again
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Two days after Colombia's central bank raised eyebrows across Latin America with an unexpected devaluation, the peso continued losing ground against the dollar Thursday, traders said. 

 The weakening came even as the bank sold millions of dollars as a support mechanism, they added. 

 The peso's average exchange rate rose to 1531.82 to the dollar from 1523.48 Wednesday, marking a depreciation. However, the peso's drop was small compared with a 5% depreciation seen the previous day, just hours after the bank announced it was shifting its preset trading band nine percentage points higher. 

 "The bank has lost a lot of credibility, and now they still have to sell the same reserves (to defend the peso)," said one trader who was disappointed with the bank's decision. 

 Asked if the peso might hit the ceiling of the new band in coming weeks he said, "For me there is no ceiling. They demonstrated to me that the band can be broken." 

 Bank board members summoned to speak before a congressional committee Thursday said the de facto devaluation had passed by a 4-3 vote, and co-director Salomon Kalmanovitz said he was one of those voting against the measure. 

 The decision came on the back of three consecutive days in which the peso's exchange rate stuck to the weak side of the band, prompting the bank to sell some $200 million as a support mechanism. 

 However, traders said the bank had to sell another $100 million on Wednesday to prevent the peso from surging towards the weak side of the new band, and some estimated the bank sold at least that amount again on Thursday. 

 Total foreign exchange volume came in at $270 million, slightly above normal levels, as banks and private companies stocked up on dollars to protect themselves from any further volatility in the future. 


The peso has fallen about 18% against the dollar so far this year.

title: Colombia 's Restrepo -3: Echos Remarks Made Friday
text:
Friday's intervention marked the third time this year the peso has required defensive measures. The last round of pressure came ahead of June's final round of presidential elections, at which time the bank chose to limit liquidity rather than pump dollars into the market. 

 That decision soon translated into a currency crunch, that in turn brought on skyrocketing interest rates. Restrepo said Monday that he hoped the current crisis could be controlled without reverting to rate hikes. 

 "Until now, Colombia has been able to maintain a monetary policy without being startled, despite the international crisis. And we haven't had to turn to the lofty interest rates of 70% or 80% that prevailed two months ago in a similar situation," he said, speaking to reporters at the Presidential Palace. Restrepo was designated to oversee domestic affairs while President Andres Pastrana completes official visits to Brazil and South Africa. 

 "We hope this new wave, that has arrived not just in Colombia, but in all the emerging countries, (we hope) we can get around it without turning again to these extravagant interest rates, that had such an effect on production and employment," Restrepo added. 

 Restrepo's remarks echoed Friday comments by Central Bank Co-director Salamon Kalmanovitz, who said Colombia would not make any decisions regarding a possible devaluation during the current global shakedown.

title: Colombia central bank intervenes  to support peso.
text:
BOGOTA, May 26 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank said it sold $82.5 million on the local foreign exchange market Tuesday in an effort to shore up the country's peso currency. 

 The bank generally refrains from commenting on its forays into the foreign exchange or interbank market. But it revealed the amount of Tuesday's intervention on its Internet page on the World Wide Web.

 The peso closed at a new historic low of 1,351.16 Monday -- on the floor of the daily exchange rate band. 

 Interbank traders said the peso has become the target of speculative attacks and that Colombian importers are snapping up greenbacks to make early payments to foreign creditors while exporters are withholding earnings in the expectation of further rises in the dollar rate. 

 In comments Monday, one trader, who did not wish to be named said he did not expect any recovery in the peso as a response to the repo rates rise until "next week at the earliest". He added that at best the peso would only gain "a maximum 10 pesos" against the dollar. 

 The peso interbank rate has lost 4.45 percent in the year so far compared to the close of 1997. The central bank has forecast a 13 percent nominal devaluation in the peso this year. 

 According to the National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF), the central bank spent $130 million propping up the peso last Thursday and Friday. 

 In the year so far, ANIF says reserves have fallen $388 million, largely as a result of central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

Colombia's net reserves stood at $9.7 billion at the close of January, the last date for which official figures are available, the central bank said.

 The volume of the foreign exchange market was $118 million in 317 separate transactions, about average by the standards of recent weeks, a trader said. 

 The central bank issued a statement on Friday in which it acknowledged buying a total of $78 million recently to slow the peso's recent upvaluation. 

 It also stated that it would buy more dollars as it considered necessary in the coming weeks to slow the peso's recent strengthening. The peso has gained about 4% on the dollar since July, boosted by exports and a weak demand for the dollar. 

 A trader at a major Colombian bank said the central bank's announcement prompted the peso to slide when the market first opened, but that it began to regain some of its lost ground when coffee exporters and investors in the petroleum sector sold dollars for pesos. 


The peso has fallen about 3.1% against the dollar so far this year.

title: Colombian government seeks to weaken buoyant peso.
text:
BOGOTA, Aug 13 (Reuter) - Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said the government was studying a number of measures aimed at weakening Colombia's buoyant peso currency to help make the country's exports more competitive abroad. 

 "It's not a matter of triggering an excessive devaluation, but we don't want an execessive appreciation either," Ocampo told reporters. 

 "Stopping the appreciation is a priority," he added. 

 The peso, which was trading at 1,070 in late June, has risen steadily in recent weeks as a flood of dollars from foreign oil sales entered the country. 

 Dealers on the country's interbank market have also attributed the rise of the peso, which closed at a six-month high of 1,030.20 Monday, to dollar sales by banks and a drop in demand for U.S. currency by the corporate sector. 

 Ocampo did not spell out what measures the government might take to halt the peso's meteoric rise. 

 But he said it had urged Colombia's central bank to intervene in the interbank market by buying dollars and undercutting the peso. 

 President Ernesto Samper urged the bank in a speech last week to push down its floating exchange rate band in a bid to weaken the peso and shore up the export sector. 

 But the bank, which likes a strong peso as a shield against inflation, has insisted that the exchange rate band will not be altered. It currently stands at 957.64 to 1,101.81 pesos to the dollar. 

 The band is set daily according to a slated pace of depreciation and the peso is currently in the middle of the band. Dealers see no problem in maintaining the current band. 

 The government had forecast a 13.6 percent devaluation of the peso this year. But the currency has lost only 5.3 percent of its value against the dollar so far.

title: Colombia's foreign reserves fall to $7.91 billion.

title: Colombian  central bank  plays down peso weakness.
text:
BOGOTA, April 18 (Reuter) - Central bank director Miguel Urrutia played down the recent weakness of Colombia's peso, saying the bank had only spent about $300 million so far this year in market interventions to prop up the currency. 

 "Given (central bank) reserves of about $8 billion, this is something we consider reasonable," Urrutia said of the Banco de la Republica's dollar sales in the local foreign exchange market. 

 "It's a limited intervention," he added in remarks to the Finance Committee of the House of Representatives. 

 The peso, under pressure from political uncertainty, has slipped 6.72 percent against the dollar so far this year. 

 The official devaluation target for the entire year is 13.5 percent and Urrutia said the central bank has no intention of altering the daily exchange rate band the peso is allowed to trade within. 

 "It's important that there be some assurance that the exchange rate is under control," he said. 

 He added that the central bank has refrained from intervening in Colombia's interbank foreign exchange market for the last three weeks.

title: Colombian peso ends down on U.S. drug report.
text:
BOGOTA, March 1 (Reuter) - Colombia's peso ended down 55 centavos at 1,049.90 to the dollar -- on the floor of the central bank's official exchange rate band, interbank traders said. 

 It was the 10th consecutive session in which the peso closed lower on spiraling political uncertainty in Colombia. 

 Traders noted that the market closed minutes before it was announced in Washington that the United States was dropping Colombia from a list of favored nations that cooperate in the international anti-drug fight. 

 But several said the move had already been discounted. 

 The central bank intervened in the market in early trade, selling up to $2 million to stabilize the peso, traders said. But they said it was generally firmer than in previous sessions this week when the central bank sold tens of millions of dollars to prop up the battered currency. 

 Though the peso could come under a new speculative assault next week, traders and market analysts say Colombia has ample reserves to intervene and inject stability into the market.

title: Colombia  Peso Slides As  Central Bank Intervenes  In  Forex
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--The Colombian central bank spent an estimated $90 million defending the peso Wednesday as foreign exchange traders remained cautious in the days before the U.S. government announces its assessment of Colombia's antinarcotics efforts. 

 The dollar's weighted exchange rate rose to 1,039.82 pesos from 1,039.23 pesos on Tuesday, with intraday trading fluctuating between 1,039.7 pesos and 1,039.85 pesos. 

 While the central bank set a floor of 1,039.82 for Wednesday's session, a trader said it allowed a few isolated exchanges to occur at 1,039.85. 

 One foreign exchange trader said the foreign exchange market remains shaken by the U.S. government's upcoming evaluation of Colombia's antinarcotics efforts. 

 U.S. President Bill Clinton has until Friday to recommend an assessment of Colombia's cooperation against illegal narcotics. A poor assessment could cost Colombia millions of dollars in direct foreign assistance, higher tariffs, and international loans. 

 "Almost no one wants to bring dollars into the country," one foreign exchange trader said. 

 The Colombian government put additional pressure on the peso Wednesday by buying dollars to pay foreign debts, the trader said. -Keefe Borden

title: Trading In  Colombia  Peso Back To Normal After  Intervention
text:
BOGOTA (Dow Jones)--Trading in the Colombian peso has returned to normal after a week of uncertainty that forced the central bank to intervene almost daily in the foreign exchange market to support the currency in late January, traders said. 

 The peso has gradually gained on the dollar since its low of 1,028.14 on Jan. 31. The peso closed at 1,024.17 on Friday. The central bank was forced to defend the peso through the end of of January, but hasn't had to intervene in the foreign exchange market since then. 

 Fernando Botero, President Ernesto Samper's former campaign director and defense minister, sparked a political scandal when he announced on Jan. 22 that the president was aware of millions of dollars in campaign contributions from drug traffickers. 

 The allegations caused a temporary run on the peso, although ING-Barings Analyst Rue Swabey noted that the central bank's level of interventions were minimal. 

 The central bank allows free market forces to determine the exchange rate within a pre-established boundaries, known as the "exchange band," which allows the peso to fall asmuch as 13.4% against the dollar in 1996. 

 The central bank sells dollars on the foreign exchange market whenever the peso hits the minimum value of the exchange band.

title: Colombia  Political Scandal Forces Daily Peso  Intervention
text:

 Fernando Botero, President Ernesto Samper's former campaign director and defense minister, last week worsened an ongoing political scandal with the explosive confirmation of allegations he'd previously denied linking the president to drug traffickers. title: Colombia peso ends down at 1,001.55.
text:
BOGOTA, Nov 24 (Reuter) - Colombia's peso slipped 1.25 against the dollar in subdued interbank trading to end the week at 1,001.55, dealers said. 

 They said exporters changing U.S. dollar earnings into pesos boosted the currency to an intraday high of 999.30 early in the session -- back above the 1,000-to-one psychological barrier broken last week. But dollar buying by banks pushed it steadily lower ahead of the close. 

 Most dealers and economic analysts expect the peso, which has already lost more than 20 pct this year, to continue losing ground until Colombia's political crisis has been resolved. 

 The crisis, and prevailing uncertainty in Colombia, stems from an investigation into charges that President Samper's 1994 election campaign was partly financed by drug lords. 

Colombia's central bank has intervened in the interbank market repeatedly in recent weeks to keep the peso within its 15- pct trading band. The crawling peg devaluation benefitted exporters, however, and helped fuel stronger-than-expected economic growth in the third quarter. 

 Dealers reported 317 operations Friday for a total of $124.2 million.

title: Colombian peso posts gains against dollar.
text:
BOGOTA, Aug 28 (Reuter) - Colombia's peso, battered over the past week by the country's deepening political crisis, strengthened against the dollar on Monday after the central bank intervened repeatedly to shore it up. 

 Finance Minister Guillermo Perry, meanwhile, said the government was studying measures to increase the supply of greenbacks in Colombia and vowed the current exchange band would remain in place. 

 "The phenomenon that we're seeing is purely a product of speculation," Perry told reporters, referring to the peso's recent drop against the dollar. 

 The peso's fall, triggered at least in part by political uncertainty stemming from allegations of drug-related contributions to President Ernesto Samper's 1994 campaign, has put a drain on Colombia's foreign reserves as the central bank intervened to stop it. 

 "The central bank intervened all morning," one dealer said of Monday's session, which ended with the dollar down 3.01 pesos on the interbank market at 970.50, off its intraday low of 974. The dealer said the central bank stopped selling dollars before midday, but the market "tended to stabilize" quickly after the bank's selling spree. 

 In his remarks to reporters, Perry did not specify the measures the government might take to increase the supply of dollars in Colombia. 

 But economic analysts say that, in addition to political uncertainty, and the resulting flight to quality into U.S. currency, the flow of dollars into Colombia has ebbed as a result of the recent crackdown on the Cali drug cartel and the arrests of all, but one of its top leaders. 

 Prior to the crackdown, the cartel controlled most of the cocaine smuggled into the United States and was a major source of foreign exchange. 

 -- Tom Brown, Bogota newsroom, 571 610 7944

title: Political Crisis Sparks Renewed Slide Of Colombian Peso

title: Colombia  peso closes weaker on bank  intervention .

BOGOTA, Jan 20 (Reuter) - The peso weakened 0.6 to end at 854.70 to the dollar after the Central Bank intervened to buy dollars when it appeared that the peso was regaining strength. 

 The peso has fallen rapidly in the past few days on importer demand and speculative selling, but traders said the dollar rally ran out of steam Friday amid sentiment it had risen too fast. 

 "The Central Bank intervened and bought (dollars) when the U.S. currency was falling to 853 pesos. We don't know why the Bank was in such a hurry to intervene," one trader said.
